nodes.title: account
nodes.summary: The login accounts a file authenticates, each bound to a privilege set
notes: ADDRESSING: by name and id -- Draco::DBUserAccountCatalog mixes in M_DBNameList (DBEngine/DBUserAccount.h:308). The wire `name` is the human-readable account name (GetUserAccountName(), DBUserAccount.h:255), not the inherited, non-human-readable GetName().
CUSTOM ORDER IS NOT EXPOSED, for the same reason `privilegeSet` does not expose it: DBUserAccountCatalog also mixes in M_DBCustomList (DBUserAccount.h:308), and nothing here reports or accepts it.

COMMIT DOMAIN: file-user, via DBFileUser::GetUserAccountCatalog() (DBFileUser.h:882) -- schema_->Commit() never reaches it, and a write goes through openForWrite() like every other file-user catalog here.

THE SEEDED GUEST ACCOUNT is listed and can be read, but update and delete both refuse it outright -- identified by its well-known member key (DBUserAccount::KGuestAccount(), DBUserAccount.h:195), never by its private-use-codepoint name.

SECURITY: binding an account to [Full Access] is the escalation vector this catalog exists to guard against. `privilegeSet` is resolved to its MEMBER KEY and refused if it is [Full Access]'s -- on both create and update -- because a display name is localized and a name-based check would be bypassable by opening a localized copy of the file. EVERY VERB on this catalog, including read, additionally requires the calling session itself to hold [Full Access].

SECRETS: an account holds password material. `hasPassword` is the only signal this catalog ever reports about it -- a boolean, never a hash, a token or the password itself, following the `authorization` catalog's own precedent.
seeAlso: privilegeSet

nodes.title: create:account
nodes.summary: Creates a login account bound to a privilege set

keys.summary: the account name a user logs in with, or the group name for a group userType, unique within the file
the privilege set to bind this account to, by name -- REFUSED if it names [Full Access]
free text stored beside the account, defaulting to empty
whether the account can log in; defaults to true
the FileMaker-native password; required for the native userType and refused for any other
the kind of account; defaults to the native FileMaker kind
force a new password to be chosen at the first login; native accounts only

semanticChecks: 'privilegeSet' is REFUSED when it resolves to [Full Access], on both create and update. This is the primary escalation vector the account catalog exists to close: binding an account to [Full Access] would give it every privilege in the file. Resolved by the privilege set's MEMBER KEY, never by its (localized) display name, so a rename cannot be used to defeat the check.

'password' is REQUIRED for a FileMaker-native account (the default 'userType') and REFUSED for every other kind. The engine itself refuses to commit a native account with no password data at all, and an external-server or OAuth account has no FileMaker password to set -- the engine stores its own placeholder for those at commit time.
'forceExpire' applies to a FileMaker-native account and is REFUSED for every other kind: it forces a new FILEMAKER password to be chosen, and no other kind of account has one.
notes: A [Full Access] SESSION IS REQUIRED to run this op at all, independent of the ordinary schema-modification lock every op needs.
`privilegeSet` is REQUIRED: an account with no binding is not a usable one, and there is no implicit default. An unknown name is `privilegeSet_not_found` with suggestions.

AN OAUTH `userType` AUTHORS THE ACCOUNT BUT CANNOT MAKE IT SIGN IN. The account is real, exportable and correctly typed in the file, but the provider it names is configured on the HOST, not in the file, so nobody can log in with it until the host is set up for that provider. Nothing in the file records whether that has been done, so this op cannot warn about it.

`userType` NAMES NINE OF THE FIFTEEN KINDS an account can be. Claris ID accounts are absent because their name is a compound of team and entity identifiers this op has no keys for; ADFS accounts are absent because FileMaker's own file format has no name for them.
`result` is the ref `{name,id,builtIn}`; `builtIn` is always false for an account this op just created.
seeAlso: `fm-cli help forms` — what JSON a key's type, its requiredness and a filter's tag each take

nodes.title: read:account
nodes.summary: Lists every account, narrowed by an optional filter, or describes one by name or id
semanticChecks: a `filter` naming no attribute is refused: it would narrow nothing, and answering it with the whole listing is indistinguishable from a filter that matched every account
notes: A [Full Access] SESSION IS REQUIRED to run this op at all -- read included. This catalog reports account existence, binding and enablement, which is itself sensitive configuration.
NOTHING HERE CAN EVER BE PASSWORD MATERIAL. `hasPassword` is a boolean; there is no key that reports a hash, a token or the password itself, on any account.

`filter` NARROWS a listing and does nothing else. Every account that comes back is reported in exactly the shape an unfiltered listing gives it, so a filter changes which accounts appear and never what any one of them says.

`privilegeSet`, `enabled` and `hasPassword` need `detail`:true: a shallow listing carries only `name`, `id` and `builtIn`, so a filter on any of the other three is refused rather than silently matching nothing.
An unknown `name` is `not_found` with closest-name suggestions; an unknown `id` is `not_found` with none.
A read never opens the account catalog for writing, so `read:account` cannot dirty the file.

nodes.title: authorization
nodes.summary: This file's half of each protected-file pairing -- FileMaker's Manage > Security > File Access
notes: ITS MEMBERS HAVE NO NAMES. There is no name list at all, so a member is addressed by the catalog's own {uuid, type} identity pair or by its `id`. This and `relation` are the two stated exceptions to "names in, IDs out", and `name` is refused rather than answered not_found.

ONE UUID, UP TO TWO MEMBERS. A pairing's two halves share the file uuid they are keyed to, so the same uuid appears once as `inbound` and once as `outbound`. That is why `type` is half the address rather than a way to select, and why selecting on it is spelled as a listing's `filter` instead.

NO VERB HERE EVER EMITS A HASH OR A TOKEN -- not in a field, not in an error message. An outbound entry's token IS the credential that opens the protected file and an inbound entry's SHA-256 is what the far side's token is checked against; what this CLI reports has only presence flags and no field a secret could be written into, so the property holds by construction.

A freshly created .fmp12 ALREADY HAS TWO authorizations: FileMaker self-authorizes at creation, one inbound and one outbound, both carrying the file's own uuid. An empty catalog is nonetheless an ordinary answer and returns `{"items":[]}`, never an error.

Only `read` and `delete` exist. `create` and `update` are declared unsupported above with their reasons, and read-only-ness is structural as well as declared: there is no create or update path underneath for a bug to reach.

children.summary: not supported — an authorization is a pairing across TWO files, not a record in this one. Creating one correctly means writing a matching entry in both files -- an outbound token here whose SHA-256 hash is the inbound entry over there -- and the second file has to be open to receive its half. The only files this tool opens alongside this one are the ones it references, and an unauthorized file refuses to be opened from here in the first place -- so at the moment a new pairing would be needed, the file that needs it is exactly the file that cannot be reached. Half a pairing does not fail loudly: it makes a file refuse to open later. Authorize files from FileMaker Pro's Manage > Security > File Access, which has both files open and will write both halves
Lists this file's authorizations, or describes one

not supported — an authorization entry has nothing safely editable. Its uuid and type are the identity the OTHER file's matching entry is keyed to, so changing either breaks the pairing at the far end, where nothing here can fix it; its hash and token are the secret material the feature rests on and this tool will not write secrets. Re-authorize from FileMaker Pro's Manage > Security > File Access with both files open, or revoke this half with delete:authorization
Revokes this file's half of one protected-file pairing

nodes.title: delete:authorization
nodes.summary: Revokes this file's half of one protected-file pairing

keys.summary: which side of the pairing to revoke
the file uuid of the half to revoke -- it needs a 'type'
the member key to revoke, from a read:authorization listing

refusedInputs.reason: authorizations have no names; address one by 'uuid' + 'type' or by 'id', or omit both to list them. There is no name list to search, so answering not_found would imply there was a name that could have matched

notes: It removes only THIS file's half. The far file still holds its side, now pointing at nothing -- the right outcome for a revocation, since access from here is denied, but not a symmetric teardown, and the other file needs cleaning up in FileMaker Pro.
`result` echoes the removed member, captured before the deletion and with the same shape as a describe -- so a caller learns which side of which pairing they just revoked, still carrying no secret.

It commits separately from other schema changes, because authorizations live outside the regular schema; skipping that separate commit would make a delete report ok, pass a same-process read, and then be silently back on reopen.
`tampered` stays false across a delete, because the commit refreshes the catalog's CRC itself -- verified rather than assumed.
seeAlso: `fm-cli help forms` — what JSON a key's type, its requiredness and a filter's tag each take

nodes.title: read:authorization
nodes.summary: Lists this file's authorizations, or describes one
notes: `tampered` is on the LIST envelope, not on each item, because it is a property of the whole catalog: it compares the catalog's stored CRC against its contents, so true means the protected-file setup should be treated as untrustworthy.

`filter` NARROWS a listing and does nothing else. Every member that comes back is reported in exactly the shape an unfiltered listing gives it, so a filter changes which members appear and never what any one of them says. It is how "every inbound entry" is asked for: a bare `type` is half an ADDRESS on this catalog and is refused as one.
`total` is how many authorizations the file has, unfiltered; `returned` counts the ones that came back, so a filtered listing reports both what matched and what it was matched against.

Matching ignores case, and `authorizedBy` takes the wildcards `*` (any run of characters) and `?` (exactly one). There is no escape, so a literal `*` or `?` cannot be matched. `uuid` is matched WHOLE rather than as a pattern -- it is an identifier, not a name -- and in either case, so a uuid copied out of a listing and one typed in lower case select the same members.

EVERY attribute given must match, so naming two of them narrows the listing further rather than widening it. `{"uuid":"...","type":"inbound"}` inside a filter therefore selects the same one member the address form describes, and returns it as a listing of one.

A filter matching nothing is `ok` with `"items":[]` and `returned` of 0. A filter selects rather than addresses, so a uuid no member carries is an empty answer and not a `not_found` -- which also means a mistyped uuid looks exactly like a file that never authorized that one.
A member whose uuid could not be read carries no `uuid` at all, and so never matches a `uuid` filter. It has no addressable identity either, which is the same fact seen twice.

The FILENAMES and the timestamp are not filterable. `filenames` is a list rather than one value, `filenamesRaw` has no delimiter this tool can promise, and `authorizedAt` is a formatted date rather than a number -- so each would answer with something other than what it appeared to ask. Read the listing and compare them yourself.

An unknown uuid or id is `not_found` with NO suggestions. Every other catalog offers closest-name hints; this one is the stated exception, because the siblings are 128-bit uuids and the nearest by edit distance is never the one the caller meant.
A malformed uuid is `invalid_field`, not `not_found`: a string that is not a uuid is bad input, and "no such member" would send a caller looking for a member when the fix is to fix the string.

`hasHash` and `hasToken` report PRESENCE and nothing else. They are gated on the entry's `type` because reading the stored value at the wrong byte count still succeeds and reports true, so an outbound token can misreport as an inbound hash and vice versa if the type is ignored.

`filenames` and `filenamesRaw` are BOTH reported. What separates two filenames is not reliably knowable, so `filenamesRaw` is verbatim and authoritative and `filenames` is a best-effort split on newline.

Whether THIS file demands authorization from its referrers is deliberately not exposed here: it is a file-level option, not a member of this catalog, and on a list of authorizations it would read as a property of the items.
A describe returns the same object a listing's item carries, plus `"kind":"authorization"`, so an item lifted out of a listing carries exactly the keys a describe of it will.

nodes.title: baseDirectory
nodes.summary: The directories externally-stored container data lives under, recorded in the file header
notes: NOTHING IN THIS CATALOG TOUCHES THE FILESYSTEM. An entry records a string: creating one does not create the directory or check that it exists, and deleting one removes nothing from disk. A path naming nowhere is a legitimate entry, since the file may later be opened on a machine where it does exist.

Paths match EXACTLY, case included -- the one deliberate exception to the case-insensitive name matching every other catalog uses. A name here is a filesystem location, and whether case matters is a property of the filesystem the data lives on, which nothing in the database file can tell. Folding `Files/` into `files/` would silently repoint container storage.
The entries are mirrored into the database file's own header, which is why a path's length is limited at all and why the limits are the header block's rather than any filesystem's.

notes: `filter` NARROWS a listing and does nothing else. Every entry that comes back is reported in exactly the shape an unfiltered listing gives it, so a filter changes which entries appear and never what any one of them says.
`total` is how many entries the file has, unfiltered; `returned` counts the ones that came back. A filtered listing therefore reports both what matched and what it was matched against.
EVERY attribute given must match, so naming both narrows the listing further rather than widening it.

A filter matching nothing is `ok` with `"items":[]` and `returned` of 0. A filter selects rather than addresses, so a pattern nothing matches is an empty answer and not an error -- which also means a misspelled pattern looks exactly like a file with no such entry.

A FILTER'S `path` IGNORES CASE and takes the wildcards `*` (any run of characters) and `?` (exactly one), which is the one place in this catalog where case does not matter. Matching exactly is a rule about ADDRESSING one stored entry, where folding case would repoint container storage; a filter only chooses which of the entries already listed are shown. There is no escape, so a literal `*` or `?` in a stored path cannot be matched.

`absolutePath` IS NOT a filter attribute, even though a listing reports it. It is whatever the entry resolves to on the machine reading the file, so filtering on it would give different answers for one unchanged file depending on where it was opened from. Filter on `path` and `relative`, which are what the file actually stores.

`absolutePath` is what the entry resolves to on THIS machine right now, so the same file opened from another directory reports a different value. It is derived and read-only: sending it back on a write is `unknown_key`, and the round trip is `path` + `relative`.
It is omitted rather than reported empty when FileMaker cannot resolve it -- absent means "FileMaker would not say", where empty would claim it resolves to nowhere.

Unlike every other catalog, the LISTING carries full detail rather than bare refs: an entry has exactly two attributes beyond its id, so withholding them would cost a round trip per entry and save nothing.
A path is matched EXACTLY, case included, so a miss is `not_found` with the closest stored paths as suggestions.

nodes.title: calculation
nodes.summary: A FileMaker formula supplied as text and thrown away -- nothing here is stored or addressable
notes: NOT A CATALOG IN THE FILE. Every other catalog here wraps a named, enumerable collection of members with keys. A calculation is a string the caller supplies, used and discarded: nothing is named, nothing is addressed by id, and no result carries one. So there is no `read:calculation` to list, and "names in, IDs out" does not apply.

IT ANSWERS NO CRUD VERB. `create`/`read`/`update`/`delete` aimed here are `invalid_op` naming both real ops, not `unsupported_operation`: there is no member to act on, so it is a grammar error rather than a missing capability.

AND ITS TWO VERBS APPLY TO NOTHING ELSE. `validate` and `evaluate` are the only entries in the verb vocabulary that are not universal; aimed at another catalog they are `invalid_op` with a `<verb>:calculation` suggestion. Every other catalog stays ignorant of these two verbs, and both halves of `<verb>:<catalog>` keep their independent did-you-mean.

NEITHER VERB IS A WRITE. A file's bytes are identical after evaluating -- including a formula that assigns a global -- so neither joins the commit lifecycle, neither reports `dry-run`, and `--dry-run` does not change what either does.

A CONTEXT CREATED EARLIER IN THE SAME UNCOMMITTED STREAM IS NOT FULLY USABLE YET. Naming it as `context` works, because the occurrence resolves by name, but resolving a field reference THROUGH it does not: FileMaker answers 106 (`table_missing`) rather than the 102/1224 the identical op earns in a later run. Left as FileMaker's own behaviour rather than papered over -- forcing a commit mid-stream would turn two read-only ops into writes.

children.summary: Parses a formula without running it and reports what parsing found
Runs a formula and returns its value as text

nodes.title: evaluate:calculation
nodes.summary: Runs a formula and returns its value as text

keys.summary: the formula text to run
the table occurrence to resolve field references from; omit for none

refusedInputs.reason: it applies to validate:calculation only. Evaluating runs the formula, and evaluation takes no slot -- notably 'Self' cannot be evaluated at all here, since there is no field or record for it to refer to. Use validate:calculation to check a field, auto-enter or validation formula

notes: `value` IS ALWAYS A JSON STRING, even when `dataType` is `number`. FileMaker's numeric type is a fixed-point decimal whose range and precision exceed IEEE 754 double, the only numeric type JSON guarantees, so emitting 1/3 or a 20-digit result as a JSON number would silently round it. `dataType` is one of `text`, `number`, `date`, `time`, `timestamp`, `container`.

A FORMULA THAT WILL NOT PARSE IS AN ERROR LINE, the inverse of `validate` on the same text: there is no value to return, so the failure is the whole answer. Measured 2026-08-03: `"Length ( "` exits 0 on validate and 1 on evaluate.

A field reference VALIDATES but does not evaluate. There is no record context -- this CLI has no notion of a current record -- so `Person::First` parses clean and then returns `calc_undefined` (1224). Validating field references against real schema is the useful half, and is why `context` exists.

`Self` cannot be evaluated at all, whatever the formula. It means the value of the field the formula belongs to, and there is neither a field nor a record here, so it fails 1225 even when it parsed fine. A `Self` formula is validate-only.

THE DESIGN FUNCTIONS EVALUATE, and answer about the file on disk. `ScriptNames`, `LayoutNames`, `TableNames`, `FieldNames`, `FieldType`, `FieldComment`, `RelationInfo` and the rest answer what FileMaker Pro answers.

BUT A DESIGN FUNCTION AND A `read:` OP DISAGREE about work this run has done. Create a layout and `read:layout` lists it immediately, while `LayoutNames ( "" )` does not until a LATER invocation. This is not a matter of committing first -- the `read:` op sees the new layout with nothing committed, in the same run, and the two answers stay different until the run ends. They are simply answering from different views of the file. Use the matching `read:` op to check work in progress: it is the authority on what this run has done, and a design function answers for the file rather than for the run.

LEAVE THE FILE ARGUMENT EMPTY. Every design function's first parameter names a file that is ALREADY OPEN -- it is looked up in the open-file list and nothing is opened to satisfy it -- and exactly one file is open, the one given to `--file`. So `ScriptNames ( "Other" )` answers empty even when `Other` is a registered externalDataSource, and `DatabaseNames` only ever names `--file`. Read another file's schema by pointing `--file` at it.

TWO OF THEM CANNOT ANSWER HERE and fail 1225 rather than answering. `ValueListItems` reads its values through a record cursor and there is no current record; `WindowNames` lists a session's open windows and nothing here opens one. They are refused rather than left to run because each would otherwise answer an EMPTY string with no error, and "this value list has no items" is a worse answer than no answer. Both still `validate` as true, so a formula calling one can be stored.

THE THREE MOBILE FUNCTIONS PARSE BUT CANNOT ANSWER EITHER. `Location`, `LocationValues` and `RangeBeacons` read a device's location or the beacons near it, and there is no device here, so each fails 1225 the same way. They are recognized so that a formula FileMaker Pro or FileMaker Go authored still validates and stores -- a field or script step calling one round-trips unchanged -- and only evaluating one is refused. Note the alternative would be worse than an error: asked with no device, each answers an EMPTY string, which reads as a location fix that found nothing rather than a question that cannot be asked here.

GLOBAL VARIABLES PERSIST for the life of the process. Evaluating `Let ( $$X = 1 ; $$X )` leaves `$$X` set for later ops in the same run. Nothing reaches the file and nothing survives exit, but ops in one stream are not isolated from each other.

The parse-error codes are DERIVED from FileMaker's own parse errors, lowercased and underscored (`calc_unknown_function` for 1208), and 1200-1225 is an open range -- so `errors` below names the measured ones rather than a closed set.
seeAlso: `fm-cli help forms` — what JSON a key's type, its requiredness and a filter's tag each take

nodes.title: validate:calculation
nodes.summary: Parses a formula without running it and reports what parsing found

keys.summary: the formula text to parse, without running it
the table occurrence to resolve field references from; omit for none
where the formula will live, which changes what is accepted

notes: AN INVALID FORMULA IS A SUCCESSFUL VALIDATE. The line is `status:"ok"` with `result.valid:false` and the run still exits 0, because the op answered the question it was asked. Branch on `result.valid`, never on `status` alone.

That split is not merely taxonomic. `--abort-on-error` defaults to true, so an error line rolls the whole batch back -- an invalid formula reported as an error would destroy every unrelated schema change in the same batch, making the op useless for the one thing it exists for.

`status:"error"` is reserved for the question being UNANSWERABLE, which today is exactly one case: an unknown `context` occurrence (`tableOccurrence_not_found`). The parse-error codes ride inside `result.error` instead, so they are not in this op's `errors` list.
On the invalid branch the body also carries a `warnings` array stating the trap outright. It is emitted only when `valid` is false, so the key means something when it appears.

`for` is echoed on every result INCLUDING the default. A caller who misspelled the key silently got `standalone` before the schema refused unknown keys; the echo is how a result stays self-describing when the verdict depends on the slot.
`errorBegin`/`errorEnd` are a half-open CHARACTER range into the submitted text, and are omitted when no position is available -- a semantic failure such as an unknown field often does not carry one.

The three non-standalone slots name the same `options` keys they check (`options.calculation`, `options.autoEnter.calculation`, `options.validation.calculation`), so this op predicts what `create:field` will accept. Measured: FileMaker does not distinguish the three -- `Self` parses in all of them and fails 1225 in `standalone`.

Cheaper and safer than `evaluate` for checking a formula about to be stored: it cannot execute anything, so it cannot set a global or read the current time. For a field calculation it is the ONLY way to check one without writing it, since `Self` and unstored references mean many valid field formulas cannot be evaluated at all.

PLUG-IN FUNCTIONS ARE THE ONE GAP. `External()` and a third-party plug-in's own functions are not registered here, so a formula using one is `valid:false` with `calc_unknown_function` even though FileMaker Pro with that plug-in installed accepts it. That is a gap in this evaluator, not in the formula. FileMaker's own design functions (`FieldNames`, `TableNames`, `ScriptNames`, `RelationInfo` and the rest) and its three mobile functions (`Location`, `LocationValues`, `RangeBeacons`) DO validate, and a formula using one can be stored.
seeAlso: `fm-cli help forms` — what JSON a key's type, its requiredness and a filter's tag each take

nodes.title: customFunction
nodes.summary: The user-defined calculation functions a formula anywhere in the file can call
notes: Custom functions are FILE-GLOBAL: they are not scoped by a table, so no verb takes a `table` key. A body may still name a field, fully qualified as "Occurrence::Field"; there is no `context` key to choose the occurrence from, so the name in the body is the whole of it.

This catalog lives in the FILE-USER commit domain, as `valueList` does: every write is only observable after the file is reopened, which is why a test that reads back in the same process sees the session's state rather than the file's.

The parameter list crosses into FileMaker as ONE STRING whose separator is locale-dependent. This CLI joins with ';' and FileMaker renders everything back with ';' regardless of what was sent. It never passes a locale, so a file it touches is always the default system type; there is no documented mapping from locale to separator, so this is MEASURED rather than derived.

Custom functions can be organised into FOLDERS, and this catalog models them: `read` reports the tree, `create` makes one with `type:"folder"`, `update` moves a function in or out with `folder`, and `delete` takes a folder and optionally its contents. A folder is purely organisational -- it does not scope a function's name, which stays file-global, and it does not affect what a formula can call.

FUNCTION NAMES ARE UNIQUE ACROSS THE WHOLE FILE regardless of folders, so moving a function never changes what it is called or how it is called. FOLDER names, by contrast, are checked for nothing at all -- FileMaker permits two at one level with the same name, and permits a folder and a function to share a name. This CLI permits both too, because refusing would make it unable to reproduce a file it can read; what it will not do is guess which member an ambiguous name meant, so every by-name op answers `ambiguous` with the candidate ids and takes an `id` instead.

nodes.title: create:customFunction
nodes.summary: Creates a custom function from a parameter list and a calculation body, or a folder

keys.summary: the function's name, unique in the file and not a built-in function's
what to create: a custom function, or a folder to group them in
the EXISTING folder to create it in, as a "/"-separated path; a folder that is not there is an error
the index within the parent, 0-based over the members a listing emits; absent appends
the ordered parameter names; `[]` for a zero-argument function, never omitted
the calculation body, as a bare string; a field in it is named "Occurrence::Field"
whether every account may call it, rather than full-access accounts only (default true)
the originating add-on UUID to stamp on it, grouping everything one add-on created
the function's own comment, shown in the Edit Custom Function dialog
one comment per parameter, by position; shorter than `parameters` leaves the rest uncommented

semanticChecks: A parameter name must not be empty or whitespace-only: FileMaker drops it, so `["a",""]` would read back as `["a"]` and the arity would not be the one that was asked for.

A parameter name must not contain ';' or ',': the list is passed to FileMaker as ONE separated string, so either character would split one name into two parameters -- the same reasoning that refuses a carriage return inside a custom value list value.

`ownerId` is 32 hexadecimal digits, hyphenated or not, in either case; braces around it are refused. A read reports it back hyphen-grouped and upper case, so a caller comparing a read-back stamp against the string it sent has to fold case and drop hyphens -- the two are equal as UUIDs and different as strings.
notes: THE BODY IS COMPILED at create time. FileMaker parses the body before storing it, so a syntax error, a call to a function that does not exist, and a reference to an undeclared parameter all surface at this op as `invalid_field` carrying FileMaker's own numeric code -- never deferred into a generic commit_failed, and never stored unparsed.

A body MAY NAME A FIELD, and the reference is resolved when this op runs. `Contacts::FullName` compiles and reads back verbatim when that occurrence and field are already IN THE FILE. A name that does not resolve fails the op: an unknown field on a real occurrence is `field_missing` / FileMaker error 102, and an unknown OCCURRENCE is `invalid_field` / error 106 -- as is a bare unqualified name, which the engine reads as an occurrence rather than as a field. Built-in calls needing no record context (`Get ( CurrentDate )`) compile fine. See `delete:field` for what happens to a body once the field it names is gone.

A FIELD REFERENCE NEEDS THE OCCURRENCE COMMITTED, and this is where it differs from a call to another custom function. A body may call a function created earlier in the same op stream, because the catalog resolves against uncommitted changes. A table occurrence does NOT: a field created earlier in the same stream is error 106 until the stream lands, because the occurrence cannot be resolved far enough to say whether the field exists. So the same body fails in the stream that builds the table and succeeds in the next one. `validate:calculation` has the same split, for the same reason.

A PARAMETER name is validated by FileMaker, not here: a reserved word or a malformed identifier is `invalid_name` naming the parameter and saying to rename it -- probed 2026-08-03, `last` and `1abc` both come back the same error, and FileMaker offers no way to tell reserved from malformed apart.

THE BODY IS NORMALIZED. FileMaker stores a parse rather than the caller's bytes: `;` and `,` are both accepted as separators on input, in the parameter list and inside the body, and everything reads back with `;`. So `Left ( x , 1 )` comes back `Left ( x ; 1 )`. This is the one visible exception to round-trippability -- re-feeding a read result produces the same function, not the same string.
A create that fails after the member is allocated deletes it, so nothing half-built reaches the file: a refused body leaves no function behind on reopen.

`comment` and `parameterComments` are FileMaker's own "Function Comment" and per-parameter comments (Edit Custom Function dialog). They are stored TOGETHER as one member with `parameters`/`body`; sending only one of the pair leaves the other absent, not left at some prior value, since there is no prior value on a create.

A FOLDER TAKES NONE OF THE ABOVE. `type:"folder"` needs only a `name`, and `parameters`, `body`, `availableToUser`, `comment` and `parameterComments` are all REFUSED on one rather than accepted and ignored -- a folder has no parameter list and no calculation, so nothing about it is compiled.

A FOLDER'S NAME FOLLOWS LOOSER RULES than a function's, and this is FileMaker's rule rather than the CLI's: a folder may be called `Length` or `My Helpers` -- a built-in function name, or a name with a space -- where a function may be neither. Folder names also have NO uniqueness requirement at all, so two folders at one level may share a name, and a folder may share a name with a function. Where that makes a later `name` ambiguous, every op says so and takes an `id` instead of guessing.

`folder` names an EXISTING folder; a path that is not there is `customFunction_not_found` with suggestions from the level that missed, never a folder created on the caller's behalf. A path component matching two folders is `ambiguous`.

A folder is TWO catalog members -- FileMaker brackets its contents between a begin marker and an end marker -- created together and stamped with the same `ownerId`, so a folder is never half-made or half-owned.
seeAlso: `fm-cli help forms` — what JSON a key's type, its requiredness and a filter's tag each take

nodes.title: delete:customFunction
nodes.summary: Deletes a custom function or folder, refusing one another calculation calls

keys.summary: the custom function or folder to delete; a duplicated name is `ambiguous`
the member to delete, by the id a listing reported
deletes a folder's whole subtree; without it a non-empty folder is refused

notes: DELETING AN IN-USE FUNCTION IS REFUSED, `in_use`, naming every referent. FileMaker would allow it and silently rewrite each calling calculation to `<Function Missing> ( ... )`, which no longer compiles -- measured 2026-07-26, and the CLI scans for referents itself rather than reporting FileMaker's verdict.

THE SCAN IS PARTIAL, and honestly so: other function bodies, all three field-calculation slots, and custom menu calculations (each menu's title and install calc, each item's name and install calc) are covered; script step calculations, layout object calculations and privilege-set calculations are not. A function referenced only from one of those still deletes.

A NAME IS MATCHED BY FILEMAKER'S RULE FOR WHAT A NAME MAY CONTAIN, so a function called `Monthly Total` or `#Ref` is guarded exactly as `Initials` is. A space, `#`, `.`, `!`, `%`, `?`, `@`, `{`, `'` and `~` are all ordinary characters inside a function name.

THE SCAN ERRS TOWARD REFUSING. Where a calculation's text is ambiguous about whether a name is a call -- a Let() variable of the same name, or a name that appears inside a longer multi-word name -- the delete is refused rather than allowed. A refusal costs one manual check; a wrong success costs an unknown number of calculations that no longer compile.
The refusal is UNCONDITIONAL -- there is no `force` flag yet, so an in-use function cannot be deleted until its callers are cleared or repointed.
`result` echoes the removed ref, `{name,id}`, with the id captured before the deletion, so a caller can log what went away.

DELETING A FOLDER TAKES BOTH OF ITS BRACKET MEMBERS, always and atomically. Deleting one alone is silent corruption -- an orphaned end marker, or a folder that never closes and adopts every later member -- which is why there is no way to ask for it.
A NON-EMPTY FOLDER IS `in_use` unless `recursive` is set, naming how many members it holds. With `recursive` the whole subtree goes, nested folders included.

A RECURSIVE DELETE IS SCANNED WHOLE AND REFUSED WHOLE. The in-use scan runs over EVERY function in the subtree before anything is deleted, and one referenced function refuses the entire op with all the referents listed -- nothing is deleted. `recursive` means "take the contents too", not "take the consequences": a partial delete would leave a half-emptied folder plus calculations that no longer compile.
A reference from INSIDE the subtree does not block it: if two functions in the same folder call each other and both are going, neither counts as a stranded referrer.

nodes.title: read:customFunction
nodes.summary: Lists the custom functions and folders, nested, or describes one by name or id
semanticChecks: a filter needs 'flatten':true. A listing is nested by default, so a filter could only test the top level and would silently drop every match inside a folder.
notes: A LISTING IS IN FILEMAKER'S DISPLAY ORDER AND NESTED BY FOLDER -- the order the Manage Custom Functions dialog shows, not id order. That is the same exception `read:script` and `read:layout` take, and for the same reason: display order is the only order a caller can write back, and it is what the folder tree is expressed in.

EVERY ITEM CARRIES `type`, `customFunction` or `folder`, and a folder additionally carries `items` -- the members inside it, nested to any depth. `total` counts every member at every depth within the scope, folders included; the folder end markers FileMaker stores are structure rather than members and never appear.

`folder` scopes the listing to one subtree and `flatten` changes its SHAPE: with `flatten:true` every member at every depth arrives in one flat array, each carrying the `folder` path it sits in. The two compose, and "everything inside this folder, however deep" is the pairing `flatten` mostly exists for.

`filter` NARROWS a listing and does nothing else, and it needs `flatten`:true. A nested listing is a tree, so a filter over it could only test the top level and would drop matches sitting inside folders; flattening puts every member in reach. Every member that comes back is reported in exactly the shape an unfiltered listing gives it, so a filter changes which members appear and never what any one of them says.
`total` is how many custom functions the file has, unfiltered; `returned` counts the ones that came back, so a filtered listing reports both what matched and what it was matched against.

Matching ignores case, and `name` is a pattern: `*` stands for any run of characters and `?` for exactly one, so `Fn*` and `*Date` both work. There is no escape, so a function whose name really contains `*` or `?` cannot be matched literally.

A filter matching nothing is `ok` with `"items":[]` and `returned` of 0 -- a filter is a test each member is put to rather than an address, so a pattern nothing matches is not `not_found`. A misspelled pattern therefore looks exactly like an empty catalog.

`name` and `type` filter an UNDETAILED listing, `type` being how a caller asks for just the folders or just the functions. `arity`, `body` and `availableToUser` filter the DETAILED item instead, so any of the three is refused with `invalid_field` unless the same op also sends `detail`:true -- and a FOLDER never matches one of them, since a folder's describe body carries none of the three (see the notes on `read:customFunction`'s filter declaration): dropping every folder from a `body` or `arity` search is correct, not a gap, because a folder has no body and no parameters to test.

`detail`:true reports each listed FUNCTION as a describe of it would, in place of the `{id,name,type,position}` summary, and leaves every FOLDER exactly as it was: a folder has no parameters and no body, and its describe is the member itself rather than its subtree, which the listing already carries as `items`. It loads each function's definition, which a plain listing does not, so the cost scales with the catalog.

A describe emits every key always, including `arity` and `prototype`, which are DERIVED BY FILEMAKER and read-only: they are what FileMaker computed when it parsed the definition, not separately stored values. `prototype` is the one place a caller can SEE which separator FileMaker round-trips, and `arity` is FileMaker's own count rather than the length of `parameters` -- if the two disagree, the definition is not what the caller thinks.

`comment` is empty string and `parameterComments` is `[]` when never set, matching how a field's `comment`/`aiAnnotation` are always reported -- a complete picture, and re-feeding it back in as a create input.

A DESCRIBE OF A FOLDER STOPS EARLY, on purpose: it carries `type`, `name`, `id`, `folder`, `position` and any `ownerId`, and no `parameters`, `body`, `arity`, `prototype`, `availableToUser` or comments. A folder has none of those, and reporting them as `[]`, `""` and `0` is exactly what used to make a folder read as a real zero-argument function.

An unknown `name`/`id` is `not_found` with closest-name suggestions -- the GENERIC code, as `read:table` uses, while the write verbs use `customFunction_not_found`. That split matches the existing table/field ops rather than introducing a new convention.

nodes.summary: Renames a custom function or folder, replaces a function's definition, or moves it

keys.summary: the member to update, by name -- the address, not a change; a duplicated name is `ambiguous`
the member to update, by id -- how to address one of two members sharing a name

semanticChecks: A parameter name must not be empty or whitespace-only: FileMaker drops it, so `["a",""]` would read back as `["a"]` and the arity would not be the one that was asked for.

A parameter name must not contain ';' or ',': the list is passed to FileMaker as ONE separated string, so either character would split one name into two parameters -- the same reasoning that refuses a carriage return inside a custom value list value.

`ownerId` is 32 hexadecimal digits, hyphenated or not, in either case; braces around it are refused. A read reports it back hyphen-grouped and upper case, so a caller comparing a read-back stamp against the string it sent has to fold case and drop hyphens -- the two are equal as UUIDs and different as strings.
notes: Anything not sent SURVIVES: a body-only update keeps the existing parameters, `availableToUser` and the originating add-on stamp.

But name, parameters and body go to FileMaker TOGETHER -- all three are rewritten at once -- so an update to any one of them re-sends the other two as currently stored, AND THE BODY IS REPARSED AGAINST THEM. A `parameters`-only update whose retained body still references the old names fails `invalid_field` / FileMaker error 106 and leaves the function untouched. Rename the parameters and the body in the same op. This is a refusal FileMaker makes, not a rule this CLI could check: nothing here reads the stored body.

A rename onto an existing name is `customFunction_exists` (matched case-insensitively); a case-only rename of the same function is allowed, because the collision check excludes the function being renamed.
`ownerId` IS NOT A CHANGE: it re-stamps the originating add-on and must accompany one of the four change keys, so an op carrying nothing but a name and an owner is refused for asking for no change.

`comment`/`parameterComments` are likewise read-modify-written as a PAIR, separately from `parameters`/`body`: an update sending only `comment` leaves the stored parameter comments as they were, and vice versa. `Set()` (the call that rewrites name/parameters/body) does not touch this member at all, so the pair survives untouched even when the other three change in the same op.
`result` is `{name,id}` with the function's id unchanged.
`folder` MOVES the member: `folder` with no `position` appends it inside that folder, and `folder:""` moves it back to the top level. `position` alone re-orders it within the parent it already has.

MOVING A FOLDER IS `unsupported_operation`, matching `update:script` and `update:layout`. A folder's contents sit between its two bracket members, so moving it means moving a contiguous run, and moving one bracket alone silently re-parents every child. Move the functions instead, or delete and recreate the folder.

A FOLDER ACCEPTS ONLY `newName` and `ownerId`. `parameters`, `body`, `availableToUser`, `comment` and `parameterComments` are refused on one as `invalid_field` naming the key -- which key is legal depends on the member this addresses, so it is a refusal the op shape cannot express and only the file can answer.

`type` IS NOT AN UPDATE KEY. A function cannot become a folder or the reverse: a folder is a bracket PAIR of members and a function is one member, so there is no in-place conversion to perform. Create the shape you want and move things into it.

Renaming a FOLDER is not checked for collisions, because FileMaker does not check either -- two folders may share a name. Renaming a FUNCTION onto another function's name is `customFunction_exists`; onto a FOLDER's name it is allowed, since the two populations do not collide.
seeAlso: `fm-cli help forms` — what JSON a key's type, its requiredness and a filter's tag each take

refusedInputs.reason: 'uuid' is output-only. create:customMenu mints one item at a time as it appends 'items', and hands every one back in 'createdItemUuids', in the same order -- there is no way to assign one yourself, on this or any other item.

'index' is output-only and POSITIONAL: it is recomputed from where an item sits in the list on every read rather than stored on the item, so there is nothing here to accept. Address a created item by the uuid 'createdItemUuids' reports instead.

'inheritedMenu' is read-only. The flag marks FileMaker's own locked built-in menu shells -- the bracketed rows in Manage Custom Menus -- and no menu you author in Pro carries it: Create Custom Menu offers only the eight standard menus FileMaker leaves unlocked as a base. Setting it on a menu that also has a 'baseMenuID' makes Pro silently discard every later edit to that menu; setting it without one leaves Pro building no menu at all. A menu meant to show a standard menu's items takes 'baseMenuID' together with those items -- which is what Pro's own copy of a standard menu produces.

semanticChecks: an `items` entry's `shortcutModifiers` is refused without a sibling `shortcutKey`: a modifier list with no key is a shortcut of nothing
an `items` entry's `shortcutKey` must be exactly one character: FileMaker stores a shortcut as a single key plus its modifiers, so there is nowhere to put a second one
a `tags` entry containing a space or a `#` is refused: the file stores the whole list as one string of space-separated `#tag` tokens, so either character inside a tag would split it in two
notes: `items` AUTHORS THE MENU'S WHOLE ITEM LIST, in the order sent -- there is no key that adds to an existing one, because create is the only write op `items` reaches (update still refuses it whole). Absent or `[]` is a menu with no items, same as today.

`createdItemUuids` IS HOW A CALLER LEARNS WHAT IT JUST MADE: one uuid per `items` entry, in the same order, readable immediately -- no need to `read:customMenu` back to get a handle onto what was just created. Omitted when `items` was absent or empty.

THE PER-KIND RULES are FileMaker Pro's own Manage Custom Menus dialog, not this tool's: `commandID`, the shortcut pair and `action` belong to a command item only; `nameCalculation` belongs to a command or a submenu, never a separator; `installCalculation` belongs to every kind, separators and submenus included; and `submenuName` is required on a submenu and refused on everything else.

AN `action` IS ANY SCRIPT STEP, not only Perform Script -- the same step object `read:customMenu` reports for an item that overrides its action, and the same one a button's `action` is (`fm-cli help layout create` / `fm-cli help script steps` for the vocabulary). Setting it also sets `overrideAction`, the way FileMaker Pro's own Action checkbox does.

A SUBMENU ITEM'S TARGET AND AN ACTION SHARE ONE STORAGE FIELD -- WHY the two can never coexist on one item, and why `submenuName` is refused everywhere but a submenu and `action` everywhere but a command: FileMaker's own CustomMenuItem keeps both in the same slot, and read:customMenu's own notes say the same about what it reports.

A STEP FILEMAKER ITSELF WILL NOT PUT ON A MENU ITEM is `unsupported_step`, and it is the same set a button refuses -- the flow-control steps, the engine-state ones, the transaction steps and the comment step -- because the editor FileMaker opens for a menu item's action is the one it opens for a button. `fm-cli help layout create` enumerates them by name. One of those is refused naming the step, and no item is written.

`position` PLACES THE MENU in FileMaker's own Manage Custom Menus order, 0-based; absent appends. The `position` the result reports is read back from the file rather than echoed, so it is where the menu actually landed.

`tags` IS AN OPEN NAMESPACE: a tag is any word, so no list of accepted values exists and none is checked. Send each tag WITHOUT the leading `#` the file stores it behind. The two characters a tag may not contain are a space and a `#`, both because the whole list is one string of space-separated `#tag` tokens.

nodes.title: read:customMenu
nodes.summary: Lists every custom menu, or describes one by name or id, including its items
semanticChecks: a `filter` naming no attribute is refused: it would narrow nothing, and answering it with the whole listing is indistinguishable from a filter that matched every menu
notes: `filter` NARROWS a listing and does nothing else: `name` matches every menu's shallow item, but `comment` needs `detail`:true because the shallow item carries only `{name,id,position}` and has nothing for that filter to compare.

A LISTING IS IN FILEMAKER'S OWN DISPLAY ORDER -- the order Manage Custom Menus shows, not id order -- and every entry reports the `position` it holds in it, 0-based. That is the same coordinate `create:customMenu` and `update:customMenu` accept, so a listing can be reordered by writing the positions back. `position` is omitted for a menu the file's order list has no entry for at all, which a menu FileMaker saved does not do; such a menu is still listed, after the ordered ones.

`tags` is the menu's own tag list, one entry per tag, WITHOUT the `#` the file stores each behind, and `[]` for a menu with none. FileMaker's own clipboard serializer carries a tag list on every menu it copies, so this is where one that arrived that way shows up. It is an OPEN NAMESPACE -- any word can be a tag -- so no list of the values to expect exists.

Each entry in `items` reports its `index`, a `uuid`, `kind` (`command`, `separator` or `submenu`), `commandID`, `overrideName` with the `nameCalculation` it gates, an `installCalculation` -- both calculations as bare strings -- `overrideShortcut` with, when present, the keyboard `shortcutKey`/`shortcutModifiers` pair it gates, `submenuName` on a `submenu` item (the target menu's name), and `overrideAction` with, when present, the `action` it gates.

The `uuid` is the STABLE handle for an item: it stays with that item across an insert, a delete or a reorder of the other items in the menu. The `index` is POSITIONAL, not an identity -- it shifts whenever another item is inserted, deleted or moved ahead of it -- so do not store an item's index and expect it to still name the same item later; hold on to the `uuid` instead. `uuid` is omitted only for an item the file itself has none for, which is not something a saved menu's items do.

`overrideName`, `overrideShortcut` and `overrideAction` are each the switch beside the value it gates: it decides whether that value takes effect, and it is exactly what FileMaker Pro shows as a checkbox in Manage Custom Menus -- the Name, Shortcut and Action tick-boxes in that pane, bound directly to these three flags. refusedInputs.reason: 'items' is create:customMenu's key, which states a menu's whole item list at once. An update names what to change instead: 'removeItems' and 'updateItems', each addressing an item by the 'uuid' a read reported, and 'addItems' to append -- applied in that order. An update naming none of the three never touches the menu's existing items.

'inheritedMenu' is read-only. The flag marks FileMaker's own locked built-in menu shells -- the bracketed rows in Manage Custom Menus -- and no menu you author in Pro carries it: Create Custom Menu offers only the eight standard menus FileMaker leaves unlocked as a base. Setting it on a menu that also has a 'baseMenuID' makes Pro silently discard every later edit to that menu; setting it without one leaves Pro building no menu at all. A menu meant to show a standard menu's items takes 'baseMenuID' together with those items -- which is what Pro's own copy of a standard menu produces.

semanticChecks: an item's `uuid` may carry ONE instruction per op: the same uuid in both `removeItems` and `updateItems`, or twice in `updateItems`, is refused rather than resolved in an order the caller cannot see

an `updateItems` entry's `shortcutModifiers` is refused without a sibling `shortcutKey`, and its `shortcutKey` must be exactly one character -- the same two rules `addItems` and create's `items` follow
an `updateItems` entry that changes an item's `kind` to `submenu` must name a `submenuName` in the same entry
`overrideName`, `overrideShortcut` and `overrideAction` each accept only `false`, which clears that override; `true` is refused
a `tags` entry containing a space or a `#` is refused, for the reason `fm-cli help customMenu create` gives
notes: AN UPDATE THAT NAMES NONE OF `removeItems`/`updateItems`/`addItems` DOES NOT TOUCH THE MENU'S ITEMS AT ALL -- it does not read, save or rewrite the item list under any circumstance, so existing items and their uuids survive a change of comment or name untouched.

THE THREE ITEM KEYS APPLY IN ONE ORDER, and it is observable: `removeItems` first, then `updateItems`, then `addItems`. So one op can replace an item, and an addition sees the count the removals left. `addItems` takes exactly the entries create's `items` takes, and its new uuids come back in `createdItemUuids`.

AN ITEM IS ADDRESSED BY `uuid`, never by `index`: an index is positional and shifts when anything ahead of it is removed -- including earlier in the same op -- while a uuid stays with its item. Read the menu, keep the uuids, edit by them.

A KIND CHANGE IS MADE IN PLACE AND THE ITEM KEEPS ITS UUID -- this is what FileMaker Pro itself does, so a command can become a submenu or a separator and back without losing its identity. Two rules come with it, both because a submenu's target and an action's script reference are stored in THE SAME PLACE: changing to `submenu` requires a `submenuName` in the same entry, and changing away from `submenu` drops the old target rather than leaving it to be read as something else.

SETTING AN `action` REWRITES THE ITEM'S STEP, and the item's two calculations are stored with it -- so an entry that sets only an `action` keeps the `nameCalculation` and `installCalculation` the item already had. Send either calculation in the same entry to change it.

TO CLEAR AN OVERRIDE, send it as `false` on the `updateItems` entry: `overrideName`, `overrideShortcut` or `overrideAction`. Each drops that one flag and leaves everything else about the item alone -- the stored calculation, key or step stays where it is, exactly as FileMaker Pro leaves it when the matching checkbox is unticked, so re-sending the value brings the override back. `true` is refused on all three: sending the VALUE is what engages an override, so each is also refused alongside the key it gates.

WHY THOSE THREE KEYS EXIST AT ALL: the engine turns every override on as a side effect of writing the value and turns none of them off, so without them an item that had ever carried a name, a shortcut or an action kept the override for good.

`position` MOVES THE MENU in FileMaker's own Manage Custom Menus order, 0-based, and the result reports where it ended up. `tags` replaces the whole tag list; `[]` clears it. Neither touches the menu's items.
A rename onto an existing name is `customMenu_exists`; the comparison is case-insensitive.

nodes.title: customMenuSet
nodes.summary: A named, ordered group of custom menus -- what a layout's menu set actually picks
notes: ADDRESSED by name -- matched case-insensitively -- or, on read, by the id a listing reports. Update and delete take the name only.

ONE NAME DOES NOT ROUND-TRIP: the built-in Standard Menu Set reports a localized display name rather than a stored one, and it cannot be addressed by that name. Recognize it by `builtIn` in a listing, and address any set whose name might not match by `id` instead.

A LISTING IS IN FILEMAKER'S OWN DISPLAY ORDER -- the order the Manage Custom Menus list shows its sets in -- and each set reports its `position` in it. `position` is writable on both write verbs, so that order is authorable rather than merely observable. The built-in holds a place in it like any other member, so position 0 is normally it.
EVERY FILE HAS EXACTLY ONE DEFAULT menu set, and `isDefault` is how a set claims it; see create/update for why it cannot be given up rather than handed over.

MEMBERSHIP IS AUTHORABLE. `menus` is the file's actual ordered list of the custom menus a menu set contains; see create/update's own notes for the replace-not-merge semantics and the omit-to-leave-untouched guarantee.

semanticChecks: a `filter` naming no attribute is refused: it would narrow nothing, and answering it with the whole listing is indistinguishable from a filter that matched every set
notes: `filter` NARROWS a listing and does nothing else: `name` and `builtIn` match every set's shallow item, but `isDefault` needs `detail`:true because the shallow item carries only `{name,id,builtIn,position}` and has nothing for that filter to compare.

A LISTING IS IN FILEMAKER'S OWN DISPLAY ORDER -- the order Manage Custom Menus shows its sets in, not id order -- and every entry reports the `position` it holds in it, 0-based. That is the same coordinate the two write verbs accept, so a listing can be reordered by writing the positions back. It is omitted for a set the file's order list has no entry for, which is still listed, after the ordered ones.

`tags` is the set's own tag list, one entry per tag, WITHOUT the `#` the file stores each behind, and `[]` for a set with none. An OPEN NAMESPACE -- any word can be a tag -- so no list of the values to expect exists.
`menus` is the ordered membership list, by name, in the same shape create/update accept.
`subMenus` is DERIVED by walking every menu in `menus` for submenu items, recursively -- it is report-only and there is no key that could author it.
`isDefault` reports whether this set is the file's current default; every file has exactly one.

A FILE THAT HAS NO CUSTOM MENU SETS LISTS NOTHING AT ALL -- not even the built-in Standard Menu Set, which is an entry in this catalog only once a file carries custom menu sets. nodes.title: extendedPrivilege
nodes.summary: The keywords a privilege set uses to permit a protocol -- fmapp, fmrest, fmxdbc and the rest
notes: THIS CATALOG CONTROLS ACCESS. A keyword is what a privilege set uses to permit a PROTOCOL: `fmapp` is FileMaker Pro / Go client access, `fmxdbc` is ODBC/JDBC, `fmrest` is the Data API, `fmodata` is OData, `fmwebdirect` is WebDirect. Granting one opens that door for every account holding the set, so a write here is not a schema edit -- it is a live change to what a hosted file exposes.

`fmapp` IS THIS FILE'S SHARING SWITCH -- the one FileMaker Pro presents as File > Sharing > Share with FileMaker Clients. Its `sharing` value is that dialog's "Network access to file" choice: `all` is All users, `specified` with `privilegeSets` is Specify users by privilege set, `off` is No users. A new file starts at `off`, so `{"op": "update:extendedPrivilege", "name": "fmapp", "sharing": "all"}` is how a file is shared, whether it was just created or has existed for years. `hidden` is the same dialog's checkbox for keeping a shared file out of the list clients browse.

SHARING A FILE TAKES TWO SETTINGS AND ONLY ONE OF THEM IS IN THE FILE. This sets the file's half, which is the half that travels with the file and is what a host reads. The other half is network sharing being switched on for the host itself, which belongs to the machine rather than to any file and has to be turned on there.

BUILT-INS CANNOT BE DELETED OR RENAMED. Everything else on a built-in IS allowed: a fresh file ships every keyword granted to nobody, and turning a channel on by granting is the entire purpose of the catalog.
Keywords are FILE-GLOBAL: they are not scoped by a table, so no verb takes a `table` key, and a keyword is addressed by its name or by the id a listing reported.
A file-user catalog, with the same commit consequence as `valueList`: a write is only observable after the file is reopened.

notes: Names are ASCII-ALPHANUMERIC and nothing else: measured 2026-07-27, `_`, `-`, `.`, `:`, a space and `é` are each refused as `invalid_name`. This is stricter than any other catalog here -- a table may be called `My Table`, an extended privilege may not.

The name is validated BEFORE the member is created. FileMaker's own order -- create, then set the name -- can leave a persisted NAMELESS member behind when the name assignment fails, a corruption that survives the commit and that no later op can address because there is no name to address it by. So a rejected create leaves the file exactly as it was.
A duplicate name is `extendedPrivilege_exists`, and that includes a built-in: `"name": "fmapp"` is an *exists* error rather than a permission one, because the keyword really is already there.
A `privilegeSets` list with no `sharing` key is sent to FileMaker as `specified`. The CLI fills it in so FileMaker sees one unambiguous instruction rather than re-deriving the caller's intent.
Defaults, when the optional keys are omitted: `description` is `""` and `sharing` is `off` -- a keyword granted to nobody, which is what a fresh file's own keywords look like.

`sharing` "all" is a RULE, not a snapshot: a privilege set created tomorrow gets the keyword automatically. FileMaker also offers a way to grant every CURRENT privilege set at once, which reads back as `specified` rather than `all`; this CLI always sets the live `all` state instead, never that snapshot.
`result` is the ref `{name,id,builtIn}` -- `builtIn` rides on every ref, so a caller can see whether they just touched a protocol keyword without a second round trip.

It is refused only once the name has been resolved to a specific member, not at the outset.
It is not `permission_denied`: nothing checked an account. It is an operation that is possible and that this tool declines to perform.

nodes.title: read:extendedPrivilege
nodes.summary: Lists every extended-privilege keyword, or describes one by name or id
notes: `filter` NARROWS a listing and does nothing else. Every keyword that comes back is reported in exactly the shape an unfiltered listing gives it, so a filter changes which keywords appear and never what any one of them says.
`total` is how many keywords the file has, unfiltered; `returned` counts the ones that came back. A filtered listing therefore reports both what matched and what it was matched against.

Matching ignores case, and `name` takes the wildcards `*` (any run of characters) and `?` (exactly one). There is no escape, so a literal `*` or `?` in a keyword cannot be matched -- which no real keyword contains, names here being ASCII alphanumerics only.
EVERY attribute given must match, so naming both narrows the listing further rather than widening it. `{"builtIn":false}` is the whole custom set, and adding a `name` pattern narrows it again.

A filter matching nothing is `ok` with `"items":[]` and `returned` of 0. A filter selects rather than addresses, so a pattern nothing matches is an empty answer and not an error -- which also means a misspelled pattern looks exactly like a file with no such keyword.

`builtIn:false` IS THE "WHICH KEYWORDS DID SOMEONE ADD HERE" QUESTION, which is the one worth asking of a file whose history is unknown. `builtIn:true` is its complement and both match, because every listed keyword carries the flag either way.
`sharing` and `enabled` need `detail`:true. Neither is on the shallow listing item, so a filter naming either without also asking for `detail`:true is refused rather than silently matching nothing.

Ordered BY NAME, not by id -- a deliberate exception, taken for the same reason `read:font` takes it. The ids here are the order FileMaker happened to stamp the seeded built-ins in, identical in every fresh file and meaningless after any edit, whereas the keyword is what a caller recognizes and what FileMaker's own UI sorts by. The sort is case-insensitive.

A fresh file has ELEVEN members, not ten: ten named built-ins plus `fmplugin`, the plug-in cross-file-security keyword. A caller enumerating "the built-ins" from a list of ten alone will be off by one, so `builtIn` is computed against the full set, case-insensitively.

Built-in descriptions read as `""`. The display text FileMaker shows for a built-in keyword is not available to this CLI without risking disagreement with a localized FileMaker Pro showing the same file. The empty string is an accurate statement about what the file stores.
`fmreauthenticate10` ships ENABLED on a fresh file, granted to all three built-in privilege sets; every other keyword ships off. That is FileMaker's default, not something this CLI does.

`enabled` reflects the current, possibly uncommitted, state of the grant rather than a cached value, which is the only correct answer inside a single op stream where a read may follow an uncommitted write.

Nothing on a describe is optional: every key -- `description`, `sharing`, `privilegeSets`, `enabled`, `builtIn` -- is always present, and `privilegeSets: []` is a real answer rather than a missing one. Names in it are sorted, so two targets can be compared. The one exception is `hidden`, reported for `fmapp` and `fmwebdirect` and absent for the rest, because the other keywords have no list of shared files to be hidden from -- reporting `false` for them would answer a question that does not apply.

An unknown `name` is `not_found` with closest-name suggestions and an unknown `id` is `not_found` with none. Lookup by name is case-insensitive (`FMREST` finds `fmrest`), because it goes through FileMaker's own name index.
A read never opens either privilege catalog for writing, so `read:extendedPrivilege` cannot dirty the file.

nodes.title: update:extendedPrivilege
nodes.summary: Turns a keyword's access on or off, or changes its grants, description or name

keys.summary: the keyword to update -- the address, and not itself a change
the new keyword to give it, refused on a built-in whose name gates a protocol
the description to store instead of the current one
who holds the keyword: every privilege set, only the listed ones, or nobody
the privilege sets to grant the keyword to, by name, replacing any others
whether to keep the file out of the list of shared files clients browse, sharing still on

semanticChecks: 'privilegeSets' applies to sharing 'specified' only: 'all' is a LIVE grant that also covers privilege sets created later and 'off' grants to nobody, so either alongside an explicit list is two contradictory instructions and is refused rather than resolved. A list with NO 'sharing' is not a contradiction -- it means 'specified'.
notes: RENAMING A BUILT-IN IS REFUSED with `unsupported_operation`, and the refusal is this CLI's rather than FileMaker's: measured 2026-07-26, the rename SUCCEEDS in FileMaker and leaves the member present with its grants intact -- but the protocol the keyword gates is matched on the keyword STRING, so the channel it gated silently goes dark. A caller who thought they were relabeling would have switched off FileMaker Pro networking, the Data API or ODBC/JDBC. It is refused only once the name has been resolved to a specific member, not upfront: the verb is legitimate on a custom keyword, and only that resolution can tell which kind of member is being addressed.

`privilegeSets` REPLACES the list; it is not a delta. Sending one set to a keyword granted to two leaves it granted to one. The change is applied as a DIFF -- revoke what is leaving, grant what is arriving -- rather than remove-all-then-re-add, so a set present in both lists is never momentarily revoked, which on a hosted file would be a live outage.

Switching to `specified` CLEARS the list first (measured 2026-07-27: switching from another sharing state empties the grant list). So when both `sharing` and `privilegeSets` are sent, the state is set first and the grants applied after -- the reverse order would discard them.
An unknown privilege set name is `privilegeSet_not_found` with suggestions, and NOTHING is applied.
A `privilegeSets` list with no `sharing` key is sent to FileMaker as `specified`, the same as on a create.
A rename onto an existing name is `extendedPrivilege_exists`; the comparison is case-insensitive and goes through FileMaker's name index.

`hidden` IS THE ONE KEY HERE THAT IS NOT A PROPERTY OF THE KEYWORD. It is a setting of the FILE, and it is accepted on `fmapp` and `fmwebdirect` only -- the two keywords whose clients browse a list of shared files. Any other keyword is `unsupported_operation`. It does not turn sharing off: the file stays shared and stays openable by name, it is just not offered in the list.

`hidden` alone is enough to satisfy "at least one change", and an update that sends only `hidden` does not write the keyword catalog at all -- so it cannot fail partway and leave a grant half-applied. It still honours `--dry-run` and still rolls back with the rest of the run.
Changing `hidden` needs the same privilege FileMaker requires to change sharing at all; without it the answer is `permission_denied` rather than a silent success.
seeAlso: `fm-cli help forms` — what JSON a key's type, its requiredness and a filter's tag each take

nodes.title: externalDataSource
nodes.summary: this file's stored pointers to other data sources, which a cross-file occurrence resolves through
notes: A REFERENCE IS A STORED STRING, NOT A CONNECTION. Nothing in this catalog resolves one, so a reference to a file that does not exist, or to a host that is not up, is created, described and renamed without complaint. That is FileMaker's own behaviour -- a data source can be defined before its target exists -- and it is what keeps a read from doing I/O the caller did not ask for.

A RELATIVE `file:` PATH IS THE DEFAULT, and usually the only entry a reference needs. `file:Other.fmp12` is resolved from the REFERRING file's own location, so one reference holds however the solution is deployed -- both files hosted on the same server, both sitting in one folder locally, or the whole thing copied from development to production -- and nothing has to be rewritten when it moves. `fmnet:/host/Name` hardcodes a server, and is for the two cases where the files genuinely are not together: the target is hosted on a DIFFERENT server than this file, or this file is local and the target is hosted. Reach for it only for one of those, because a hardcoded host is what breaks when the solution is moved or copied.

`fmnet:/` TAKES A SINGLE SLASH. That is FileMaker's own path syntax, and it is NOT the two-slash `fmnet://host/Name` URL this CLI's own `--file=` takes -- the resemblance is what invites copying a `--file=` target straight into `paths`, which would be wrong twice over: wrong spelling, and a hardcoded host where a relative `file:` path was wanted. The engine REFUSES the two-slash form outright -- `create_failed`, "the engine rejected the path list", and the batch rolls back (measured 2026-09-13). Path SYNTAX is checked; whether the file exists is not, so the mistake that survives a write is a well-formed path naming the wrong place.

PATHS ARE STORED DECODED, so write -> read is not byte-identity. FileMaker accepts percent-hex and decodes on the way in: `file:a%20b.fmp12` reads back as `file:a b.fmp12`. A path with no prefix at all is normalized rather than refused, which is the same effect from the other direction -- `Other.fmp12` reads back as `file:Other.fmp12` (measured 2026-09-13), confirming a relative file path is what the engine assumes when told nothing. What round-trippability needs is a FIXED POINT, and it is one -- feeding a read result straight back into a create stores and reports the same string (measured 2026-07-26). Prefer sending already-decoded paths.

ODBC authentication, stored auth tokens, Magnolia attributes and the ODBC filter properties are real FileMaker file-reference capabilities this CLI deliberately does not expose: the first three are credential material, which does not belong in a schema-diffing tool's plaintext NDJSON, and the last is a sub-object shape of its own, orthogonal to identifying the source.

nodes.title: read:externalDataSource
nodes.summary: Lists every file reference, or describes one by name or id
notes: `filter` NARROWS a listing and does nothing else. Every reference that comes back is reported in exactly the shape an unfiltered listing gives it, so a filter changes which members appear and never what any one of them says.
`total` is how many references the file holds, unfiltered; `returned` counts the ones that came back, so a filtered listing reports both what matched and what it was matched against.

Matching ignores case, and `name` is a pattern: `*` stands for any run of characters and `?` for exactly one, so `Invoices*` and `*_backup` both work. There is no escape, so a reference whose name really contains `*` or `?` cannot be matched literally.

A filter matching nothing is `ok` with `"items":[]` and `returned` of 0 -- a filter is a test each member is put to rather than an address, so a pattern nothing matches is not `not_found`. A misspelled pattern therefore looks exactly like an empty catalog.

`name` filters an UNDETAILED listing, which is `{name,id}` and nothing else. `dsn` filters the DETAILED item instead, so it is refused with `invalid_field` unless the same op also sends `detail`:true. `sourceType`, `paths` and `hasData` remain unfilterable at any depth.

A describe reports `sourceType` -- filemaker, odbc, magnolia or unknown -- which is READ-ONLY and derived from the path's scheme. There is no verb to set it: you write an `odbc:` path and the reference becomes one. It is not called `type` precisely because `type` is settable elsewhere in this CLI, and reusing the name would invite a caller to try.

`hasData` is always reported, so a named reference with no stored path is VISIBLE rather than reported as an ordinary reference that happens to have zero paths -- one written by something other than this CLI can be in that state.
`dsn` appears on an ODBC reference only, and only when non-empty. It is derived: it is the body of the `odbc:` path, not a separate attribute, which is why it is not accepted as input on any verb.
An unknown name or id is `not_found` -- the GENERIC code, matching read:valueList. The write verbs use `externalDataSource_not_found` for the same miss.
Reading never opens the referenced file: for an `fmnet:` path, opening it would mean a network connect and possibly a login, as a side effect of what the caller asked to be a read.

nodes.title: field
nodes.summary: The columns of a base table -- a data type plus the storage, auto-enter and validation attributes
notes: TWO type-ish keys, and they answer different questions. The op's `type` is the DATA type (text, number, date, ...); `options.fieldType` is whether the field stores its value, calculates it, or summarizes another field. `"type":"calculation"` is not a thing, and it answers `unknown_field_type` rather than being quietly reinterpreted.

Every formula slot -- `options.calculation`, `options.autoEnter.calculation`, `options.validation.calculation` -- is the object `{text, context}`, and the `context` names a table OCCURRENCE rather than a base table. A formula resolves its field references from an occurrence's position in the relationship graph, so text alone is under-specified; the two names coincide only while a table has just its auto-created occurrence.

EVERY REFERENCE TO ANOTHER FIELD IS THE OBJECT `{occurrence, field}`, never a bare name: FileMaker stores a table alongside every one of them, and field ids start at 1 in every table, so a name with no occurrence resolves against whichever table is asked and answers with a real, plausible, wrong field. That is `options.autoEnter.lookup.source`, `options.summary.field` and `options.summary.auxiliaryField`. The two summary keys may omit `occurrence`, which means this field's own table; a lookup's source may not.
A field is addressed by `table` + `name` on every write verb, because names and ids are both per-table. A `read:field` by id alone works, but a `table` sent with it still scopes the lookup.
