nodes.title: create:field
nodes.summary: Creates a field in a table, with its storage, auto-enter and validation attributes

keys.summary: the table to add the field to
the field's name, unique within the table
the field's data type
the field's attributes; an absent key takes FileMaker's default
the originating add-on UUID to stamp on it, grouping everything one add-on created
where the field goes in this table's own field order, 0-based; absent appends

semanticChecks: `options.global` with `options.stored` false is refused: a global field holds a value and an unstored one does not, and FileMaker accepts the pair without complaint
`options.autoEnter.increment` may not be 0 -- a serial that never advances

`options.primaryKey` true is refused when another field of the same table already carries the mark. FileMaker keeps the mark as an object tag it documents as unique within the table and leaves to its caller to keep that way; two of them would leave FileMaker's own "which field is the primary key" answer depending on which it enumerated first.

`options.summary.auxiliaryField` is required precisely when FileMaker's own `SummaryDef::NeedsAuxField()` says the type/`variant` combination needs one -- a variant `average` or `fraction` summary -- and refused otherwise; neither half of that condition can be a declared `requiredWhen`/`forbiddenUnless` because it depends on TWO keys together, not one key's value.

`options.summary.field` may not carry an `occurrence`: FileMaker does not summarize a field in another table, and its engine refuses one outright. `auxiliaryField` MAY carry one. Both are the same object shape so that a read can report what a file holds, so the difference is checked against the value rather than declared on the key.

`options.autoEnter.lookup.source.occurrence` must be RELATED to `context` and must not BE `context`. FileMaker restricts its own lookup dialog to exactly that, and the engine reports nothing for a pair with no relationship between them -- it just never copies anything -- so the check has to be here.

`options.validation.range` bounds are STRINGS that FileMaker reads in the field's own data type, so a date field's bounds want date literals and a number field's want numerals -- the pair is passed through as written and never parsed here.

`options.autoEnter.next` is a string rather than a number so a serial may carry a non-numeric prefix. How the stored value advances is FileMaker's, not this CLI's: `increment` is handed over as given.

`options.autoEnter.type` `previous` is FileMaker's "value from the last visited record" and takes no operand -- there is nothing to carry beside it, which is why no sibling key is required with it and every one of them is refused.

`ownerId` is 32 hexadecimal digits, hyphenated or not, in either case; braces around it are refused. A read reports it back hyphen-grouped and upper case, so a caller comparing a read-back stamp against the string it sent has to fold case and drop hyphens -- the two are equal as UUIDs and different as strings.
notes: For a `summary` field the op's `type` is IGNORED: a summary's data type is derived by FileMaker from the field being summarized. The key is still required by the op shape; `"number"` reads most honestly.

`options.autoEnter.alwaysEvaluate` true is refused unless the field ends up with a LIVE auto-enter calculation -- `type` `calc`, or `calculationEnabled` true beside another mode -- checked against the field's resulting state rather than the request: the bit is stored only while the calculation is enabled and reads back false otherwise.

`options.autoEnter.calculationEnabled` false is refused alongside `type` `calc`, which is that same bit raised: the pair asks for the calculation and turns it off at once. To keep a formula the field does not evaluate, send `type` `none` with the `calculation`.

`options.indexing` is a REQUEST. FileMaker raises it when another option needs an index -- `validation.unique` forces at least `minimal` -- so an explicit `"indexing":"none"` alongside `unique` reads back `minimal`. It is never lowered.

AN OPTION THE FIELD WILL NOT KEEP IS REFUSED rather than quietly dropped, the same rule `options.validation` follows below. FileMaker rewrites a field's options on commit down to what that field can carry: a calculated field enters no value of its own, so it takes no `autoEnter`; a summary field takes no `autoEnter`, no `global`, no `indexing` and no `autoIndex`; a date, time or timestamp field cannot auto-enter a serial; a container field cannot auto-enter a constant or a serial and cannot be indexed; `stored` false belongs to a calculated field, which is the only kind FileMaker leaves unstored; `container.external` belongs to an ordinary container field; and neither a global nor an unstored field is indexed. Which auto-enter VARIABLES survive depends on the data type too -- a date field takes only the creation and modification date.

`options.validation` IS NOT a request in the same sense: a setting the field will not keep is refused rather than quietly dropped. FileMaker rewrites a field's validation on commit down to what that field can carry -- a calculated or summary field carries none at all, and its own field dialog offers none either; a container keeps neither `unique`, `existingValue`, `range`, `valueList` nor the strict data checks; a date or timestamp drops `strictNumber` and `strictTimeOfDay`; a time drops `strictNumber` and `strictFourDigitYear`. Sending one of those as `false` asks for nothing and is never refused, which is what keeps a `read:field` result feeding straight back in.

FIVE VALIDATION SETTINGS ARE CLEARED BY SENDING `null`: `options.validation.maxLength`, `range`, `valueList`, `calculation` and `messageCalculation`. Each turns its rule on by being present, and nothing else in the object turns one back off -- unlike the flags, which take `false`, and `validation.message`, which takes `""`. `null` is refused on every other key, so it cannot clear something the request did not name. Clearing a rule leaves the number or formula behind it stored but unreachable, exactly as unticking the box in FileMaker Pro's field dialog does; sending a value again brings the rule back.
A create whose options are rejected at either layer leaves NOTHING behind: the half-built field is deleted, so the next `read:field` will not list a name the caller was told had failed.

`Self` is available in all three calculation slots, so a formula can refer to the field it is attached to. `validate:calculation` with the matching `"for"` checks a formula the same way, which is how it can be validated before it is sent.

`options.comment` and `options.aiAnnotation` are two DISTINCT stored values -- FileMaker's field "Comment" and 22.1's separate per-field AI annotation, which FileMaker prefers when describing a field to a model or to OData. Setting one does not touch the other.

A `name` that is legal but cannot be used unquoted in a calculation (a leading digit, a leading or trailing space, or certain punctuation) is still created as given -- `result` then also carries a `warnings` array saying so. `warnings` is absent, not `[]`, on a clean name.

`position` PUTS THE FIELD SOMEWHERE IN ITS TABLE'S FIELD LIST -- FileMaker's own Manage Database > Fields order for that table, 0-based, the one a person drags rows around in. Absent appends, which is what a create does on its own. `result` reports where the field landed.

ASKING FOR ONE HAS A FILE-WIDE SIDE EFFECT, and it is FileMaker's rather than this CLI's: the field list's "View by" setting is a single preference for the whole FILE, not a per-table one, so ordering one table's fields switches every table's field list into custom order. FileMaker Pro does exactly the same thing when a developer drags a field row on one table's page. Without it the order would be stored and never shown, and FileMaker would rebuild it from creation order on the first drag.

A FIELD MAY BE NAMED BY ITS ID INSTEAD OF BY NAME, and exactly one of the two is given. This is for a field whose occurrence is based in a file this one cannot open -- unreachable, absent, or not authorized -- because a NAME only becomes a key by being looked up in that file's field catalog, and there is nothing to look it up in. An id needs nothing opened. NOTHING VALIDATES AN ID: a wrong one writes a reference to a field that may not exist, exactly as `tableId` on create:tableOccurrence does, so prefer the name whenever the file can be reached. A read reports the id in place of the name ONLY when it could not resolve the name, so a read can always be fed straight back in.

AN AUTO-ENTER LOOKUP NAMES TWO OCCURRENCES, and they are different ones. `context` is where the lookup RUNS -- an occurrence of this field's own table, holding the record being filled -- and `source.occurrence` is the RELATED occurrence the value is copied from. FileMaker's Lookup dialog has the same two popups, "starting with table" and the relationship it travels; naming one occurrence for both describes a lookup that commits and never fires.

A lookup takes the id spelling on its source field -- `options.autoEnter.lookup.source.fieldId` -- but never on `context` or `source.occurrence`, which need none: an occurrence is a member of THIS file's catalog and resolves whatever state the file it points at is in.
seeAlso: `fm-cli help forms` — what JSON a key's type, its requiredness and a filter's tag each take

nodes.title: read:field
nodes.summary: Lists a table's fields, or describes one field in full
semanticChecks: a `filter` naming no attribute is refused: it would narrow nothing, and answering it with the whole listing is indistinguishable from a filter that matched every field
notes: A describe writes `options` in FULL canonical form -- every attribute that applies, defaults included -- so the result feeds straight back in as a `create:field` input.

The round trip holds ONE WAY ONLY. A describe round-trips into a create; a create does not round-trip into a describe, because FileMaker normalizes on write and a read reports defaults the request left out. Never diff a read against the request that produced it.

Attributes whose ABSENCE is meaningful appear only when set: `calculation` on a calculated field, `summary` on a summary field, `autoEnter.next`/`increment`/`generate` on a serial, `validation.maxLength`/`range`/`calculation` when their flag is on.

FileMaker's auto-enter options are independent CHECKBOXES, so one field can carry several at once while `autoEnter.type` names one. The one reported is the one FileMaker's own serializer reports, in its order: a creation/modification variable, then a serial, then the value from the last visited record, then constant data, then a calculation, then a lookup. A field carrying both constant data and a calculation therefore reads as `constant`, which is what FileMaker's own field dialog shows as the value the field enters. The formula still comes back under `autoEnter.calculation`, because it is reported off the stored slot rather than off the mode -- so a create fed the result keeps both, and neither is silently dropped. `autoEnter.calculationEnabled` is what tells you whether that formula EVALUATES: `type` cannot, having already been spent naming the option FileMaker reports.
A stored formula whose `context` no longer names a live occurrence is reported as NO calculation rather than as one with an empty context, which is a shape this CLI's own parser refuses.
A listing carries `{name,id,type,table,position}` per item and no `options`; `summary.field` renders as `{"field": <name>}`, with an empty name if that field is gone.

`position` is the field's index in FileMaker's own Manage Database > Fields order for this table, 0-based, reported by a listing and by a describe alike. A listing is still ordered BY ID, so sort on `position` for FileMaker's own sequence. It is absent for a field the table's order list has no entry for, which is not the same as being first.

EVERY FIELD REFERENCE REPORTS ITS OCCURRENCE, because the engine stores one: `autoEnter.lookup.source` always, and `summary.auxiliaryField` when the file holds a reference to a related table. A reference to this field's own table omits `occurrence` entirely, which is the only spelling of that a create takes back. Where the name cannot be resolved -- a field in a file this one cannot open -- `fieldId` appears in place of `field`.

`filter` SUBSETS a listing and never changes an item's shape: a field that comes back carries exactly what it would without a filter. `table` is still what chooses which table's fields are listed, and a filter narrows that listing rather than replacing it.

Every attribute inside `filter` must match, so two of them narrow further than one. `total` stays the table's whole field count and `returned` counts what came back, so a caller can see how much the filter excluded.

Matching is case-insensitive. `filter.name` is a pattern: `*` stands for any run of characters and `?` for one, so `"*date*"` is the way to ask for names CONTAINING "date". There is no escape for a literal `*` or `?` in a name.

A filter that matches nothing is `ok` with `"items":[]` and `"returned":0`, never an error -- a filter is a predicate and not an address, so a value naming something no field has is an empty result rather than `not_found`. An unknown `table` is still `table_not_found` with suggestions.

`filter.type` is the DATA type (text, number, date, ...). Narrowing a listing to the calculated or summary fields is `filter.fieldType` instead, and it needs `detail`:true: that attribute lives only on the detailed item, so asking for it without `detail` is refused rather than answered with an empty result.
Reads never mutate and always report `ok`/`error` regardless of `--dry-run`.

nodes.title: update:field
nodes.summary: Renames, retypes and re-options one field

keys.summary: the table holding the field
the field to change
the name to give it
the data type to change it to
the attributes to change; an absent key is left as it is
moves the field to this index in this table's own field order, 0-based

semanticChecks: an `options` object that is present but sets nothing does not count as a change, so an update carrying only `"options":{}` is refused
`options.global` with `options.stored` false is refused: a global field holds a value and an unstored one does not, and FileMaker accepts the pair without complaint
`options.autoEnter.increment` may not be 0 -- a serial that never advances

`options.primaryKey` true is refused when ANOTHER field of the same table already carries the mark, which is create:field's rule read against the table as it now is: re-asserting it on the field that already has it is fine.

`options.summary.auxiliaryField` is required/refused by the same `NeedsAuxField()` combination create:field's semanticChecks describes -- checked against the field's resulting type/`variant`, not the request alone.
`options.summary.field` may not carry an `occurrence`, and an auto-enter lookup's `source.occurrence` must be related to `context` without being `context` -- both as create:field describes them.

`options.validation.range` bounds are STRINGS that FileMaker reads in the field's own data type, so a date field's bounds want date literals and a number field's want numerals -- the pair is passed through as written and never parsed here.

`options.autoEnter.next` is a string rather than a number so a serial may carry a non-numeric prefix. How the stored value advances is FileMaker's, not this CLI's: `increment` is handed over as given.
notes: `options` is a PARTIAL edit: only the keys present are written and everything else on the field survives, including attributes this CLI does not model -- the option and validation bitfields are read-modify-written, never rebuilt.

The two create-only completeness rules are relaxed here, which is the whole difference between the two `options` views: `{"fieldType":"calculated"}` alone is a legitimate reassertion on a field that already carries a formula.

One rule is evaluated against the field's RESULTING state rather than the request: `options.autoEnter.alwaysEvaluate` true needs the field to be a calc auto-enter AFTER the update, so asking for it in the same op that switches to `serial` is refused.

AN EDIT CAN COST THE FIELD VALIDATION IT ALREADY HAD, and that is honoured with a `warnings` array naming every setting lost rather than refused: retyping a number field to a date drops its `strictNumber`, and making a field calculated drops all of its validation. The request is a coherent one FileMaker Pro answers the same way. NAMING one of those settings as a request in the same op is still refused, as create:field describes.

THE SAME GOES FOR OPTIONS the edit puts out of reach: retyping a number field to a date drops a serial `autoEnter`, turning a field into a summary drops its `autoEnter`, `global`, `indexing` and `autoIndex` at once, and retyping a container to text drops `container.external`. Each is warned about by name. `options.indexing` is warned about only when the field ends up with NO index at all -- FileMaker drops a number field's word index because a number field has none to want, and the answer is still `all`.

TO CONSENT TO EITHER LOSS AND SILENCE ITS WARNING, turn the settings off in the same op, sending each as the value the field ends up with: `false` or `true` on a flag, `"none"` on `autoEnter.type` or `indexing`, `""` on `validation.message`, and `null` on the five validation settings that take it. The warning is for a loss the caller did not ask for, so asking for it is what removes the warning.
The field's id is unchanged. An `options` FileMaker rejects leaves the field as it was -- the member is aborted, not committed.
A `newName` that is legal but cannot be used unquoted in a calculation is still applied as given, with a `warnings` array on `result` saying so -- same as create:field.

`position` MOVES THE FIELD in its table's field order and is a change in its own right, so `{table, name, position}` is a complete update. `result` reports where it ended up rather than what was asked for, so a shift the engine declined does not read as a success. It carries the same file-wide "View by" side effect create:field describes.

notes: READ-ONLY, and enforced structurally rather than by convention: there is no font write method at all, so there is no font write path for a bug to reach.
Entries appear when layout content references a typeface and disappear when that content does. The way to change which fonts a file has is to change its layouts.

`--dry-run` does not soften the three refusals. "dry-run" means "this would have worked; I just did not commit it", which is a promise an impossible op cannot keep -- and a batch that passed the pre-flight check and then failed the real run is the failure `--dry-run` exists to catch.

nodes.title: read:font
nodes.summary: Lists the interned fonts, or describes one by name or by id
notes: Ordered by NAME, not by id. A font id is interning order -- the position in which layout content happened to first mention the typeface -- so it is neither stable across files nor meaningful to a caller, whereas the name is the thing they recognize. Every other catalog orders by id.

An empty catalog is `{"items":[]}` with `total` and `returned` of 0, never an error. A file with no layout content has no fonts, and that is an ordinary answer; a caller enumerating fonts should not have to tell "no fonts" apart from "the op failed".

`filter` NARROWS a listing and does nothing else. Every entry that comes back is reported in exactly the shape an unfiltered listing gives it, so a filter changes which entries appear and never what any one of them says.
`total` is how many fonts the file has, unfiltered; `returned` counts the ones that came back. A filtered listing therefore reports both what matched and what it was matched against.

Matching ignores case, and `name` and `postScriptName` take the wildcards `*` (any run of characters) and `?` (exactly one). There is no escape, so a literal `*` or `?` in a name cannot be matched. `codeSet` is matched whole rather than as a pattern.
EVERY attribute given must match, so naming two of them narrows the listing further rather than widening it.

A filter matching nothing is `ok` with `"items":[]` and `returned` of 0. A filter selects rather than addresses, so a name no font carries is an empty answer and not a `not_found` -- which also means a misspelled pattern looks exactly like a file that never used that typeface.

An entry with no recorded character set carries no `codeSet` and so never matches a `codeSet` filter, including one asking for the value it would most likely have had. "Nothing was recorded" is a different fact from any particular character set, and the listing reports it as an absence rather than a guess.
`name` is matched CASE-INSENSITIVELY, because the lookup goes through FileMaker's own name index rather than a hand-rolled scan. Leading and trailing whitespace IS significant.
An unknown `name` is `not_found` with closest-name suggestions. An unknown `id` is `not_found` with none: suggesting names for a numeric miss would not help.

`id` is OMITTED, never reported as 65535. That value is FileMaker's "this is not a real font" sentinel; publishing it would look exactly like an addressable id, and a caller feeding it back would get an unexplainable `not_found`. Listings drop such entries outright. Ids start at 0, so 0 is a real id.

`codeSet` is omitted, never guessed. When FileMaker cannot determine a character set it says so, a different fact from any particular character set. A value outside the known set is reported as `unknown(<n>)` rather than dropped.

`postScriptName` is the entry's STORED name -- the one recorded in the file, not one synthesized from the fonts installed on the machine running this CLI. Synthesizing one would make the output a property of the reader rather than of the file. An entry interned for a face the host lacks therefore reports "", which is kept rather than omitted: it is a successful read of a file that records no PostScript name.
A describe returns the same object a listing's item carries, plus `"kind":"font"`, so an item taken straight out of a list carries exactly the keys a describe of it will.
A read never opens the font catalog for writing, so it cannot dirty the file.

notes: Every key on an item's page is printed as its name, its form, its requiredness and a sentence. `Forms` and `Conditions` below say what those two middle columns mean; `Filters` says what the bracketed tag on a listing's keys means.

`<key>`, `<value>` and `<group>` in the requiredness column are placeholders here. On a real key they are filled in with the name of the other key the rule is about, the value it must have, and the name tying a set of keys together.

A key may carry more than one rule, joined with `; ` -- `requiredWhen:type=calc; forbiddenUnless:type=calc` is one key that is required with that type and refused without it. Every rule listed has to hold.

nodes.title: graphNote
nodes.summary: The notes drawn on FileMaker's relationships graph -- text, a box, its colours and its type
notes: A note is PRESENTATION, not schema: no query resolves differently because of one. It is stored in the file and survives a reopen, and it is what tells the next person why a region of the graph is shaped the way it is.
Notes have NO NAMES and no order of their own. A note is addressed by the `id` or the `uuid` a create or a listing reported -- the `id` within one file, the `uuid` across copies of it.
Notes are independent of the graph's nodes: deleting a table, an occurrence or a relation leaves every note exactly where it was, even one that was describing what just went away.

Notes are drawing objects on the relationships graph rather than named members of a catalog, so there is nothing for a name to address and no name to report. semanticChecks: 'bounds' width and height must be greater than zero: a note zero points wide is invisible on the graph, which is the worst way to find that out.

'backgroundColor' and 'textColor' are six or eight hex digits with an optional leading '#' -- "#FFF2A8" or "#FFF2A880", where the last pair is alpha. Six digits mean fully opaque. Three-digit shorthand is not accepted.

'font' is a typeface NAME, as `read:font` reports it -- "Helvetica", "Courier New". Naming a typeface the file has not used before adds it to the file's font list, which is what FileMaker does when a font is picked from its own menus. `fontId` is reported by a read but is not accepted by a write: it can name one specific face of a family, and a write is deliberately limited to the families a person picks from.
notes: `bounds` IS REQUIRED. Nothing places a note automatically, so a note without one would sit at the origin with no size -- present but invisible.

Leaving `backgroundColor` out gives the note FileMaker's own note yellow. It is not an error, and it is deliberately not left unset: an unset background is fully transparent, which would put an invisible note on the graph.

`font`, `fontSize` and `textColor` are LEFT UNSET when omitted, unlike the background. An unset one draws in FileMaker's own default, which is a note a person can read, so there is nothing to default and a read reports the key as absent.

A SECOND NOTE WITH THE SAME `text` IN THE SAME `bounds` IS REFUSED with `graphNote_exists`, and the error names the existing note's `id` and `uuid` so it can be updated instead. That is what makes re-running a create safe: a replay reports the refusal rather than quietly stacking a duplicate note on top of the first. Only both together count as a duplicate -- the same wording elsewhere on the graph is an ordinary second note, since a region label often repeats.
`result` is the whole note. Keep the `id` or the `uuid`: they are the only ways to address the note again.

nodes.title: layout
nodes.summary: The Layouts menu: the views records are seen through, and the folders and separators around them
notes: Names are NOT unique -- FileMaker permits duplicates and accepts them silently -- so a name naming two members is `ambiguous` with the candidate ids, and every write reports the layout's `id`.

A folder is a Begin/End bracket PAIR of catalog members rather than one member that owns them, which is why `type` is a create-time decision, why a folder delete takes both markers, why a folder copy copies a whole RUN of the display order, and why a folder cannot be moved.

A SEPARATOR IS A LAYOUT NAMED "-", detected by name because FileMaker stores no separator flag -- measured 0 on every member of every real file tested. FileMaker's own Save As XML derives it the same way, and the `script` catalog derives its separators identically. A FOLDER named "-" stays a folder. A separator otherwise reads and writes exactly as a layout does, occurrence and theme included, because that is what it is.

Seventeen object kinds are writable and `type` lists them. The one that is not is the CHART, readable through `read:layout`'s `detail` only. That is why an update ADDS, CHANGES and REMOVES named objects rather than replacing the set: a wholesale replace would delete the objects this CLI cannot recreate.

A button is writable AS AN OBJECT -- its geometry, its name, the text on its face -- and its ACTION is one script step, written as `action`: the same step object a `contents` read reports and the same object one line of a script's `body` is. Sixteen of FileMaker's step ids cannot go on a button, because FileMaker itself refuses them there, and those are the flow-control and engine-state steps. An existing button's action is PRESERVED by an edit to anything else about it, so a button on a layout someone else built is safe to move, rename and relabel.

Writes are committed to the file rather than held in memory for the session, the same as `script` writes. Verified in a second process: names, occurrence, custom-order position, folder nesting and the whole object store including portals all read back.

Script triggers come at TWO LEVELS and this catalog reaches both. A LAYOUT's own are the twelve events a layout stores, reported by `read:layout` and set by `scriptTriggers` on a create or `setTriggers` on an update. An OBJECT's are eight different events, reported on the object by `read:layout` with `detail` and set by `setTriggers` inside an `updateObjects` entry. The two vocabularies do not overlap, so naming one level's event at the other is refused. The FILE-level events (File Options' OnFirstWindowOpen and friends) belong to no layout at all.

refusedInputs.reason: it was the older spelling of 'baseWidth', which is the name a describe reports the layout's own width under. Send 'baseWidth' instead.
it was the older spelling of 'bodyHeight', which is the name a describe reports the body part's height under. Send 'bodyHeight' instead.

semanticChecks: 'bounds' width and height must be greater than zero: a zero-sized object is invisible on the layout, which is the worst way to find that out. A LINE is the exception -- one of the two may be zero, which is what makes it horizontal or vertical. On an 'updateObjects' entry the kind is not known until the 'id' resolves, so a zero extent there is refused by the engine with the kind the id landed on, rather than by the schema.
'baseWidth' and 'bodyHeight' must be greater than zero: a zero-wide layout or a body with no room for an object is not a mistake this CLI will make quietly.

'width' and 'height' were the older spelling of 'baseWidth' and 'bodyHeight' and are no longer accepted. One name per setting: 'baseWidth' and 'bodyHeight' are what a describe reports these two under `geometry`, so a value read can be handed straight back.
An object inside a portal must be of type 'field': a label there would repeat on every row, and FileMaker allows no portal inside a portal.

'text' belongs to a 'label' and to a 'button' -- the same characters in the same place, which is why one key serves both. It is REQUIRED on a label and OPTIONAL on a button, because a button with nothing written on it is ordinary and an empty text object is almost always a mistake. On any other kind it is refused rather than dropped. A button inside a BUTTON BAR is the one case where those characters are stored somewhere else -- FileMaker keeps a segment's label in a different slot from a free-standing button's face -- and the key is the same either way, because which slot to write is FileMaker's decision and it makes it from the parent.

'objects' belongs to a kind that HOLDS OTHER OBJECTS, and seven do: 'portal', 'tabControl', 'slideControl', 'tabPanel', 'slidePanel', 'buttonBar' and 'group'. What each one accepts is FileMaker's rule rather than this CLI's -- a control holds only its own kind of panel, a bar holds only buttons, a portal holds only fields, and a panel or a group holds anything except another panel of its own sort. An 'objects' on any other kind is refused rather than dropped, and so is a child the object it is going into will not hold.

A 'tabControl' and a 'slideControl' must be created WITH their panels, and a 'buttonBar' with its segments, so 'objects' is required and may not be empty on those three. FileMaker's own model permits a control with no panels, and its accessors do not survive one -- a later read of that layout fails rather than reporting an empty control. A 'group' and a 'portal' may be created empty, which is a reasonable state while a layout is built up over several ops.

On an entry that CREATES an object -- 'objects' or 'addObjects' -- 'parent' is the `id` of an object that ALREADY EXISTS and that holds other objects, and it is how something gets inside one after the fact: a field into a tab panel, a button into a popover, anything into a group. It is refused on an entry nested inside another entry's 'objects', where the enclosing entry already says where the object goes. An id naming an object that holds nothing is refused with the kind it landed on.

A 'tabPanel', a 'slidePanel' and a SEGMENT take no 'bounds'. A panel's rectangle is its control's, which FileMaker keeps equal as the control is resized, so resizing the CONTROL is what resizes its panels. A segment's is the bar's rectangle divided by the number of segments, and is never stored at all. Sending 'bounds' for either is refused rather than accepted and then overwritten.

'title' is the text on a TAB PANEL's tab, and on 'updateObjects' also a POPOVER's heading. It is stored as a LITERAL and quoted into a calculation for you, which is what FileMaker's own Tab Control Setup dialog offers. A slide panel has no title at all -- FileMaker stores none. A title that is a live CALCULATION is reported by `read:layout` with `detail` as 'titleCalculation' and cannot be written here; an entry that does not mention 'title' leaves such a calculation alone.

A 'graphic' is a PICTURE, and 'picture' is the file it shows -- a path on the machine running this CLI, read while the op runs. THE BYTES ARE COPIED INTO THE FILEMAKER FILE and the path is not stored, so the picture travels with the file and this works against a file hosted on FileMaker Server. FORMATS: JPEG, PNG, GIF, BMP, TIFF, HEIC, WebP, AVIF and PDF. FileMaker Pro also takes EPS and Windows metafiles, through conversions that live in Pro rather than in the database engine, so those are refused here. ONE COPY PER DISTINCT PICTURE: FileMaker keys its image library by a checksum over the picture's data AND its filename, so the same FILE sent twice, or an object duplicated, leaves one copy that both objects show -- which `read:layout` with `detail` says outright, as the same 'pictureId' on both. Two files whose bytes match under different names are two copies.

A 'graphic' with no 'bounds' takes THE PICTURE'S OWN SIZE, corrected for its DPI, which is what FileMaker Pro's Insert > Picture does. A 288-pixel-wide screenshot tagged 144 DPI lands 144 points wide, and the same pixels tagged 72 DPI land 288. Send 'bounds' for anything exact -- the picture is then scaled into the rectangle, and so it is after an 'updateObjects' that replaces the picture without saying anything about 'bounds'.

A 'button' AND A 'group' each take 'action', which is the ONE script step it performs when clicked, written as the step object `read:layout` with `detail` reports for it -- 'stepID' says which step and the remaining keys are that step's own. It is the same object one entry of a script's 'body' is, so `fm-cli help script steps` is the vocabulary for both. Absent makes a button that does nothing, which is what FileMaker Pro's own Insert > Button gives you and is a perfectly ordinary button; '{"stepID":0}' says the same thing explicitly and is what a read reports for one. A GROUP TAKES THE SAME KEY because FileMaker turns a group into a button by giving it a script step -- select several objects in Pro and choose Button Setup and what you have is a group with an action. A group with no action is an ordinary group rather than a broken button, and a read reports '{"stepID":0}' for one. A 'popoverButton' takes no 'action' at all: opening its popover is the whole of what it does.

SIXTEEN STEPS CANNOT GO ON A BUTTON, and FileMaker itself is what refuses them: the flow-control steps (If, Else, Else If, End If, Loop, Exit Loop If, End Loop), the engine-state ones (Allow User Abort, Set Error Capture, Set Layout Object Animation, Set Revert Transaction on Error, Set Script Triggers), the transaction steps (Open/Commit/Revert Transaction) and the comment step. One of those is refused naming the step, and nothing is written. A NAME IN A CALCULATION MUST ALREADY BE IN THE FILE when the op runs: a table or field created by an EARLIER op in the same stream is not yet visible to the calculation parser, so put such a write in a later invocation -- the same limitation `update:script`'s bodies have.
A 'webViewer' needs EXACTLY ONE of 'url' and 'urlCalculation': 'url' is a literal address that is quoted into a calculation for you, 'urlCalculation' is the formula itself.

Two objects on one layout MAY share a name, and a write that leaves them that way says so in 'warnings', naming every id holding the name. FileMaker permits the pair, so it is not refused; what it costs is addressability, because 'objectName' matches every object holding the name rather than reporting an ambiguity -- so a later edit or removal naming it reaches all of them. A copy made by 'duplicateObjects' cannot cause this unless its own 'objectName' says so: an unnamed copy is named by FileMaker's own generator, which picks a name no other object holds.

A trigger's 'event' is one of the twelve LAYOUT-level events: OnLayoutEnter, OnLayoutExit, OnLayoutKeystroke, OnLayoutSizeChange, OnRecordLoad, OnRecordCommit, OnRecordRevert, OnModeEnter, OnModeExit, OnViewChange, OnGestureTap, OnExternalCommandReceived. Object-level events belong to an OBJECT rather than to the layout, so they are refused here and are set through an `updateObjects` entry's own 'setTriggers'; file-level ones (OnFirstWindowOpen, OnTimer) are stored on no layout at all.

'modes' holds any of 'browse', 'find' and 'preview', and absent means all three. It is not a cosmetic setting: a trigger has no separate on/off switch, so the modes ARE where it is enabled, and '[]' is refused because a trigger that fires nowhere is not something to ask for.

A trigger's 'parameter' is a CALCULATION, exactly as it is in FileMaker Pro's own dialog, and it is parsed in the layout's table occurrence. So a literal string needs quoting -- "parameter": "\"done\"" -- and an unquoted bare word is refused rather than quietly turned into one, which is what the engine's own auto-quoting would have done.

`ownerId` is 32 hexadecimal digits, hyphenated or not, in either case; braces around it are refused. A read reports it back hyphen-grouped and upper case, so a caller comparing a read-back stamp against the string it sent has to fold case and drop hyphens -- the two are equal as UUIDs and different as strings.
notes: `tableOccurrence` is required for a layout and refused for a folder. A layout is a view of one occurrence, and one based on nothing is a layout the Data API can read nothing through; a folder marker's stored occurrence key is zero-length, so setting one would assert a property a folder does not have. A folder takes no `theme` and no `objects` either, for the same reason.
`objectsAdded` is not `objects.length`: a field WITH a label is two objects, so the two numbers differ by design and the count is reported rather than left to be inferred.

A bare `field` name resolves against the occurrence of whatever it sits in -- the layout's, or the portal's for a field inside one -- which is the same defaulting FileMaker's calculation grammar does. The qualified form is what `read:layout` with `detail` emits, so read -> create round-trips.

`label` has THREE states: absent labels the field with its own name (what FileMaker's New Layout assistant does), "" means no label, and a string is that text. A field inside a PORTAL gets no automatic label, because a label in a portal row repeats on every row.

Geometry is automatic unless `bounds` is given: fields stack down the body with labels in a left-hand column. Mixing is fine, and the automatic cursor skips past explicitly placed objects rather than overlapping them. For a Data API layout none of it matters -- the Data API reads the field list, never the geometry.

`baseWidth` and `bodyHeight` size the LAYOUT, and are for the person who opens it in FileMaker Pro rather than for the Data API, which never sees geometry. Absent, both take the engine's defaults (1024 wide, a 500pt body), which is what every layout this CLI wrote before these keys existed got. A caller placing more fields than fit legibly should widen or deepen the layout rather than shrink the fields.

A LAYOUT IS NEVER LEFT WITHOUT A THEME, and that is a rule rather than a default: a themeless layout renders with the style system's bare fallbacks instead of a theme. Absent, `theme` takes the file's MOST-USED theme so a new layout blends in. A name the file has never had is installed if it is one of FileMaker Pro's built-ins, so a file carrying no themes of its own is not a dead end -- and a file `--create` made already carries FileMaker Pro's default, installed for the layout it was created with. Only a name that is neither in the file nor built in fails, and a custom theme cannot be created.

DUPLICATE NAMES ARE ALLOWED, unlike create:script. FileMaker permits them (a real file ships two layouts named "-") and FileMaker accepts them silently, so refusing would make this CLI unable to reproduce a file it can read. The cost is that the layout may not be addressable by name afterwards, which is why `id` comes back.

`type`:"folder" makes a Begin/End bracket PAIR of catalog members, created atomically. `type`:"separator" makes an ordinary layout that FileMaker draws as a divider in the Layouts menu, and it takes the name "-" -- the name is the whole of what makes it one, because FileMaker stores no separator flag (measured 0 on every member of every real file tested). It still needs a `tableOccurrence`, because it is a layout.
A `folder` that does not exist is an error rather than an auto-create, and the message names the failing path component.

A label's `text` is stored LITERALLY: "<<Occurrence::Field>>" produces a label displaying those characters, not a merge field. Reading merge labels authored in FileMaker does work (read:layout with `detail`).

A `webViewer`'s address is a CALCULATION, which is what FileMaker's "Web Address" box is.`url` is the friendly spelling -- a literal address, quoted for you, with any quote or backslash in it escaped -- and `urlCalculation` is the formula, which is what a per-record address needs and what `read:layout` with `detail` reports back. A field inside `urlCalculation` must be named "Occurrence::Field": a layout object's calculation stores no table context, so there is no occurrence for a bare name to resolve against. A formula FileMaker cannot parse fails the op rather than storing a web viewer that shows nothing.

A `webViewer`'s six settings are FileMaker's Web Viewer Setup checkboxes. Absent, they take the set that makes the object usable -- interaction, progress bar and status messages on, automatic URL encoding on, Find-mode content and JavaScript-to-FileMaker-scripts off. That is NOT what FileMaker Pro's palette produces: dragging one out there stores no settings at all and relies on you clicking through its dialog, which this CLI has no equivalent of.
A `webViewer` with no `bounds` is placed 300 x 150 points down the body, which is FileMaker's own default size for one. It gets no label: a caption belongs to a field.

A `webViewer` is created with NO BORDER on any side, whatever the layout's theme would draw. A web viewer is a window onto a page and the page draws its own frame, so a theme's line around one reads as a grey rectangle framing the page. There is no key for it: add a border in FileMaker's Inspector, where its width, colour and radius can be set too.

THE FOUR SHAPES -- `line`, `rectangle`, `roundedRectangle`, `oval` -- carry nothing but `bounds`, `objectName` and `anchors`. Fill, border and corner radius belong to the THEME, which is why there is no key for any of them and why a rounded rectangle needs no radius: FileMaker Pro's own Insert menu sets nothing on the shape it has just drawn either. With no `bounds` each gets FileMaker Pro's own size on a row of its own -- 100 x 50 points, and a `line` 100 x 0, which is a horizontal line rather than a number left out.

A `line` runs from its box's TOP-LEFT corner to the bottom-right, which is what FileMaker Pro's Insert > Line draws. The direction is not on the wire: `read:layout` with `detail` reports a line's `bounds` and not its endpoints, so a direction key could not be read back. The cost is that a line whose box is both tall and wide always slopes down to the right; a horizontal or vertical line pays nothing, because the two corners meet once the box has no height or no width.

A `button` PERFORMS ONE SCRIPT STEP, or nothing, and `action` is that step: `{"type":"button","text":"Go","action":{"stepID":1,"script":"Invoice","parameter":"\"hi\""}}` performs a script, `{"stepID":6,"layout":"Summary"}` goes to a layout. Absent `action` makes a button that does nothing, which is exactly what FileMaker Pro's own Insert > Button gives you before you fill in its dialog and is a perfectly ordinary button; "Do Nothing" is one of the choices in that dialog too.

THE STEP OBJECT IS THE ONE `read:script` AND `read:layout` REPORT, so `fm-cli help script steps` is where a step's own keys are listed and nothing about it is layout-specific. A CALCULATION inside it is a calculation, as it is in FileMaker Pro -- a literal string is quoted, `"invoice"` and not `invoice`. FileMaker's "Specify: by name" variant of Perform Script is writable like any other slot, and a button using it cannot be told which script it will reach, because that is decided when the button is clicked. A button gets NO ICON: an icon is a reference-counted library member, and this CLI does not write one.

AN EXISTING BUTTON'S ACTION IS PRESERVED when `updateObjects` changes its `bounds`, its `objectName` or its `text` -- including the sixteen steps that cannot be written onto a button in the first place. Moving, renaming or relabelling a button authored in FileMaker Pro is safe: the action is left exactly as it was, not cleared. `removeObjects` does delete it along with the button, the same as removing a label deletes its text.

A `button` with no `bounds` is placed 100 x 28 points on a row of its own. The width is FileMaker Pro's own; the height is not -- Pro measures the theme's button font and sizes the button to it, so the two differ deliberately, and 28 points is the row height this CLI uses for everything else it places. Send `bounds` for anything exact. A button gets no label object beside it: its text is on its face.

Seventeen object kinds are writable, and `type` lists them. ONE FileMaker object type is READ by `read:layout` with `detail` and cannot be created: the CHART, which is why an unknown `type` is a vocabulary miss rather than a missing feature. A chart is the same engine object as a web viewer and is unwritable for good: its definition is a serialised chart model rather than a formula and six flags.

SEVEN KINDS HOLD OTHER OBJECTS, and each takes its children in `objects`: a `portal` (fields only), a `tabControl` and a `slideControl` (panels only), a `tabPanel` and a `slidePanel` (anything but another panel of the same sort), a `buttonBar` (buttons only) and a `group` (anything). A control is created WITH its panels and a bar WITH its segments, because a control with no panels is a file a later read crashes on. A group may be created empty, the same as a portal, since it is a reasonable intermediate state while a layout is built up.

`objects` GOES ONE LEVEL DEEP. A tab control arrives with its panels and the panels arrive empty; to put a field inside a panel, send a second `addObjects` entry carrying `parent` set to the panel's `id`, which comes back in `createdObjectIds`. So building a populated tab control is two invocations rather than one, because the second needs ids the first mints.

A `popoverButton` MAKES TWO OBJECTS -- the button and the popover it opens -- and both ids come back, the button first. There is no `popover` type word, because a popover button whose popover is missing is corrupt by FileMaker's own rule, so half the pair is not something to ask for. The popover is reported at the layout's TOP LEVEL rather than under its button, which is where FileMaker stores it; put objects in it with `parent` set to the popover's id.

A BUTTON BAR'S SEGMENTS ARE ORDINARY BUTTONS. There is no `segment` type: FileMaker derives "this is a segment" from the parent being a bar, so a bar's `objects` holds `button` entries, each with its own `text` and its own `action`. A segment takes no `bounds` -- they are the bar's rectangle divided by the number of segments -- and neither does a panel, whose rectangle is its control's.

`baseWidth` and `bodyHeight` are the layout's own size: `baseWidth` is the layout's base width and `bodyHeight` is the body part's height, the only part this CLI ever adds. Absent, each keeps its own default rather than the other's -- `baseWidth` whatever the engine assigns a brand-new layout, `bodyHeight` 500 points. `width` and `height` are the older spelling of the two and still work.

`anchors` sets an object's autoresize behaviour -- FileMaker's Inspector "Position" tab. All four true is what makes an object fill the window as it resizes; absent is FileMaker's own default, top+left only, which pins the object in place and resizes nothing. All four keys are required together: a partial `anchors` has no unambiguous reading for a brand-new object. ON A TAB PANEL OR A SLIDE PANEL IT LANDS ON THE CONTROL and on every panel of it, because that is the only place FileMaker stores it and a read of a panel reports its control's -- so two panels of one control cannot be given different anchors, in this CLI or in Pro.

`scriptTriggers` names the SCRIPT, and it must be a script this file already has -- a trigger pointing at nothing is a trigger that cannot run. Put `create:script` earlier in the same stream and the layout can name it. A trigger targeting a script in ANOTHER file can be read but not written: the binding stores a key belonging to that file's own catalog, which cannot be resolved from a name here.
One trigger per event, because that is the file's own shape: a layout's triggers are keyed by event, so naming the same event twice in one `scriptTriggers` array leaves one trigger -- the last one.

A FIELD MAY BE NAMED BY ITS ID INSTEAD OF BY NAME, and exactly one of the two is given. This is for a field whose occurrence is based in a file this one cannot open -- unreachable, absent, or not authorized -- because a NAME only becomes a key by being looked up in that file's field catalog, and there is nothing to look it up in. An id needs nothing opened. NOTHING VALIDATES AN ID: a wrong one writes a reference to a field that may not exist, exactly as `tableId` on create:tableOccurrence does, so prefer the name whenever the file can be reached. A read reports the id in place of the name ONLY when it could not resolve the name, so a read can always be fed straight back in.

ON A FIELD OBJECT the id spelling is two keys, `fieldOccurrence` and `fieldId`, both or neither, each refused alongside `field` -- a field object names its field as a single string rather than as an object, so there is nowhere inside it to put an id. See `update:layout` for the matching address on `removeObjects`.
seeAlso: `fm-cli help forms` — what JSON a key's type, its requiredness and a filter's tag each take

nodes.title: delete:layout
nodes.summary: Deletes a layout, or a folder and everything it brackets

keys.summary: the layout or folder to delete
deletes a FOLDER with everything in it; without it a non-empty folder is `in_use`

notes: A folder is deleted as BOTH BRACKETS, always. Deleting the Begin alone promotes the contents to depth 0 and orphans the End; deleting the End alone means the folder never closes and every later member becomes its child forever. FileMaker reports success for either and cascades nothing.

A non-empty folder is refused (`in_use`) without `recursive`: a folder brackets its contents rather than owning them, so "delete the folder" has two honest meanings and neither is a safe default. Identical treatment to delete:script.

NOTHING checks what referred to the layout. A layout is named by script steps, buttons and portals, and this CLI does not chase those, so a delete can leave a `Go to Layout` step pointing at nothing. FileMaker Pro's own delete warns; this does not.
`result` echoes `{id, name}` with `objectsRemoved` counting the CATALOG MEMBERS removed -- 1 for a layout, and for a folder the Begin, the End and everything between.

THE LAST LAYOUT CANNOT GO (`layout_required`), whether on its own or inside a `recursive` folder delete. Every FileMaker window shows a layout, so a file with nothing to show cannot be opened far enough to be given something -- create the replacement first. Folder brackets and separators do not count as layouts for this.
