refusedInputs.reason: 'type' cannot be updated: a folder is a pair of BRACKET members, so turning a layout into one is a delete plus two creates plus a re-parent of everything meant to be inside. A separator is a layout named "-", so that direction is a rename.

update:layout has no 'objects': that would mean "make the contents exactly this", which would delete the objects this CLI cannot recreate (a chart). Use 'addObjects', 'updateObjects', 'duplicateObjects' and 'removeObjects'.
it was the older spelling of 'baseWidth', which is the name a describe reports the layout's own width under. Send 'baseWidth' instead.
it was the older spelling of 'bodyHeight', which is the name a describe reports the body part's height under. Send 'bodyHeight' instead.

semanticChecks: 'bounds' width and height must be greater than zero: a zero-sized object is invisible on the layout, which is the worst way to find that out. A LINE is the exception -- one of the two may be zero, which is what makes it horizontal or vertical. On an 'updateObjects' entry the kind is not known until the 'id' resolves, so a zero extent there is refused by the engine with the kind the id landed on, rather than by the schema.
An object inside a portal must be of type 'field': a label there would repeat on every row, and FileMaker allows no portal inside a portal.

'text' belongs to a 'label' and to a 'button' -- the same characters in the same place, which is why one key serves both. It is REQUIRED on a label and OPTIONAL on a button, because a button with nothing written on it is ordinary and an empty text object is almost always a mistake. On any other kind it is refused rather than dropped. A button inside a BUTTON BAR is the one case where those characters are stored somewhere else -- FileMaker keeps a segment's label in a different slot from a free-standing button's face -- and the key is the same either way, because which slot to write is FileMaker's decision and it makes it from the parent.

A 'button' AND A 'group' each take 'action', which is the ONE script step it performs when clicked, written as the step object `read:layout` with `detail` reports for it -- 'stepID' says which step and the remaining keys are that step's own. It is the same object one entry of a script's 'body' is, so `fm-cli help script steps` is the vocabulary for both. Absent makes a button that does nothing, which is what FileMaker Pro's own Insert > Button gives you and is a perfectly ordinary button; '{"stepID":0}' says the same thing explicitly and is what a read reports for one. A GROUP TAKES THE SAME KEY because FileMaker turns a group into a button by giving it a script step -- select several objects in Pro and choose Button Setup and what you have is a group with an action. A group with no action is an ordinary group rather than a broken button, and a read reports '{"stepID":0}' for one. A 'popoverButton' takes no 'action' at all: opening its popover is the whole of what it does.

'action' states the WHOLE step and REPLACES what the button held; it is not merged into it. So a key you leave out is that step's default rather than a value carried over -- changing '{"stepID":1,"script":"A","parameter":"\"p\""}' to '{"stepID":1,"script":"B"}' leaves a button with no parameter. That is what makes a change from one step to another safe, because the calculation slots mean different things on different steps. To remove an action entirely, send '{"stepID":0}' -- FileMaker's own "Do Nothing".

SIXTEEN STEPS CANNOT GO ON A BUTTON, and FileMaker itself is what refuses them: the flow-control steps (If, Else, Else If, End If, Loop, Exit Loop If, End Loop), the engine-state ones (Allow User Abort, Set Error Capture, Set Layout Object Animation, Set Revert Transaction on Error, Set Script Triggers), the transaction steps (Open/Commit/Revert Transaction) and the comment step. One of those is refused naming the step, and nothing is written. A NAME IN A CALCULATION MUST ALREADY BE IN THE FILE when the op runs: a table or field created by an EARLIER op in the same stream is not yet visible to the calculation parser, so put such a write in a later invocation -- the same limitation `update:script`'s bodies have.
A 'webViewer' needs EXACTLY ONE of 'url' and 'urlCalculation': 'url' is a literal address that is quoted into a calculation for you, 'urlCalculation' is the formula itself.
'baseWidth' and 'bodyHeight' must be greater than zero: a zero-wide layout or a body with no room for an object is not a mistake this CLI will make quietly.

'width' and 'height' were the older spelling of 'baseWidth' and 'bodyHeight' and are no longer accepted. One name per setting: 'baseWidth' and 'bodyHeight' are what a describe reports these two under `geometry`, so a value read can be handed straight back.

Two objects on one layout MAY share a name, and a write that leaves them that way says so in 'warnings', naming every id holding the name. FileMaker permits the pair, so it is not refused; what it costs is addressability, because 'objectName' matches every object holding the name rather than reporting an ambiguity -- so a later edit or removal naming it reaches all of them. A copy made by 'duplicateObjects' cannot cause this unless its own 'objectName' says so: an unnamed copy is named by FileMaker's own generator, which picks a name no other object holds.

A 'graphic' is a PICTURE, and 'picture' is the file it shows -- a path on the machine running this CLI, read while the op runs. THE BYTES ARE COPIED INTO THE FILEMAKER FILE and the path is not stored, so the picture travels with the file and this works against a file hosted on FileMaker Server. FORMATS: JPEG, PNG, GIF, BMP, TIFF, HEIC, WebP, AVIF and PDF. FileMaker Pro also takes EPS and Windows metafiles, through conversions that live in Pro rather than in the database engine, so those are refused here. ONE COPY PER DISTINCT PICTURE: FileMaker keys its image library by a checksum over the picture's data AND its filename, so the same FILE sent twice, or an object duplicated, leaves one copy that both objects show -- which `read:layout` with `detail` says outright, as the same 'pictureId' on both. Two files whose bytes match under different names are two copies.

A 'graphic' with no 'bounds' takes THE PICTURE'S OWN SIZE, corrected for its DPI, which is what FileMaker Pro's Insert > Picture does. A 288-pixel-wide screenshot tagged 144 DPI lands 144 points wide, and the same pixels tagged 72 DPI land 288. Send 'bounds' for anything exact -- the picture is then scaled into the rectangle, and so it is after an 'updateObjects' that replaces the picture without saying anything about 'bounds'.

'objects' belongs to a kind that HOLDS OTHER OBJECTS, and seven do: 'portal', 'tabControl', 'slideControl', 'tabPanel', 'slidePanel', 'buttonBar' and 'group'. What each one accepts is FileMaker's rule rather than this CLI's -- a control holds only its own kind of panel, a bar holds only buttons, a portal holds only fields, and a panel or a group holds anything except another panel of its own sort. An 'objects' on any other kind is refused rather than dropped, and so is a child the object it is going into will not hold.

A 'tabControl' and a 'slideControl' must be created WITH their panels, and a 'buttonBar' with its segments, so 'objects' is required and may not be empty on those three. FileMaker's own model permits a control with no panels, and its accessors do not survive one -- a later read of that layout fails rather than reporting an empty control. A 'group' and a 'portal' may be created empty, which is a reasonable state while a layout is built up over several ops.

On an entry that CREATES an object -- 'objects' or 'addObjects' -- 'parent' is the `id` of an object that ALREADY EXISTS and that holds other objects, and it is how something gets inside one after the fact: a field into a tab panel, a button into a popover, anything into a group. It is refused on an entry nested inside another entry's 'objects', where the enclosing entry already says where the object goes. An id naming an object that holds nothing is refused with the kind it landed on.

A 'tabPanel', a 'slidePanel' and a SEGMENT take no 'bounds'. A panel's rectangle is its control's, which FileMaker keeps equal as the control is resized, so resizing the CONTROL is what resizes its panels. A segment's is the bar's rectangle divided by the number of segments, and is never stored at all. Sending 'bounds' for either is refused rather than accepted and then overwritten.

'title' is the text on a TAB PANEL's tab, and on 'updateObjects' also a POPOVER's heading. It is stored as a LITERAL and quoted into a calculation for you, which is what FileMaker's own Tab Control Setup dialog offers. A slide panel has no title at all -- FileMaker stores none. A title that is a live CALCULATION is reported by `read:layout` with `detail` as 'titleCalculation' and cannot be written here; an entry that does not mention 'title' leaves such a calculation alone.

A trigger's 'event' is one of the twelve LAYOUT-level events: OnLayoutEnter, OnLayoutExit, OnLayoutKeystroke, OnLayoutSizeChange, OnRecordLoad, OnRecordCommit, OnRecordRevert, OnModeEnter, OnModeExit, OnViewChange, OnGestureTap, OnExternalCommandReceived. Object-level events belong to an OBJECT rather than to the layout, so they are refused here and are set through an `updateObjects` entry's own 'setTriggers'; file-level ones (OnFirstWindowOpen, OnTimer) are stored on no layout at all.

'modes' holds any of 'browse', 'find' and 'preview', and absent means all three. It is not a cosmetic setting: a trigger has no separate on/off switch, so the modes ARE where it is enabled, and '[]' is refused because a trigger that fires nowhere is not something to ask for.

A trigger's 'parameter' is a CALCULATION, exactly as it is in FileMaker Pro's own dialog, and it is parsed in the layout's table occurrence. So a literal string needs quoting -- "parameter": "\"done\"" -- and an unquoted bare word is refused rather than quietly turned into one, which is what the engine's own auto-quoting would have done.
An 'updateObjects' entry takes at most ONE of 'url' and 'urlCalculation'. Neither leaves the web viewer's address as it is.

An 'updateObjects' entry may carry only the keys its object's KIND has: 'field' on a field, 'text' on a label or a button, 'action' on a button or a GROUP, 'tableOccurrence' and 'rows' on a portal, 'title' on a tab panel or a popover, 'picture' on a graphic, 'popoverArrow' and 'showTitleBar' on a popover, 'orientation' on a button bar, the address and the six settings on a web viewer, 'showNavigationDots' and 'enableSwipeGestures' on a slide control, the four Tab Control Setup keys on a tab control, the ten Behavior-section keys and eleven Data-section keys on a field, 'quickFind' on either a field or a label, 'scrollBarVisibility' on either a field or a portal, the four Graphic-tab keys 'graphicSizing', 'maintainOriginalProportions', 'horizontalAlignment' and 'verticalAlignment' on either a field or a graphic, 'optimizeFor', 'autoPlay', 'noContextMenu' and 'preservePdfTransparency' on a field, 'placeholderText' and 'entryCalculation' on a field, 'setTriggers' and 'removeTriggers' on the nine kinds that can hold an object script trigger, 'icon', 'iconSize' and 'iconPosition' on a button or a popover button, 'showHandCursor' on either of those or on a group carrying an 'action', and 'initialRow', 'allowVerticalScrolling', 'scrollBarVisibility', 'allowDelete' and 'resetScrollBarOnExit' on a portal. 'id', 'bounds', 'anchors', 'objectName', 'arrange', 'parent', 'style', 'rotation', 'locked', 'hideWhenPrinting', 'slideLeft', 'slideUp', 'slideBasedOn', 'resizeEnclosingPart', 'tooltip', 'hideCondition', 'applyInFindMode', 'accessibilityTitle', 'accessibilityHelp' and 'accessibilityLabel' apply to every kind, and a SHAPE takes nothing but those. TWO KINDS TAKE NO 'bounds': a panel, whose rectangle is its control's, and a segment, whose rectangle is the bar's divided by the segment count. A SEGMENT ALSO TAKES NO 'anchors' AND NO SLIDING, for the same reason and as in Pro; its 'locked' is accepted and applies to the bar. A key belonging to another kind is refused with the kind the `id` actually names, because the usual cause is a read that has gone stale rather than a typo.

'style' binds an object to a NAMED THEME STYLE by the display name Pro's Inspector shows -- the same name `read:layout` with `detail` reports under 'style'. "" removes the binding and leaves the object on its theme's default for its kind, which is where most objects are. IT CANNOT CREATE A STYLE: the name has to already be in the layout's theme, and a name that is not there is refused with the closest ones that are. ONE NAME CAN BE SEVERAL STYLES -- 'Transparent' is fourteen different styles in Apex Blue, one per kind of object -- so the object's own kind picks which one is applied, and a name defined only for OTHER kinds is refused with the list of what this object can wear. 'style' applies to every kind, unlike the per-kind keys above.

'rotation' takes 0, 90, 180 or 270 -- whole degrees, and nothing in between. FileMaker turns an object in quarter turns only, so 45 is REFUSED rather than rounded to 90: the engine would store it and draw the object upright, and the write would report ok having changed nothing anybody can see. 0 turns an object back upright and absent leaves the angle alone. 'rotation' DOES NOT MOVE OR RESIZE ANYTHING -- the rectangle 'bounds' reports is the stored one whatever the angle is, so a turned field still occupies the rectangle it did before.

'popoverArrow' names which of the POPOVER's OWN edges carries the arrow pointing at its button -- so the popover opens on the OPPOSITE side: 'left' puts the arrow on the popover's left edge and the popover to the RIGHT of its button. The words are FileMaker's own, and a DDR export uses the same ones. IT IS A PREFERENCE RATHER THAN A PLACEMENT: FileMaker tries this edge first when the popover opens and falls back through the others when it does not fit the screen, and in Layout mode the popover keeps its own rectangle, which 'bounds' is what moves. Send it for the POPOVER, not for the button that opens it -- a read reports the popover's `id` on the button under 'popover'.

'showTitleBar' is Pro's own checkbox and reads the way Pro's does: false hides the strip along the top of a POPOVER. IT DOES NOT CLEAR THE TITLE -- the title stays stored and stays reported, so showing the bar again shows it. Send it for the POPOVER rather than for the button that opens it, the same as 'popoverArrow'. 'orientation' is which way a BUTTON BAR runs, 'horizontal' or 'vertical', and it RE-LAYS-OUT EVERY SEGMENT: segment rectangles are the bar's own rectangle divided along whichever axis this names, so one write moves them all without any of them being addressed. It leaves the BAR's 'bounds' alone -- a wide bar turned vertical stays wide and stacks its segments inside the rectangle it has, and 'bounds' is how a caller reshapes it. Send it for the BAR: a SEGMENT is refused, with the bar's `id` named.

'showNavigationDots' and 'enableSwipeGestures' are the two checkboxes in Pro's Slide Control Setup dialog and they read the same way it does: true shows the dots and allows the swipe. THE FILE STORES THE OPPOSITE, as a hidden bit and a disabled bit, so a DDR export's raw `slideFlagSet` number is the negation of these and this CLI converts. Send them for the SLIDE CONTROL, not for one of its panels -- the panels are what a caller clicks in Pro, and a read reports the control as the object they are nested under. NEITHER CHANGES THE CONTROL'S GEOMETRY: hiding the dots does not reclaim the space they occupied, because that space comes from the control's style rather than from the flag.

'initialRow', 'allowVerticalScrolling', 'scrollBarVisibility', 'allowDelete' and 'resetScrollBarOnExit' are Pro's Portal Setup dialog, in the dialog's own sense: true shows the bar, allows the deletion, and resets the scroll on exit. WATCH THE TWO SCROLL-BAR KEYS -- 'allowVerticalScrolling' is the CHECKBOX and 'scrollBarVisibility' is the picker beside it, which is the control the dialog labels "Show scroll bar:". Pro greys the picker out until the checkbox is on and this CLI accepts either alone, so setting the picker on a portal with no bar is allowed and does nothing visible. 'initialRow' is 1-BASED, the row of the found set the portal starts at. THREE OF PORTAL SETUP'S CONTROLS ARE NOT HERE and a portal is not fully described by these five: the SORT and the FILTER are backed by a stored sort order and a calculation rather than by a setting and are not yet writable, and the new-record row is not in the dialog this CLI's engine ships. The alternate-row and active-row checkboxes are styling, which this verb does not cover for any kind.

'locked' is Pro's padlock and 'hideWhenPrinting', 'slideLeft', 'slideUp', 'slideBasedOn' and 'resizeEnclosingPart' are its Sliding & Visibility section. EVERY KIND TAKES ALL SIX, because each is one setting of the word every object carries, and a read reports all six on every object. TWO THINGS ABOUT WHERE THEY LAND. A PANEL DOES NOT OWN ITS OWN: sending any of the six -- or 'anchors' -- for one panel of a tab or slide control applies it to the CONTROL, which is the only place FileMaker stores it, so it affects every panel of that control and a read of any of them reports it. That is what Pro does: select a panel in Pro and the checkboxes shown are the control's. 'anchors' IN A PANEL'S OWN 'addObjects' SPEC LANDS THERE TOO, so creating a panel with anchors sets its control's. AND 'locked' CASCADES -- locking a group locks everything inside it, locking a control locks its panels, locking a bar locks its segments, exactly as Pro's Arrange > Lock does. A SEGMENT REFUSES all of them but 'locked', because its rectangle is the bar's divided by the segment count and it has no position of its own; send them for the bar. 'slideBasedOn' takes effect when 'slideUp' is on and is stored either way, so it is accepted either way.

'tabWidthStyle', 'tabWidthModifier', 'tabWidthUnits' and 'tabsShareSingleStyle' are the stored parts of Pro's Tab Control Setup dialog, and they belong to the TAB CONTROL -- sending one for a tab panel is refused with the control's own id. 'tabWidthModifier' IS ALWAYS IN POINTS whatever 'tabWidthUnits' says: FileMaker stores the width in points and remembers the unit only so its dialog can reopen in the one you last used, so changing the unit changes nothing a user sees. THE MODIFIER IS USED BY THREE OF THE FIVE WIDTH STYLES, the ones whose picker item ends in a number; Pro greys the field out for the other two and this CLI accepts it anyway, because the value is stored either way and becomes meaningful when the style changes. THREE CONTROLS IN THAT DIALOG ARE NOT KEYS HERE, and none is an oversight: the tab list is each panel's own 'title', the default front tab is 'defaultPanel', and the tab justification is styling. NOR IS THE TAB POSITION OR THE TAB HEIGHT: nothing in FileMaker reads the position and its drawing code puts tabs at the top unconditionally, and the height is recomputed from the font every time the layout is laid out, so a write to either would be ignored or overwritten.

'browseEntry', 'findEntry', 'selectContentsOnEntry', 'exitOnTab', 'exitOnReturn', 'exitOnEnter', 'applyVisualSpellChecking', 'quickFind', 'inputMode' and 'keyboardType' are Pro's Inspector Behavior section, and they belong to a FIELD only. THE TWO ENTRY PICKERS TAKE PRO'S OWN WORDS: 'edit', 'selectOnly' and 'viewOnly'. Read them as the picker means them rather than as they might sound -- 'selectOnly' means the contents can be selected and copied but not changed, and 'viewOnly' means the field cannot be entered at all. 'setByCalculation' IS THE FOURTH VALUE AND IT NEEDS 'entryCalculation' BESIDE IT: the picker says the field is entered by calculation and the calculation says when, and a field in that state holding no calculation cannot be entered at all. The two are separate keys because Pro shows them as separate controls, and either can be set without the other. THE THREE EXIT KEYS ARE INDEPENDENT and any combination is legal, including none. 'applyVisualSpellChecking' AND 'quickFind' ARE POSITIVE: true means misspellings are underlined and the field is searched, so 'applyVisualSpellChecking' false is Pro's "Do not apply visual spell-checking" ticked. 'keyboardType' CHANGES NOTHING ON A DESKTOP -- it picks the on-screen keyboard a touch device offers, and 'inputMode' is the input method for Japanese text entry. 'quickFind' IS THE ONE OF THE TEN A LABEL TAKES AS WELL, and what it means there is different: a label's Quick Find searches the FIELDS its merge fields reference rather than its own characters, so it needs at least one merge field naming a field that is itself quick-findable. A label that has none is refused, because FileMaker's own setter ignores the value on such a label rather than storing it. This CLI stores 'text' literally and does not interpret merge syntax, so a label it created can never qualify and only a label authored in FileMaker Pro can take the key.

'control', 'valueList', 'repetition', 'repetitionCount', 'repetitionOrientation', 'allowEntryOfOtherValues', 'allowEditingOfValueList', 'includeShowHideIcon', 'autoComplete', 'showVerticalScrollBar', 'scrollBarVisibility', 'showPlaceholderInFindMode' and 'overrideDataFormattingWithValueList' are Pro's Inspector Data section, on a FIELD -- 'scrollBarVisibility' is the one of them a PORTAL also takes. 'control' AND 'valueList' GO TOGETHER: the drop-down list, pop-up menu, checkbox set and radio button set styles draw their choices from a value list, so setting one of those on a field that has no list is refused rather than leaving a control that shows nothing. Send both in the same entry, or switch between two list styles and the field's existing list is kept. 'selectionList' IS REPORTED BY A READ AND REFUSED BY A WRITE: FileMaker's own picker has no such item. 'repetition' AND 'repetitionCount' ARE A SPAN, Pro's "show repetitions N through M": the first is where the object starts and the second is how many it shows FROM there. Moving the start does not move the count, so a start that would push the object's existing span past the field's last repetition is refused -- send both keys in one entry to move a span that no longer fits. 'repetitionCount' RESIZES THE OBJECT, because more repetitions need more room and FileMaker grows the object the same way -- so it can be refused by the rules that keep an object inside a portal row or a clipping container, and it refreshes an enclosing group's rectangle. Both are bounded by the FIELD's own maximum repetitions, which is Pro's own limit. THE ORIENTATION IS THE SIGN OF ONE STORED NUMBER, so sending one of the two keys keeps whatever the other was. 'showPlaceholderInFindMode' AND 'overrideDataFormattingWithValueList' ARE POSITIVE: true means the placeholder keeps showing and the value list decides the formatting, which is the opposite sense from the bits the file stores.

'graphicSizing', 'maintainOriginalProportions', 'horizontalAlignment' and 'verticalAlignment' are the Graphic tab of Pro's Data Formatting section, and they apply to a container FIELD AND TO A GRAPHIC alike -- both hold the setting in one place and Pro shows both the same controls. 'optimizeFor', 'autoPlay', 'noContextMenu' and 'preservePdfTransparency' are the rest of the same tab and belong to a FIELD ONLY: a graphic cannot show interactive content, so a read leaves those four out on one and a write is refused. THE TWO PRODUCERS DIFFER, which matters to anyone comparing objects: a field this CLI creates reads 'cropToFrame' with proportions false, a field FileMaker Pro creates reads 'reduceToFit' with proportions TRUE, and a GRAPHIC this CLI creates reads 'reduceOrEnlargeToFit' with proportions FALSE -- so a picture put on a layout by this CLI is stretched to the object's rectangle until 'maintainOriginalProportions' is set. 'noContextMenu' IS NOT AN INVERTED KEY: true suppresses the shortcut menu, which is the sense FileMaker's own export writes it in. WHAT PRO GREYS OUT IS STILL ACCEPTED HERE: 'maintainOriginalProportions' with 'cropToFrame', and the interactive-content settings on a field optimized for images or showing several repetitions. FileMaker stores each either way and a Pro-authored field can already hold the combination, so refusing it would make the ORDER of two keys in one entry decide whether a legal end state is reachable.

'tooltip', 'hideCondition', 'accessibilityTitle', 'accessibilityHelp', 'placeholderText' and 'entryCalculation' EACH HOLD A CALCULATION, exactly as the box in FileMaker Pro does. A literal string is a quoted expression: send '"Save this record"', with the quotes, not 'Save this record'. A VALUE THAT DOES NOT PARSE IS REFUSED and the message names the quoted form -- FileMaker's own setters would quote an unparseable word for you, which would store a formula meaning something other than what you sent while this reported success. A FIELD REFERENCE HAS TO NAME ITS TABLE OCCURRENCE, 'Contacts::Name' rather than 'Name', which is what Pro's own field list writes. "" CLEARS the calculation, the way it does for 'title' and 'text'. THE OTHER TWO KEYS OF THE GROUP ARE NOT CALCULATIONS: 'applyInFindMode' is the checkbox beside the hide condition and does nothing without one, and 'accessibilityLabel' is another object's `id`. 'hideCondition' AND 'applyInFindMode' ON A TAB OR SLIDE PANEL LAND ON ITS CONTROL, which is where FileMaker keeps them and what a read of the panel reports back. 'entryCalculation' DOES NOT SET EITHER ENTRY PICKER: a field only consults it once 'browseEntry' or 'findEntry' is 'setByCalculation', and a field in that state with NO calculation cannot be entered at all.

AN `updateObjects` ENTRY'S 'setTriggers' AND 'removeTriggers' ARE THE OBJECT'S OWN, and they are a different set of events from the layout's: OnObjectEnter, OnObjectExit, OnObjectModify, OnObjectSave, OnObjectKeystroke, OnObjectValidate, OnObjectAVPlayerChange, and OnPanelSwitch on a tab or slide CONTROL. The eight are Pro's Set Script Triggers dialog with an object selected. A LAYOUT's twelve go in the update's own 'setTriggers', outside the entry. 'setTriggers' UPSERTS BY EVENT -- an object holds one trigger per event, so re-running the same call is safe and every event you do not name is left alone -- and 'removeTriggers' runs FIRST, so one entry can repoint an event. Removing an event that is not bound is a WARNING rather than an error, because that is what an idempotent re-run looks like. NINE KINDS TAKE ONE: a button, a popover button, a field, a web viewer, a portal, a popover, a tab control, a slide control, and a GROUP once it has an 'action' -- FileMaker makes a group a button by giving it a script step, and an entry that sets 'action' and a trigger together works because the action is written first. Anything else is refused, because the engine's own write would store nothing there and report success. A CHART CAN HOLD ONE AND CANNOT BE WRITTEN HERE: a read reports a chart's triggers and every write to a chart is refused, the same as for its other settings. A trigger's 'parameter' is a CALCULATION, so quote a literal -- "parameter": "\"done\"" -- and 'modes' works exactly as a layout trigger's does. Pro hides the Preview checkbox for an object trigger, saying none of these events is useful there; 'preview' is accepted because the engine's mode test reads the same bit at both levels.

'icon' is Pro's Button Setup icon, as a PATH ON THIS MACHINE, and its BYTES ARE COPIED into the FileMaker file's own image library -- so the path is not stored, and a hosted file carries its icons with it. That is what 'picture' does for a graphic, into the same library. "" TAKES THE ICON AWAY. PNG AND SVG ONLY, and by the FILE'S EXTENSION rather than by what is in it: FileMaker's glyph loader refuses anything else, so a JPEG that 'picture' accepts is not a legal icon. SVG is what Pro's own icons are, and an SVG is rewritten on the way in so FileMaker can recolour it to the theme. 'iconSize' is how big the icon is DRAWN, in points, 8 to 128 -- Pro's own slider range, and nothing to do with the pixels in the file. 'iconPosition' is whether the button draws its label, its icon or both, and which side the icon is on; 'none' is Pro's "Display only a label", which draws no icon and LEAVES THE STORED ICON ALONE. THE THREE KEYS ARE INDEPENDENT, and Pro's dialog is not: Pro picks an icon for you when you choose a position on a button that has none, and clears the icon when you choose label-only. Neither is done here -- both would change something you did not ask for -- so 'iconPosition':'left' on a button with no icon is accepted and reserves the space. AN ICON DRIVEN BY A CALCULATION IS INVISIBLE TO THIS CLI: FileMaker can compute one as SVG, the engine this builds against cannot be asked about it, and such a button reports and accepts these three keys normally -- so a reported icon can be one a formula overrides when the button is drawn. Send them for a BUTTON or a POPOVER BUTTON; a button bar SEGMENT is a button and takes all three, one icon per segment, which is what Pro's Button Bar Setup does.

'showHandCursor' is Pro's "Change cursor to hand over button" checkbox, beside the icon controls in the same dialog. IT GOES WHEREVER FILEMAKER READS IT, which is anything that IS a button: a BUTTON, a POPOVER BUTTON, a button bar SEGMENT, and a GROUP once it carries an 'action' -- FileMaker makes a group a button by giving it a script step, which is the same thing that lets a group hold a script trigger. A group with no action is REFUSED, because the flag would be stored and read by nothing; send 'action' in the same entry and both apply, since the action is written first. PRO SETS IT FOR YOU AND THIS DOES NOT: choosing an action in Button Setup ticks the checkbox and removing the action unticks it, while this CLI changes only what you name. So a button given an 'action' here keeps whatever hand cursor it had.

WHAT HOLDS AN OBJECT IS STATED, NEVER INFERRED FROM ITS COORDINATES. FileMaker stores it as a link, not as a position, so bounds that land squarely on a tab panel move the object over that panel and leave it belonging to whatever held it before -- it then draws on every panel of the control rather than on one, and does not hide or scroll with it. To put an object inside something, send 'parent' with that object's `id`; to take it back out to the layout, send 'parent':0. A move whose bounds NEWLY put an object entirely inside something it is not parented to is refused, and the message names what it landed on so the id is to hand. Overlap on its own is ordinary layout work and is left alone -- a border drawn over a tab control stays where it was put.

'bounds' IS OPTIONAL BESIDE 'parent' AND THE TWO READINGS DIFFER. Left out, the object keeps the place it occupies on screen -- its bounds are rebased against its new parent's origin, which is what "move this into the tab panel" means. Sent, they are the NEW parent's own coordinates and are written as sent. Either way they must fall INSIDE the new parent, because a panel, a button bar and a popover clip their children when they draw: a child outside is not misplaced, it is invisible and cannot be clicked. A GROUP is the exception -- its rectangle is the union of whatever is in it.

THREE KINDS TAKE NO 'parent'. A POPOVER is kept at the layout's top level beside the button that opens it, wherever that button sits, and it is drawn over the layout rather than on it. A TAB PANEL and a SLIDE PANEL are pages of one control and are made by that control, so a panel belongs to nothing else -- move the CONTROL instead. And a button cannot become or stop being a SEGMENT this way: FileMaker keeps a segment's label in a different slot from a free-standing button's face, so the move would leave the characters behind. Add a segment to the bar and remove the button.
'addObjects' must not be empty: an update that changes nothing is a mistake, not a no-op, and atLeastOneOf counts a key's mere presence.
'removeObjects' must not be empty, for the same reason.
'updateObjects' must not be empty either, and neither may one of its entries carry an 'id' and nothing else.
'duplicateObjects' must not be empty either -- but one of ITS entries may carry an 'id' and nothing else, because that is a complete request: it asks for another one of that object.
'setTriggers' and 'removeTriggers' must not be empty either, for the same reason.
notes: `removeObjects` runs BEFORE `addObjects`, so one op can replace an object: remove it, then add it back with different geometry.

THE FOUR OBJECT KEYS RUN IN ONE ORDER: `removeObjects`, then `updateObjects`, then `duplicateObjects`, then `addObjects`. The two that MINT ids run last, so neither an edit nor a removal can be about an object this same op created -- a caller cannot know an id that does not exist when the op is written. The middle positions are observable rather than arbitrary: an added object with no `bounds` is placed below the LOWEST object on the layout, so a move made by `updateObjects` and a copy made by `duplicateObjects` are both things the automatic placement sees.

`updateObjects` addresses ONE object by `id` and nothing else -- none of the four searches `removeObjects` accepts. The reason is a collision: `field` and `objectName` are each both a way to FIND an object and a thing to CHANGE about it, and one key cannot be both without a second `new`-prefixed spelling of half the vocabulary. So every key of an entry means the same thing it means in `addObjects`, and a search that matches two objects cannot silently move both to one place.

`objectsUpdated` counts the `updateObjects` ENTRIES applied, not the objects that ended up different: two entries naming one `id` count two, and they are applied in order, so the second sees what the first did. An entry that resolves and then changes nothing observable -- `arrange`:"bringToFront" on the object already at the front -- still counts, because the entry was applied.

`duplicateObjects` COPIES AN OBJECT THE LAYOUT ALREADY HAS, addressed by `id` alone -- the same address `updateObjects` takes, for the same reason: `bounds` and `objectName` on the entry describe the COPY, and a search matching two objects would have one set of bounds and one name to give both of them. An entry carrying nothing but an `id` is complete, which is where this differs from `updateObjects`: "another one of these" is the whole request.

A COPY IS DEEP AND ITS IDS ARE ALL NEW. A portal is copied with the fields inside it, and every object in the copy gets an `id` of its own, so nothing a caller recorded about the original names any part of the copy. Without `bounds` the copy is offset from the original by 12 points down and right, which is what FileMaker Pro's own Duplicate does -- a copy landing exactly on the original would be indistinguishable from it on the layout. That offset is measured from the ORIGINAL every time, so two copies of one object land on each other; give each its own `bounds` when making several. Without `objectName` the copy's name is derived from the original's the way FileMaker derives it: "Save" becomes "Save Copy", then "Save Copy2". An UNNAMED original gives an unnamed copy, because FileMaker requires no object name and inventing one is not this CLI's to do.

`createdObjectIds` IS HOW A CALLER LEARNS WHAT IT JUST MADE, without reading the layout back. It holds the `id` of every object the op created, grouped by the entry that created it and in the order the two keys ran -- `duplicateObjects`, then `addObjects`. Each group leads with the object its entry named, the copy or the field, and then holds what came with it: the copy's own contents, or the label created beside a field. So it lines up index for index with the request only where every entry made exactly one object, which is the ordinary case for a duplicate and never the case for a field with a label. It is omitted when the op created nothing. `objectsDuplicated` counts OBJECTS rather than entries, the same as `objectsAdded` does -- copying a portal that holds three fields is four -- so the two counts together are the length of that list.

IN AN `updateObjects` ENTRY, ABSENT MEANS LEAVE IT ALONE. That is the opposite of `addObjects`, where an absent key takes a default -- there is no default to take for an object that already exists. `bounds` is the one exception to how little a caller must send: all four numbers are required, the same as on a create, so that one word does not have two shapes on one op. A caller holding an `id` has read the object and has its other numbers.

`arrange` moves an object in its parent's stacking order, which is its position in that parent's child list -- `bringToFront`, `sendToBack`, `bringForward`, `sendBackward`, FileMaker Pro's own Arrange menu. `bringForward` and `sendBackward` move ONE POSITION, which differs from Pro: Pro walks up the stack to the next object that visually OVERLAPS and stops there, so one of its commands can jump several positions or none. A step whose size depends on where things are drawn is not one to build on. An object already at the front of its parent stays there and the op still reports ok.

`baseWidth` and `bodyHeight` are applied AFTER the object changes, so they are measured against the objects the op leaves behind. A `bodyHeight` that would leave an object below the bottom of the body is REFUSED -- FileMaker still stores such an object and the Data API still reports it, so a silent clip would hide a field from the person reading the layout while every other surface insisted it was there. A `baseWidth` narrower than the rightmost object only warns, because FileMaker Pro itself allows and draws an object past the boundary.

A remove that matches NOTHING is an error (`layoutObject_not_found`), and the whole op fails with it -- nothing the op would have changed is written. An address comes from a picture of the layout, so an address that names nothing means that picture is wrong, and the ops after it in the batch are built on the same picture. Read the layout first if you need the run-it-twice shape. `objectsRemoved` is still what to check for how many went, because one address can match several objects (a field may be placed twice).
`removeObjects` entries are applied IN ORDER, and removing an object removes whatever is inside it -- so an entry naming a child of something an earlier entry already removed fails as a miss.

`id` addresses ONE object, by the `id` `read:layout` with `detail` reported for it, and it is the only way to reach an object that has no name, no field spec and no text. An `id` is scoped to ONE LAYOUT: ids count from one in every layout, so one read from a different layout resolves to a different object here or to nothing.

`objectName` and `id` match only the object kinds this CLI can write -- the seventeen `type` lists -- never a chart, even though a chart carries a name and an id too. The update path's safety story is that it never removes what it cannot recreate, and an object of another kind answers `unsupported_operation` rather than being removed, changed or copied -- which is true of an `updateObjects` or `duplicateObjects` `id` as much as of a `removeObjects` one. `objectName` and `id` are also the only ways to address a web viewer, a shape, a button, a panel or a tab control for removal -- none of them has a field spec, text or an occurrence to name it by.

A BUTTON IS EDITABLE AND ITS ACTION IS PRESERVED. Changing a button's `bounds`, `anchors`, `objectName`, `arrange` or `text` leaves the script step it performs exactly as it was: this CLI changes the object in place and never rewrites the parts of it that it does not model. So moving, renaming or relabelling a button someone built in FileMaker Pro is an ordinary thing to do, and there is no need to avoid buttons for fear of breaking them.

A BUTTON'S ACTION IS SETTABLE with `action`, which is the whole step object a `contents` read reports for it: `{"id":7,"action":{"stepID":6,"layout":"Summary"}}` makes the button go to a layout, whatever it did before. It REPLACES the step rather than merging into it, so nothing from the old step survives under a key the new one happens to share -- which is what makes changing from one step to another safe. `{"stepID":0}` is "Do Nothing", so there is a way to remove an action. Any step FileMaker allows on a button can be set here; the sixteen it does not allow are refused naming the step. `removeObjects` deletes the action along with the button.

Changing `tableOccurrence` ORPHANS the fields already on the layout, exactly as it does in FileMaker Pro: each field object keeps its own occurrence and FileMaker renders it as <Table Missing>. Nothing cascades, and a warning says so rather than this CLI silently rewriting objects the caller did not mention.
`folder`:"" moves a layout to the top level. `folder` without `position` appends; `position` without `folder` repositions within the current parent.

An update REPAIRS a layout that has no theme even when it says nothing about themes: the layout gets the file's default theme and the result carries a warning. Layouts created by releases before 2026-07-31 in a fresh file are the population this finds; a layout that already has a theme keeps it.

A FOLDER cannot be moved (`unsupported_operation`). FileMaker's ordering primitive moves one member at a time with no understanding of brackets, so a move would separate a folder from its end marker and report success.
Addressed BY NAME, so a duplicated name is `ambiguous` with the candidate ids -- the same rule the describe follows.

Any write RESTAMPS the member's whole modification record -- `modified.by`, `modified.account` and `modified.timestamp` are all rewritten, not just whatever the request asked to change. The name written to `modified.by` identifies this tool and its build rather than a person, so it does not say who asked for the change even when a person did. Not specific to layouts.
`baseWidth` changes the layout's base width; `bodyHeight` resizes the BODY part specifically, and is refused (`invalid_field`) on a layout with no body part rather than adding one.

`setTriggers` UPSERTS by event and `removeTriggers` runs before it, so one op can repoint a trigger at a different script or narrow its modes. Events the op does not name keep whatever trigger they had -- an update never replaces the whole set, for the same reason it adds and removes objects rather than replacing them.

Removing a trigger for an event that has none is a WARNING, not an error, unlike a `removeObjects` address that matches nothing. The difference is what the request says: an object address names a thing the caller believes is there, while `removeTriggers` names an event that is to end up unbound, and it already is. `triggersRemoved` is what to check when you want certainty.
A FOLDER has no script triggers, so `setTriggers` and `removeTriggers` are refused on one, the same as `theme` and the object keys.

A FIELD MAY BE NAMED BY ITS ID INSTEAD OF BY NAME, and exactly one of the two is given. This is for a field whose occurrence is based in a file this one cannot open -- unreachable, absent, or not authorized -- because a NAME only becomes a key by being looked up in that file's field catalog, and there is nothing to look it up in. An id needs nothing opened. NOTHING VALIDATES AN ID: a wrong one writes a reference to a field that may not exist, exactly as `tableId` on create:tableOccurrence does, so prefer the name whenever the file can be reached. A read reports the id in place of the name ONLY when it could not resolve the name, so a read can always be fed straight back in.

HERE THE ID SPELLING IS TWO KEYS, `fieldOccurrence` and `fieldId`, because a field object names its field as a single string rather than as an object. Both or neither, and each is refused alongside `field`. A describe reports the same pair -- `field.tableOccurrence.name` and `field.id` -- and OMITS `field.name` when it could not resolve it, so an absent name is the signal to address that object by id.

`removeObjects` TAKES THE ID ADDRESS TOO, and that is the half that matters most: a field object whose name cannot be resolved has no other address -- `objectName` reaches it only if one was set, `portal` only inside a portal -- so without it a dangling cross-file reference could not be removed from the layout at all.
seeAlso: `fm-cli help forms` — what JSON a key's type, its requiredness and a filter's tag each take

children.summary: lay the printed report out in columns; null prints in one
fixed page margins in points; null lets the printer decide
parts to add, each placed by its type's own position on the layout
objects to APPEND, placed below whatever is already on the layout
changes to objects already on the layout, each addressed by `id`
objects to COPY, each addressed by `id`; the new ids come back in `createdObjectIds`
objects to remove, applied BEFORE addObjects so one op can replace one
script triggers to set, replacing any the layout already has for that event

keys.summary: which writable object kind this entry is
explicit geometry in points, relative to the parent; absent means auto-placement
the name `Go to Object` addresses; absent leaves the object unnamed, and on a field it also names that field's label "<name>.label"
the field to place, as "Occurrence::Field" or bare for the occurrence of whatever it sits in
the occurrence the field belongs to, with 'fieldId' instead of 'field'
the field's id in the file that holds it, with 'fieldOccurrence'
the text placed beside a FIELD, "" for none; a label object's own text is `text`
a label's text, or a BUTTON's; stored literally, and merge syntax is not interpreted
the occurrence whose RELATED records a portal shows, which is not the layout's own
how many portal rows; 999 is FileMaker's own cap in the Portal Setup dialog
the objects inside a CONTAINER -- a portal's fields, a control's panels, a bar's segments, a group's contents -- whose geometry is relative to it

nodes.title: persistentData
nodes.summary: FileMaker's per-file key/value store for add-on state, keyed by (instance, key)
notes: This is what the `Configure Persistent Data` script step (id 238) writes and the `GetPersistentData` calculation function reads. Before these ops it was unreachable from this CLI, which runs no scripts and whose engine registers no `SetPersistentData` calculation function at all.

AN ENTRY IS ADDRESSED BY A PAIR, never by a name. `instance` is an add-on instance UUID and a scoping parent, much as `table` is to a field: the same key legitimately exists under several instances holding different values, so `key` alone is half an address rather than a lookup that might work.

`instance` IS OPTIONAL, AND THAT HALF OF THE PAIR MAY BE EMPTY. An entry written with no `instance` belongs to no instance, which is a namespace of its own rather than a default or a wildcard: it holds its own entries, and a key in it is unrelated to the same key under any UUID. FileMaker stores the pair as a single name, `key-instance`, so `key-` is an ordinary name -- and this is what the `Configure Persistent Data` script step writes when its instance slot is left blank.

OMITTING `instance` AND SENDING `""` ARE THE SAME WRITE, and describe the same entry. FileMaker stores an empty instance by writing no instance at all, so nothing downstream can tell the two apart. A LISTING IS THE ONE EXCEPTION: there, omitting `instance` spans every instance while `""` scopes to the entries belonging to none.

Addresses are case-insensitive on BOTH halves, and the stored spelling is the first one written: writing `Licence` then `licence` updates one entry, which afterwards still reports `"key":"Licence"` while holding the second value. So a read may get back a different spelling than it asked with. This is the opposite of baseDirectory, which matches exactly -- in both places the rule is to match the way the thing that WRITES matches, and the two engines differ.

AN ENTRY HAS NO `id` ANYWHERE IN THIS CATALOG, in or out. FileMaker files an entry under one name built from the pair, so the pair is the whole identity and the internal serial adds nothing to address by. There is no rename either -- a different pair is a different entry -- so unlike a table or a field, the address a listing reports stays the address forever.

WRITES ARE HELD UNTIL THE RUN COMMITS, like every other write in this CLI: `--dry-run` withholds them and `--abort-on-error` rolls them back, so `"rolledBack":true` covers this catalog too. Within a run they are visible -- a read sees what the ops before it wrote.

nodes.title: read:persistentData
nodes.summary: Lists persistent data entries, or describes one by (instance, key)
semanticChecks: `instance` and `key` share ONE 99-character budget, because FileMaker stores them as a single catalog member name capped at 100 characters, less one separator. Neither half is limited on its own: a 36-character instance UUID leaves 63 for the key
notes: `filter` NARROWS a listing and does nothing else. Every entry that comes back is reported in exactly the shape an unfiltered listing gives it, so a filter changes which entries appear and never what any one of them says.

`total` is how many entries the listing covers, unfiltered; `returned` counts the ones that came back. Under an `instance` scope `total` is that instance's count, because the scope decides what the listing is OF and the filter only chooses within it.

`instance` AND `filter` COMPOSE, and together they are the pairing to reach for: `{"instance":"...","filter":{"key":"licence_*"}}` is "this add-on's licence entries". `instance` is a SCOPE and stays where it is -- it is not a filter attribute, because narrowing before the entries are read is both cheaper and the address vocabulary the catalog already has.

Matching ignores case, and `key` takes the wildcards `*` (any run of characters) and `?` (exactly one). There is no escape, so a literal `*` or `?` in a stored key cannot be matched. Case-insensitivity matches how an address resolves here, so a filter and a describe agree about which entry is which.
EVERY attribute given must match, so naming both narrows the listing further rather than widening it.

A filter matching nothing is `ok` with `"items":[]` and `returned` of 0. A filter selects rather than addresses, so a pattern nothing matches is an empty answer and not an error -- which also means a misspelled pattern looks exactly like an instance with no such entry.

`dataType` matches the type name a listing reports -- `text`, `number`, `date`, `time`, `timestamp`, `container`, `boolean`, `json` or `unknown` -- compared without case. It is a free string rather than a fixed vocabulary, so a value outside that set is an empty answer rather than a refusal, and `unknown` really is what a freshly written entry reports.

`value` IS NOT a filter attribute, though a listing reports it. A stored value is an opaque payload rather than a label, so a pattern over it is guesswork whose empty answer says nothing -- and `*` and `?` occur in real payloads with no way to escape them. Read the entries and search the values if that is the question.

AN UNSCOPED LISTING IS THE ONLY WAY TO DISCOVER AN INSTANCE. Nothing in a .fmp12 enumerates instances -- an instance exists exactly insofar as some entry names it -- so omitting `instance` spans every instance in the file rather than failing.

SEND `"instance":""` TO LIST ONLY THE ENTRIES BELONGING TO NO INSTANCE. This is the one place in the catalog where omitting `instance` and sending `""` differ, and they have to: omitting is already the unscoped listing, and `filter` has no `instance` attribute to narrow with, so `""` is the only spelling that question has.

A DESCRIBE MUST STATE ITS SCOPE even though a write may omit it: `{"key":"licence"}` is `missing_field`, and the entry belonging to no instance is described with an explicit `{"key":"licence","instance":""}`. Forgetting a real UUID is the mistake that gets made, and naming it beats answering `not_found` from a namespace the caller did not mean.

An unwritten instance lists EMPTY rather than answering `not_found`. With no instance catalog to miss against, "unknown instance" and "instance with no entries" are the same state and cannot be told apart.
Ordered as the file stores the entries, not by name: identity is the pair, so there is no single name to sort by.

AN ENTRY HAS NO `id`, and none is reported. FileMaker files an entry under one name built from the pair, so its internal serial says nothing the address does not -- and since a rename is impossible here (a different pair is a different entry), the address never goes stale the way a name does elsewhere. `{"instance":...,"key":...}` is the durable handle.

`instance` is echoed back as an object carrying `name` and NO `id` -- the one place this catalog cannot honour "names in, IDs out", because an instance is not a catalog member and FileMaker assigns it no key.

`value` is always a JSON string, never a bare number, for the same reason evaluate:calculation's is. `dataType` says what the string holds, and a fresh entry can report `unknown` -- that is FileMaker's own default type, not an error.

A miss on `instance` + `key` is `not_found` with suggestions drawn from sibling keys in the SAME instance only; a suggestion from another instance would name an entry the caller's address could never reach.

A READ ANSWERS OVER THE WRITES STAGED EARLIER IN THE SAME BATCH, so it reports what the run would leave behind rather than what is on disk now. Neither read is a write and neither reports `dry-run`: under `--dry-run` a read still answers over the staged writes, which are then discarded rather than reaching the file.

nodes.summary: The named access-level sets accounts are assigned -- built in or custom
notes: ADDRESSING: by name and id, the same shape `extendedPrivilege` uses. Draco::DBPrivilegesCatalog mixes in M_DBNameList (DBEngine/DBPrivileges.h:275).
CUSTOM ORDER IS NOT EXPOSED. DBPrivilegesCatalog also mixes in M_DBCustomList (DBPrivileges.h:275) -- the order Manage Security's own list shows -- and no key here reports or accepts it.

COMMIT DOMAIN: file-user, not schema. The catalog hangs off DBFileUser::GetPrivilegesCatalog() (DBFileUser.h:874), so schema_->Commit() never reaches it -- the same second commit domain `valueList` and `extendedPrivilege` are in, and a write goes through openForWrite().

SCOPE: the file-level privileges (the `fileOptions` object), the description, the password-policy pair, and the whole of Manage Security's Data Access and Design pane -- per-table record access with its limited-access formulas, per-field access, and the per-layout, per-script and per-value-list grants.

SECURITY: [Full Access] is identified by a well-known internal key, never by its (localized) display name, so renaming a set cannot be used to dodge a check. FileMaker already refuses to open any of the three built-in sets for editing or deletion, and this tool never uses the engine's escape hatch for that. No account can be created as, or promoted to, [Full Access] through this tool. EVERY VERB on this catalog, including read, additionally requires the calling session itself to hold [Full Access].

semanticChecks: 'fileOptions.canModifyAccounts' and 'fileOptions.canManageDatabase' grant file-level administrative control: the first lets an account holding this set create and manage OTHER accounts, the second grants control over the database, external data sources and containers. Both are accepted, on create and on update, because neither can reach [Full Access] -- binding an account to [Full Access] requires the caller to hold [Full Access] already, and create:account and update:account refuse it outright.

'create' is accepted only as "yes" or "no". FileMaker offers no limited-by-formula state for creating records -- the Create dropdown has two entries -- so "limited" there would name a grant the product could never show back.

A row access of "limited" and its formula require each other: 'view':"limited" needs 'viewCalculation', 'edit':"limited" needs 'editCalculation', 'delete':"limited" needs 'deleteCalculation', and each formula is refused where the matching level is not, and will not be, "limited".

'edit' is refused where 'view' is "no": FileMaker makes editing unavailable to an account that cannot see the record. The view level checked is the one the request leaves in place, so raising edit on a table whose stored view is "no" needs view raised in the same request.

'allowCreation':true requires the matching new-object access to be modifiable -- 'layouts.newLayouts.access', 'scripts.newScripts.access' or 'valueLists.newValueLists.access'. FileMaker refuses to both allow new objects to be made and forbid changing the ones just made.

'records' on a layout grant requires that layout's own 'access' not be "noAccess": records reached through a layout the account cannot open is a grant with nothing to apply to. The key is declared under 'layouts' only -- a value list has no records reached through it.

'fileOptions.canManageDatabase':true sets record access to "createEditDelete" for the whole set. An account able to change the file's tables and fields necessarily reaches every record in them, so a narrower record grant cannot stand beside it.
notes: Every file already ships [Full Access], [Data Entry Only] and [Read-Only Access]; this creates a FOURTH (or later) set alongside them.

The whole of Manage Security's Data Access and Design pane is settable here: 'records' carries per-table row access with its limited-access formulas and the per-field grants under it, and 'layouts', 'scripts' and 'valueLists' carry the per-item grants plus the 'allowCreation' flag for each. An axis left out is left exactly as a brand-new privilege set starts.

ON EACH AXIS -- 'records', 'layouts', 'scripts', 'valueLists' -- 'access' IS A BULK PRESET, not a default with the overrides left standing: it writes the default AND clears every override beneath it, exactly as choosing from that row's dropdown in Manage Security does. That is why 'access' and the per-item list are refused together. It is also why there is no "custom" to set: FileMaker shows "Custom" on that row when any item carries an override of its own, so the word is derived from the list rather than chosen.

AN ITEM WITH NO GRANT OF ITS OWN CARRIES NO ENTRY AT ALL, which is not the same as any access level. Sending "default" for an item's access removes its override and returns it to the axis default. On a table entry, 'access':"default" drops the whole override -- the four row answers and the field access together -- so the other keys have nothing to add beside it.

'newTables', 'newFields', 'newLayouts', 'newScripts' and 'newValueLists' address the rows Manage Security lists as [Any New Table], [Any New Field] and so on: the grant an item added to the file LATER starts with, before anything gives it one of its own. They are the axis default itself, not an item, which is why none of them takes a name.
A [Full Access] SESSION IS REQUIRED to run this op at all, independent of the ordinary schema-modification lock every op needs -- see the catalog's own notes.
`result` is the ref `{name,id,builtIn}`; `builtIn` is always false for a set this op just created.

nodes.summary: Changes a custom privilege set's name, description, file-level privileges, password policy or access grants

semanticChecks: 'create' is accepted only as "yes" or "no". FileMaker offers no limited-by-formula state for creating records -- the Create dropdown has two entries -- so "limited" there would name a grant the product could never show back.

A row access of "limited" and its formula require each other: 'view':"limited" needs 'viewCalculation', 'edit':"limited" needs 'editCalculation', 'delete':"limited" needs 'deleteCalculation', and each formula is refused where the matching level is not, and will not be, "limited".

'edit' is refused where 'view' is "no": FileMaker makes editing unavailable to an account that cannot see the record. The view level checked is the one the request leaves in place, so raising edit on a table whose stored view is "no" needs view raised in the same request.

'allowCreation':true requires the matching new-object access to be modifiable -- 'layouts.newLayouts.access', 'scripts.newScripts.access' or 'valueLists.newValueLists.access'. FileMaker refuses to both allow new objects to be made and forbid changing the ones just made.

'records' on a layout grant requires that layout's own 'access' not be "noAccess": records reached through a layout the account cannot open is a grant with nothing to apply to. The key is declared under 'layouts' only -- a value list has no records reached through it.

'fileOptions.canManageDatabase':true sets record access to "createEditDelete" for the whole set. An account able to change the file's tables and fields necessarily reaches every record in them, so a narrower record grant cannot stand beside it.
notes: REFUSED OUTRIGHT on [Full Access], [Data Entry Only] or [Read-Only Access] -- the three built-ins -- with `unsupported_operation`. The engine already refuses this (kNotAllowedOnAdministrator); this restates it in the CLI's own vocabulary rather than surfacing the bare engine code. The built-in is identified by its WELL-KNOWN MEMBER KEY, never by name, so a rename cannot be used to dodge the check on a later op.

AN ACCESS AXIS THIS OP DOES NOT NAME IS NOT TOUCHED, and within a named axis only the items listed are. Sending 'records' with two tables in it leaves every other table's grant exactly as it was -- unless 'access' is sent, which clears them all by design.

ON EACH AXIS -- 'records', 'layouts', 'scripts', 'valueLists' -- 'access' IS A BULK PRESET, not a default with the overrides left standing: it writes the default AND clears every override beneath it, exactly as choosing from that row's dropdown in Manage Security does. That is why 'access' and the per-item list are refused together. It is also why there is no "custom" to set: FileMaker shows "Custom" on that row when any item carries an override of its own, so the word is derived from the list rather than chosen.

AN ITEM WITH NO GRANT OF ITS OWN CARRIES NO ENTRY AT ALL, which is not the same as any access level. Sending "default" for an item's access removes its override and returns it to the axis default. On a table entry, 'access':"default" drops the whole override -- the four row answers and the field access together -- so the other keys have nothing to add beside it.

'newTables', 'newFields', 'newLayouts', 'newScripts' and 'newValueLists' address the rows Manage Security lists as [Any New Table], [Any New Field] and so on: the grant an item added to the file LATER starts with, before anything gives it one of its own. They are the axis default itself, not an item, which is why none of them takes a name.

`fileOptions.canModifyAccounts` and `fileOptions.canManageDatabase` may be changed here, as on create. The built-in refusal above is what stops this catalog from ever making a BUILT-IN more dangerous.
A rename onto an existing name is `privilegeSet_exists`; the comparison is case-insensitive.
seeAlso: `fm-cli help forms` — what JSON a key's type, its requiredness and a filter's tag each take

nodes.title: relation
nodes.summary: The edges of FileMaker's relationship graph, joining two table occurrences by field predicates
notes: A RELATION HAS NO NAME. It is an edge, so every verb but `create` addresses it by its `left`/`right` occurrence pair -- in either order -- or by the `id` a previous op reported, and no verb takes a `name`.

The endpoints are table OCCURRENCES, not base tables. The `tableOccurrence` catalog owns the nodes; this one owns the edges between them, and a predicate's fields are resolved against each endpoint's base table.

Each direction's flags act on the FAR table -- `leftToRight` configures `right` -- and each direction may be spelled either as the traversal (`leftToRight`, `rightToLeft`) or as the table its flags govern (`onRightTable`, `onLeftTable`).

A DIRECTION'S SORT ORDER IS `sortSpec`, and `sortRelated` is only the switch that turns it on. They are two separately stored things: sending a `sortSpec` and no `sortRelated` turns the switch on when the order has levels and off when it does not, which is the rule FileMaker's own import applies -- a relation marked sorted with no levels is a state FileMaker discards on the way through. Sending both is taken literally.
Not supported on any verb: setting a predicate's operator per-direction, since a predicate stores exactly one operator regardless of which way it is traversed.

A relation has NO APPEARANCE of its own -- no colour, no position. FileMaker draws the edge between its two endpoint boxes and computes the line from where those sit, so there is nothing on a relation to place or colour. What IS adjustable is the boxes: see `tableOccurrence`'s `graph` for a node's position, colour and view state, and the `graphNote` catalog for the notes drawn beside them.

Replaces a relation's predicates, or merges its per-direction flags

keys.summary: the occurrence at the left end of the edge, not a base table

the join predicates, at least one, each {leftField, op, rightField}
flags governing the RIGHT occurrence's records, named as the traversal to them

flags governing the LEFT occurrence's records, named as the traversal to them

semanticChecks: 'leftToRight' and 'onRightTable' are two spellings of ONE direction, as are 'rightToLeft' and 'onLeftTable'; both spellings of one direction in one op is refused rather than merged or resolved by precedence, because a silent winner is the mistake the alias exists to prevent.
'predicates' must hold at least one entry: a relation with no join predicate matches nothing, and FileMaker will not validate it.
Every operator except the Cartesian product '×' requires BOTH 'leftField' and 'rightField'; '×' joins every record to every record and takes neither, so sending a field with it is refused.

A predicate's 'op' is checked against the join operator vocabulary -- the seven glyphs plus the ASCII aliases -- and an unrecognized one is 'unknown_field_type' with the accepted spellings as suggestions.

Each 'sortSpec.fields' level needs a 'field' (or the 'fieldKey' of one that no longer resolves) and an 'order'; 'descending' is accepted only under 'valueList' and 'predefined', whose word has taken the 'order' slot, and a level carrying a value list must say order 'valueList'. A level naming a field or value list that does not exist is 'field_not_found' or 'valueList_not_found' with suggestions, and any other malformed level is 'invalid_field' naming the level by its position.
notes: A DIRECTION FLAG ACTS ON THE FAR TABLE: `leftToRight` configures the `right` occurrence and `rightToLeft` configures the `left` one. Each direction is a direction of TRAVEL -- "what would be the direction starting from this table?" -- and every flag is phrased about the far end reached by that travel, such as "do we allow creation of RELATED records". With left `Orders` and right `OrderLines`, `leftToRight.cascadeDelete` deletes the ORDERLINES of a deleted order -- the usual intent -- and `rightToLeft.cascadeDelete` deletes the whole ORDER when one line goes. Confirmed against FileMaker's own reporting rather than assumed from how the flag is set: `hasCascade` on read:tableOccurrence is true on the LEFT occurrence for `leftToRight` (measured 2026-08-03).

GETTING THE DIRECTION BACKWARDS CANNOT BE CAUGHT BY read:relation, which reports back whichever direction was asked for -- a transposed pair round-trips perfectly. read:tableOccurrence's `hasCascade` is the one read-based check that can catch it, and only for `cascadeDelete`: there is no way to read back `createRelated`, `cascadeUpdate` or `sortRelated`, and `hasCascade` is one boolean per occurrence across all of its edges. Use `onRightTable`/`onLeftTable` when working from FileMaker's UI or a DDR, which present these options per TABLE -- turning "the option belongs on OrderLines" into a traversal is the inference that inverts a cascade delete.

Omitted flags default to false on create, and both directions are independent. A read always reports all four flags of both directions, so there is no partial state to infer. `sortSpec` is the exception and appears only on a direction that stores one.

`sortSpec` IS THE SORT ORDER ITSELF and `sortRelated` is only its switch. `sortSpec.fields` is the list of levels, outermost first, each naming a `field` as 'Occurrence::Field' and an `order` of `ascending`, `descending`, `valueList` (with the `valueList` it sorts by) or `predefined`; `descending` carries the direction for the latter two, whose word has taken the `order` slot. `maintain` and `blanksLast` are the two checkboxes beside the list. IT IS THE SAME SHAPE `create:script`'s Sort Records step takes, key for key -- one stored structure, one vocabulary -- so a sort order copied from a script body is accepted here unchanged. A `fields` of `[]` means SORT BY NOTHING and clears a stored order; omitting `sortSpec` leaves it alone.

`left` and `right` name OCCURRENCES -- the nodes FileMaker's relationship graph shows -- not base tables. Creating a table mints one same-named occurrence, so for a simple schema the two names coincide, but an unknown one is `tableOccurrence_not_found` with suggestions.
A predicate's fields are resolved against each endpoint's BASE TABLE, so a bad name is `field_not_found` with suggestions drawn from that endpoint rather than from the file.

FILEMAKER VALIDATES THE GRAPH and its refusals are reported as its own: `create_failed` carries FileMaker's numeric error code plus a message naming the cause -- 8201 would create a cycle, 8202 cannot join an occurrence to itself, 8203 the join fields are not of joinable types, 8204 too many tables in the join graph.

ONE RELATION PER OCCURRENCE PAIR. A second relation between an already-joined pair is refused with 8201 in EITHER orientation -- an existing A->B makes both another A->B and a B->A a cycle. That is what makes the endpoint pair a usable address.

On a self-join -- a table joined to its own second occurrence -- either direction's `cascadeDelete` destroys records of the SAME table, so neither is a safe default to copy. State the outcome to a user before applying one.
`effects` is derived read-only output and is refused as an unknown key on a write, so a read body feeds back into a create only with `id`, `kind` and `effects` stripped.

A FIELD MAY BE NAMED BY ITS ID INSTEAD OF BY NAME, and exactly one of the two is given. This is for a field whose occurrence is based in a file this one cannot open -- unreachable, absent, or not authorized -- because a NAME only becomes a key by being looked up in that file's field catalog, and there is nothing to look it up in. An id needs nothing opened. NOTHING VALIDATES AN ID: a wrong one writes a reference to a field that may not exist, exactly as `tableId` on create:tableOccurrence does, so prefer the name whenever the file can be reached. A read reports the id in place of the name ONLY when it could not resolve the name, so a read can always be fed straight back in.

A PREDICATE'S id spelling is `leftFieldId`/`rightFieldId`, each refused alongside its own name key. A Cartesian product takes neither spelling on either side. Reachability is only needed for a side that has a NAME to resolve, so a predicate naming the far field by id does not require the far file to be openable.

So an edge in the way is removed here, by name, before its occurrence can go.

nodes.title: read:relation
nodes.summary: Lists every relation, or describes one by its endpoint pair or id
notes: RELATIONS HAVE NO NAME, and that is a limitation of FileMaker's own schema rather than this CLI's choice: relations have no name list to draw from. It is a reasoned exception to the "names in, IDs out" convention -- the address is either the endpoint pair, which IS named, or the id a previous op returned.

The pair form matches in EITHER orientation: "the relation between A and B" is one edge whichever way it is named, and which endpoint FileMaker stored as `left` is an artifact of how it was created. The output always reports the STORED orientation, not the one asked with.

A LISTING'S `filter` DOES NOT: `left` and `right` each test the STORED endpoint, so `{"filter":{"left":"Contacts"}}` finds the relations where Contacts is the stored left endpoint and NOT the ones where it is the stored right endpoint -- even though the describe address would have found either. That difference is the one thing to know about filtering this catalog.

SO "EVERY RELATION TOUCHING X" IS TWO OPS, and the union of their `items` is the complete answer: one listing filtered `left`:X and one filtered `right`:X, both on the same NDJSON invocation. The two results cannot overlap -- an occurrence cannot be joined to itself -- so nothing is double-counted, and every relation carries an `id` to key on. Asking with one half only is what silently returns a subset.

`filter` NARROWS a listing and does nothing else. Every relation that comes back is reported in exactly the shape an unfiltered listing gives it -- `{id,left,right}` -- so a filter changes which members appear and never what any one of them says.
`total` is how many relations the file has, unfiltered; `returned` counts the ones that came back, so a filtered listing reports both what matched and what it was matched against.

Endpoint matching ignores case and is a whole-name comparison, not a pattern: `*` and `?` have no special meaning in either attribute, because each names an occurrence that exists rather than describing a shape of name.

Both attributes given must match, so `{"left":"A","right":"B"}` narrows to the one edge stored that way round rather than widening to either. A filter matching nothing is `ok` with `"items":[]` and `returned` of 0 -- a filter is a test each relation is put to rather than an address, so an occurrence that is joined to nothing, one that does not exist, and one that is joined only the other way round all give the same empty answer.

A describe reports `predicates` in stored order, plus `leftToRight` and `rightToLeft` with all four flags each -- never a partial object -- so a caller sees the whole state without having to know the defaults. A direction that stores a sort order also carries `sortSpec`, in the shape the write verbs accept it, so a read feeds back in unchanged.

`effects` is DERIVED: each set flag is spelled out as a sentence naming the occurrence whose records it affects, so a caller verifying intent cannot be misled by a direction they read the wrong way round. A relation with no flags set reports an empty list.

A pair or id matching nothing is `not_found` -- the GENERIC code, as `read:table` uses, while the write verbs use `relation_not_found`. That split matches the existing ops rather than introducing a new convention.

`ambiguous` is in the vocabulary for a pair matching more than one relation and is unreachable through this CLI, because FileMaker enforces one relation per pair on every path this CLI uses to create one. It is kept as a guard: a file authored elsewhere could still present two.

`sortSpec` REPLACES like `predicates` do, not merges like the flags: a level has no wire identity either, so supplying one puts the whole list in place of what was stored.

nodes.title: script
nodes.summary: The scripts, folders and separators of the Script Workspace, and the steps a script holds
notes: A FOLDER IS A BRACKET PAIR of real catalog members, not a path string: a Begin member, the contents, and an End member with a junk name. Only the Begin is surfaced, and that is why `type` is a create-time decision with no update.

A SEPARATOR IS A SCRIPT NAMED "-". No separator flag distinguishes it in the data -- that was measured 0 on every member of every file tested -- and FileMaker's own Save As XML emits isSeparatorItem="True" for exactly the members named "-", so it is detected by name and surfaced as its own kind.
Every write here is committed under the file's own user, so a same-process read-back proves nothing and a change is only observable after a reopen.

A step's own key surface is a separate tier: `fm-cli help script steps` lists the step ids by palette group and `help script steps "Set Variable"` describes one. It comes from the same static table the projector and the elaborator read, so it cannot drift from what the CLI accepts.
Each key on a step's page is tagged with a form and a slot group, and those two vocabularies are what decide the JSON to send for it. `fm-cli help script steps forms` defines both.
