semanticChecks: Every `body` entry is an object carrying an integer `stepID`, the discriminator every step is read through; an empty array is a valid empty script.
The `type` vocabulary is 'script', 'folder' or 'separator'; an unknown one is unknown_field_type with did-you-mean.

`ownerId` is 32 hexadecimal digits, hyphenated or not, in either case; braces around it are refused. A read reports it back hyphen-grouped and upper case, so a caller comparing a read-back stamp against the string it sent has to fold case and drop hyphens -- the two are equal as UUIDs and different as strings.
notes: A `folder` that does not exist is `script_not_found` WITH SUGGESTIONS, never an auto-create: naming a thing that does not exist is a mistake rather than a request, which is this CLI's names-in convention everywhere.

A SEPARATOR IS A SCRIPT NAMED "-", not a flagged member -- no separator flag distinguishes it in the data; that was measured 0 on every member of every file tested. `type` exists so a caller does not have to know that convention.

A NAME ALREADY IN USE IS REFUSED as `script_exists`, compared case-insensitively (so `Foo` collides with `foo`) against both scripts and folders. FileMaker itself does not enforce this: it accepts a second member of the same name silently and the duplicate persists, which is why this CLI enforces it instead. Separators are EXEMPT, or they would become uncreatable.
A folder is created as a Begin/End bracket PAIR of members, atomically. The End marker is a real member and is never surfaced by a read.

A body is elaborated BEFORE anything is written, and `--dry-run` does not soften that: an unknown step or an unresolvable field name is reported with every other diagnostic in `error.details` and nothing is created.

WHAT A PASSING DRY RUN DOES NOT PROVE. Step identity, block balance, calculation syntax, every name that has to resolve, and every choice with a named list of values are all checked. What is NOT checked is whether the step MAKES SENSE: no step option is required, none excludes another, and a plain number whose meaning FileMaker does not name is written as given. A step with no target, no value, or two contradictory targets is accepted and stored. So a dry run that passes says the body is well formed, not that it is the script intended -- only reading it back says that. See `fm-cli help script steps forms`.

A projected step carries two structural keys beside its named options. `flags` is the integer holding every on/off option of that step, and `slots` holds every value the step stores that has no name of its own, keyed by kind and then by slot number. Both are accepted on a write: send back what a read gave you, or omit `flags` and let the values written imply their own bits.
`result` is `{name,id}`, the id being FileMaker's -- the "names in, IDs out" convention.
seeAlso: `fm-cli help forms` — what JSON a key's type, its requiredness and a filter's tag each take

keys.summary: the script, folder or separator to delete
deletes a folder's whole subtree; without it a non-empty folder is refused

notes: A NON-EMPTY FOLDER IS `in_use` WITHOUT `recursive`. The alternative -- delete the bracket pair and promote the contents one level -- moves scripts the caller never mentioned.

Both brackets always go together. Deleting one is the measured catastrophe this op exists to prevent: the Begin alone orphans the End, and the End alone makes every later member a child of the folder forever -- and FileMaker allows both without complaint.
Deleting a member leaves the surrounding custom order intact and re-numbers the remaining positions.

nodes.title: read:script
nodes.summary: Lists scripts in FileMaker's custom order, or describes one with its body and problem steps
semanticChecks: a filter needs 'flatten':true. A listing is nested by default, so a filter could only test the top level and would silently drop every match inside a folder.
notes: The listing is NESTED by default and in FileMaker's CUSTOM order, which is this CLI's one knowing divergence from the usual "items ordered by id ascending" -- custom order with folders is the point of this catalog rather than a rendering choice.

`filter` narrows a listing to the members matching every attribute given, and needs `flatten`:true. A nested listing is a tree, so a filter over it could only test the top level and would drop matches sitting inside folders; flattening puts every member in reach. `total` still counts every member the listing covers and `returned` counts what matched, so a filter that matches nothing is an empty `items` rather than an error.

`flatten` returns the SAME members as one flat array instead of a tree, each carrying the `folder` path it sits in -- absolute, "/"-separated, and "" at the top level, so it feeds straight back into create:script's or update:script's own `folder`. Folders and separators are still reported (an empty folder would otherwise be invisible) but a folder carries no `items`, so `type` is the discriminator in every mode. Order is depth-first: a folder, then its contents, which is the Script Workspace read top to bottom.

`position` is PARENT-relative in both modes and is never renumbered across a flattened list, so the same member reports the same number either way and `folder` plus `position` stays the address an ordering write targets.

`folder` scopes a listing to one folder's subtree and composes with `flatten`, which is the pairing to reach for: it answers "every member inside this folder, however deep". `total` then counts that subtree rather than the file. A path component matching two folders at one level is `ambiguous` with the candidate ids rather than a guess at which subtree was meant.

AN AMBIGUOUS NAME IS AN ERROR, NOT A GUESS. Real files hold duplicate names and FileMaker resolves a name lookup to an arbitrary one of them, so a name matching more than one member is `ambiguous` with the candidate ids and `id` is the escape hatch. This CLI can READ duplicates it cannot CREATE.

`body` is a LOSSLESS PROJECTION, not a summary: it elaborates back into a byte-identical tree. An empty script is `[]`, never null and never "" -- the difference between "no steps" and "no body was reported" is what stops a caller overwriting a script it believed was empty.
A describe carries the `token` an `update:script` body write requires. Folders and separators have no body, so they carry no token.
`steps` is reported on the listing AND on a describe, so an empty script can be told from a 200-step one without projecting every body.

EVERY STEP CARRIES A `uuid`, its durable handle, and `update:script`'s `edits` accepts one in place of a step index -- so an edit can name the step it means instead of counting to it. It is read-only: a body may carry it and a write ignores it. Absent only on a step in a file old enough never to have been re-saved by a FileMaker that stores them, and unique within a script rather than within the file, which is all an edit path needs.

A BLOCK STEP CARRIES ITS EXTENT: `"block": {"role": "opener", "start": 3, "end": 11}` on every `If`, `Else`, `Else If`, `Loop`, `End Loop`, `Open Transaction` and `Commit Transaction`. `start` and `end` are the indexes of the steps that open and close that step's block, both inclusive, and they read the same from either end of it -- so a caller learns which `End If` is which without counting openers and closers itself. `role` is opener, branch or closer. Pass `"block": true` on an `update:script` delete addressed at the opener to remove the whole thing. The body stays FLAT: this is derived from the step ids on every read, never stored, and it is read-only on a write. A key is ABSENT where there is nothing true to say: a step with no block role has none at all, a DISABLED block step has none either (FileMaker gives one no role, so a disabled `If` pairs with nothing), and an unclosed `If` reports its `start` with no `end` rather than a guess.

A step whose options this CLI cannot yet read is projected with `opaque: true` and `editable: false` rather than as a plausible-looking complete object. Its stored options SURVIVE a write of the body it appears in -- they are carried across rather than re-authored -- so writing back what you read does not clear them.

A DESCRIBE ALSO REPORTS `problems`: steps whose stored field, layout, script or calculation references no longer resolve, the same live re-check that puts FileMaker Pro's red "problem step" flag on a step in the Script Workspace. This CLI validates a body only at the moment it is WRITTEN (create:script/update:script); a reference broken afterwards -- a later delete:layout or delete:field in the same batch, an edit made in FileMaker Pro, a rename -- used to read back looking clean, and `problems` is what closes that gap. Each entry is `{"path":"/N","step":"..."}`: `path` is a JSON Pointer into `body` (the same addressing a validate/update diagnostic uses), and `step` is copied from that step's own name in `body` rather than named a second way. ALWAYS PRESENT, `[]` when none are found. It does NOT check value-list references or most table-occurrence references, and it says nothing about whether a step makes sense (see the values-unchecked note on create/update) -- an empty array is not a certificate that every reference is good, only that this check found none broken. It is reported on a describe only, never on the listing: computing it needs the whole step list loaded and re-checked, which a describe already pays for while building `body` and a listing across every script in the file does not.

A projected step carries two structural keys beside its named options. `flags` is the integer holding every on/off option of that step, and `slots` holds every value the step stores that has no name of its own, keyed by kind and then by slot number. Both are accepted on a write: send back what a read gave you, or omit `flags` and let the values written imply their own bits.

A path component matching two folders at one level is `ambiguous` with the candidate ids rather than a guess at which subtree was meant.

AN AMBIGUOUS NAME IS AN ERROR, NOT A GUESS. Real files hold duplicate names and FileMaker resolves a name lookup to an arbitrary one of them, so a name matching more than one member is `ambiguous` with the candidate ids and `id` is the escape hatch. This CLI can READ duplicates it cannot CREATE.

`body` is a LOSSLESS PROJECTION, not a summary: it elaborates back into a byte-identical tree. An empty script is `[]`, never null and never "" -- the difference between "no steps" and "no body was reported" is what stops a caller overwriting a script it believed was empty.
A describe carries the `token` an `update:script` body write requires. Folders and separators have no body, so they carry no token.
`steps` is reported on the listing AND on a describe, so an empty script can be told from a 200-step one without projecting every body.

EVERY STEP CARRIES A `uuid`, its durable handle, and `update:script`'s `edits` accepts one in place of a step index -- so an edit can name the step it means instead of counting to it. It is read-only: a body may carry it and a write ignores it. Absent only on a step in a file old enough never to have been re-saved by a FileMaker that stores them, and unique within a script rather than within the file, which is all an edit path needs.

A BLOCK STEP CARRIES ITS EXTENT: `"block": {"role": "opener", "start": 3, "end": 11}` on every `If`, `Else`, `Else If`, `Loop`, `End Loop`, `Open Transaction` and `Commit Transaction`. `start` and `end` are the indexes of the steps that open and close that step's block, both inclusive, and they read the same from either end of it -- so a caller learns which `End If` is which without counting openers and closers itself. `role` is opener, branch or closer. Pass `"block": true` on an `update:script` delete addressed at the opener to remove the whole thing. The body stays FLAT: this is derived from the step ids on every read, never stored, and it is read-only on a write. A key is ABSENT where there is nothing true to say: a step with no block role has none at all, a DISABLED block step has none either (FileMaker gives one no role, so a disabled `If` pairs with nothing), and an unclosed `If` reports its `start` with no `end` rather than a guess.

A step whose options this CLI cannot yet read is projected with `opaque: true` and `editable: false` rather than as a plausible-looking complete object. Its stored options SURVIVE a write of the body it appears in -- they are carried across rather than re-authored -- so writing back what you read does not clear them.

A DESCRIBE ALSO REPORTS `problems`: steps whose stored field, layout, script or calculation references no longer resolve, the same live re-check that puts FileMaker Pro's red "problem step" flag on a step in the Script Workspace. This CLI validates a body only at the moment it is WRITTEN (create:script/update:script); a reference broken afterwards -- a later delete:layout or delete:field in the same batch, an edit made in FileMaker Pro, a rename -- used to read back looking clean, and `problems` is what closes that gap. Each entry is `{"path":"/N","step":"..."}`: `path` is a JSON Pointer into `body` (the same addressing a validate/update diagnostic uses), and `step` is copied from that step's own name in `body` rather than named a second way. ALWAYS PRESENT, `[]` when none are found. It does NOT check value-list references or most table-occurrence references, and it says nothing about whether a step makes sense (see the values-unchecked note on create/update) -- an empty array is not a certificate that every reference is good, only that this check found none broken. It is reported on a describe only, never on the listing: computing it needs the whole step list loaded and re-checked, which a describe already pays for while building `body` and a listing across every script in the file does not.

A projected step carries two structural keys beside its named options. `flags` is the integer holding every on/off option of that step, and `slots` holds every value the step stores that has no name of its own, keyed by kind and then by slot number. Both are accepted on a write: send back what a read gave you, or omit `flags` and let the values written imply their own bits.

nodes.title: forms
nodes.summary: what a step key's form and slot group mean, and what JSON each one takes

forms.writes: `true` turns the option on and `false` turns it off; `null` leaves it unset. Anything else is refused. A read reports the state either way -- `true` or `false`, never an absent key -- so a body you read carries every switch the step has and hands back the same settings it came with

SEVERAL LABELS AT ONCE, because the value is a bitfield rather than a choice -- a window can be a card AND dim its parent AND have a close button. `set` names the flags that are on, from the list on the key's own line, and is what a write acts on. `raw` is the whole stored word as hex, and it carries any bit that has no label: send it back with `set` and those bits survive an edit that only changed `set`. Send `set` alone to write exactly the flags you name and nothing else. If both are sent and they disagree about a LABELLED flag, neither is guessed -- the write is refused

forms.json: one of the labels from the list on the key's own line
forms.writes: THE LABEL, NOT THE INTEGER. A read emits the label and a write takes only the label, so the round-trip is a literal echo. The integer is refused even when it is the right integer -- the diagnostic names the label it meant -- because as long as `1` worked, a body could avoid the vocabulary entirely and never be checked against it. The labels are FileMaker's own, extracted from the serializer behind its Database Design Report

forms.json: whatever the key's slot group takes
forms.writes: FileMaker writes this one with its label showing; that is a display difference only, and it does not change what you send

forms.json: whatever the key's slot group takes
forms.writes: FileMaker writes this one as the step's bare subject, with no label; that is a display difference only, and it does not change what you send
stored as given, and NOT range-checked: the number's meaning is FileMaker's, this CLI has no list of the values it allows, and one it does not recognize is written rather than refused

three distinguishable states: `true`, `false`, and unset. Unlike a bareFlag, which is always one or the other, an unset triState is a state of its own: the key is absent from a read, and `null` on a write clears the choice rather than storing one

slotGroups.holds: a string holding a FileMaker calculation
slotGroups.notes: compiled when the step is written, so a syntax error or an unresolvable field name is refused rather than stored

slotGroups.holds: a string naming a field, written `Occurrence::Field`
slotGroups.notes: resolved against TABLE OCCURRENCES, not base tables

slotGroups.holds: an integer counting from 1, or a string holding a FileMaker calculation
slotGroups.notes: WHICH REPETITION of a repeating field the step is on -- `Contacts::Notes[3]`. Not a slot of its own: it is stored inside the field reference beside it, which is why a 1 is never reported (FileMaker does not show `[1]` either) and why sending one without a field or variable target is refused. The string form is the calculated repetition, `Notes[$i]`, and only a step's PRIMARY reference can carry one -- on the others the value is a number. A 0 is FileMaker's own spelling for 'the repetition is a calculation', reported where the calculation itself is under another key

slotGroups.holds: a string naming an existing external data source, or the literal "Current File"
slotGroups.notes: resolved when the step is written, so an unknown name is refused. "Current File" is not a catalog member -- it is what an unset reference reads back as -- and is written by writing nothing, leaving the step pointed at the current file. A non-string is refused too; to write a raw stored key, send `slots`: {"fileReferenceKey": <id>}

slotGroups.holds: no slot of its own: the value is one bit of the step's `flags` word
slotGroups.notes: the trailing number on the key's line is always 0 and addresses nothing

slotGroups.holds: an integer, or the label string where the key's line lists them
slotGroups.notes: one of the step's numbered value slots. A 0 IS reported back where the key has labels, because there 0 is a value like any other; on an unlabelled slot the number itself is the output and a 0 there is not reported, being indistinguishable from a slot nobody set

slotGroups.holds: a string naming an existing layout or table occurrence, depending on the step
slotGroups.notes: resolved when the step is written, so an unknown name is refused. A non-string is refused too; to write a raw stored key, send `slots`: {"memberKey": <id>}

slotGroups.holds: an integer, or the label string where the key's line lists them
slotGroups.notes: one of the step's numbered number slots -- the same numbering as `calc`, and a slot holds one or the other, never both. A 0 IS reported back where the key has labels: the slot is checked for whether it EXISTS rather than for whether it is non-zero, so an option whose lowest value means something reads correctly when it is set to it. On an unlabelled slot a 0 is not reported, being indistinguishable from a slot nobody set

slotGroups.holds: an array of strings, each a FileMaker path expression such as `filemac:/...` or `$variable`
slotGroups.notes: a list of ALTERNATIVES, tried in order; a single string is accepted and stored as a one-entry list

slotGroups.holds: a string naming an existing script
slotGroups.notes: resolved when the step is written; an unknown name is refused

slotGroups.holds: no slot of its own: the value is the step's single `stepValue` number
slotGroups.notes: a step has exactly one, so the trailing number on the key's line is always 0 and addresses nothing
not a calculation and not parsed

slotGroups.holds: a string: either a field, written `Occurrence::Field`, or a `$variable`
slotGroups.notes: one slot that holds either kind. The field form resolves against TABLE OCCURRENCES, not base tables, so a base-table name is refused even when a field of that name exists

notes: Each line of a step's key table is a key, then its form, then its slot group and a number. The form says what JSON to send; the slot group says what kind of value it is.

The trailing number is the value's SLOT -- its address within the step. It matters for a value that is not individually named: those round-trip under the step's `slots` object, keyed by slot group and then by that number. For a `flag` or a `stepValue` it is always 0 and addresses nothing.

A step read back carries two structural keys alongside its named options. `flags` is an integer holding every on/off option of that step plus the internal markers saying which of its slots are in use, and `slots` holds every value the step stores that has no name of its own. Both are accepted on a write: send back the `flags` a read gave you unchanged, or omit it and let the values you write imply their own markers.

A few steps carry a third key, `spec`, holding options that FileMaker stores as one structured group rather than as separate values -- a Sort Records step's sort order is one. It is an object with a `type` saying which group it is, and it is all-or-nothing: send it to replace the whole group, or LEAVE IT OUT to keep what is already stored. Omitting it never clears it.

No step key is required: a step may be written with no target and no value, and it is stored as given. Two keys that write the SAME slot are refused, though -- only one of them could survive, so which one you meant is asked rather than guessed.
seeAlso: `fm-cli help forms` — the same question for a CATALOG's keys, which carry a type, a requiredness and, on a listing, a filter tag

refusedInputs.reason: 'type' is a create-time decision: a folder is a Begin/End bracket pair of members, so a script cannot become one in place. Delete and recreate. A separator is a script named "-", so that direction is a rename.

semanticChecks: Every `body` entry is an object carrying an integer `stepID`, the discriminator every step is read through; an empty array is a valid empty script.

Each `edits` entry is an object with a string `op` (set, replace, insert or delete) and a `path` that looks like a JSON Pointer -- empty, or starting with '/'. The path's first token is a step index or the `uuid` a read reported for that step. An entry takes no keys beyond op, path, value, expect and block: an unknown one is refused with did-you-mean rather than ignored, because a typo in the optional `expect` would silently drop the miscount guard.

A delete edit takes no `value`; set, replace and insert each require one. `expect` is any JSON value and is matched as a subset of the actual value, so nothing about its shape is checked here. `block` is boolean and belongs only to a delete.
`edits` must not be empty: an update that changes nothing is a mistake, not a no-op, and the at-least-one-change group counts mere presence.
notes: `token` is REQUIRED WITH `body` OR `edits` AND IGNORED WITHOUT THEM. A rename or a move is attribute-addressed and cannot clobber a concurrent change; a body write is the only update that can silently discard someone else's work.
A `newName` ALREADY IN USE IS REFUSED as `script_exists`, on the same case-insensitive rule create:script applies -- FileMaker would accept the collision silently, so this CLI does not.

THE TOKEN IS OPAQUE and spans more than the script: a projection resolves field, occurrence, layout, script, value-list and custom-function names, so a rename in ANY of those makes it stale. A token covering only the script would report "unchanged" after a field rename and the caller's patch would apply against text that no longer exists.
`body` and `edits` are mutually exclusive because an edit's path resolves against the body AS READ, never against a partially edited one, so a line carrying both has no single meaning.

EVERY EDIT PATH RESOLVES AGAINST THE BODY AS READ and all edits apply in one pass, the way `diff` does it -- so edit 2 cannot shift edit 3's index. Two inserts at the same path apply in the order listed.

AN EDIT PATH'S FIRST TOKEN IS A STEP INDEX OR A STEP HANDLE, and the handle is worth preferring. `read:script` reports a `uuid` on every step, and `"/A1B2C3D4-.../value"` addresses that step wherever it now sits -- so composing an edit needs no counting, and a miscount, which would otherwise address a different real step and succeed, becomes impossible. A handle survives the edits you make through it, including one that rewrites the step, so a sequence of edits to the same step can all name it the same way. It can still go stale if someone changes that step's TYPE in FileMaker, which mints a new one; an unresolvable handle is `edit_path_not_found` with the near misses from the script. Indexes keep working, and appending still needs one: there is no handle for a step that does not exist yet.

`edits` WRITES ONLY THE STEPS IT NAMES, and that is the reason to prefer it over `body` for a change to an existing script. A step no edit addresses is left alone rather than re-created from its description -- so a step written by a newer FileMaker keeps working, and a script containing one is still editable elsewhere. `body` replaces every step in the script.

THE ONE EXCEPTION is the jump targets FileMaker itself computes. Inserting or deleting a step re-computes every one of them, even though no edit named the steps that hold them, because the alternative is a script that jumps to the wrong line. It is more than the block steps: `If`, `Else If` and `Else` each store the next branch in their own chain (and `Else If` also stores its matching `End If`), `Loop` and `End Loop` store each other, `Open Transaction` and `Commit Transaction` both store the commit's line, and `Exit Loop If`, `Go to Record/Request/Page` and `Go to Portal Row` each store the `End Loop` they escape to -- or -1 when no `Loop` encloses them. None of those targets is part of a step's readable options, so none of them appears in a body, and nothing a caller writes can set them.

`expect` is optional but strongly recommended on every edit: the token covers someone ELSE changing the file, and nothing underneath can detect the caller miscounting its own index. A disagreement is `edit_expect_mismatch`, reported with the value actually found.

The whole edit set is ATOMIC, and block balance is re-checked after applying: deleting an `If` without its `End If` is `script_unbalanced_block` with nothing written, because FileMaker would otherwise store the corrupt result without objecting.

`"block": true` ON A DELETE REMOVES THE WHOLE BLOCK -- the `If`, its `End If`, every branch and nested block between them -- so a block comes out in one edit that names one step. Without it, removing an `If` meant counting openers and closers to find the matching closer and then emitting a delete per step, and a miscount there addresses real steps and succeeds. It goes on the step that OPENS the block, which is what `block.start` in the body you read gives you from any step in that block; asking for it on an `End If`, an `Else`, a disabled block step or a step with no block role at all is `edit_op_invalid` naming which of those it was. An `opaque` step inside the range loses its stored options, on the same footing as deleting one on its own: the steps were asked for.

Every calc write is read back and compared. FileMaker auto-quotes an unresolvable calculation silently and reports success, so `Contacts::Emial` becomes the STRING "Contacts::Emial" with no error; a mismatch is `calc_autoquoted`.

AN `opaque` STEP CAN BE DELETED, AND ITS `disabled` CAN BE SET. Anything else is `step_not_editable`: that object is not a complete description of the step, so an edit asking for its `flags`, its `stepID`, its `breakpoint` or a whole-step `replace` cannot be honored. Its stored options are carried through the two edits that ARE allowed, and through any edit to another step.

WHAT A PASSING DRY RUN DOES NOT PROVE. Step identity, block balance, calculation syntax, every name that has to resolve, and every choice with a named list of values are all checked. What is NOT checked is whether the step MAKES SENSE: no step option is required, none excludes another, and a plain number whose meaning FileMaker does not name is written as given. A step with no target, no value, or two contradictory targets is accepted and stored. So a dry run that passes says the body is well formed, not that it is the script intended -- only reading it back says that. See `fm-cli help script steps forms`.

A projected step carries two structural keys beside its named options. `flags` is the integer holding every on/off option of that step, and `slots` holds every value the step stores that has no name of its own, keyed by kind and then by slot number. Both are accepted on a write: send back what a read gave you, or omit `flags` and let the values written imply their own bits.
`result` is `{name,id}` with the script's id unchanged.
seeAlso: `fm-cli help forms` — what JSON a key's type, its requiredness and a filter's tag each take

nodes.title: tableOccurrence
nodes.summary: The nodes of FileMaker's relationships graph -- named references to a base table
notes: An occurrence is NOT its base table: the two are separate catalog members with separate ids, and one base table may have any number of occurrences. Layouts, relations, value lists and calculations all address the OCCURRENCE, which is why the distinction is worth the second catalog.

A node's BASE TABLE can be changed after the fact -- `table` or `dataSource` on an update -- and doing so moves nothing else. Everything that addressed the occurrence still addresses it, by (occurrence, field) pair, so those field ids come to resolve against the new base table's fields. FileMaker's own Specify Table dialog behaves identically; see the note on update:tableOccurrence before using it.
Occurrences are FILE-GLOBAL and are not scoped by their base table, so a name is unique across the whole graph rather than per table.

A node carries PRESENTATION as well as identity -- where its box sits on the graph, what colour it is, and how much of its field list is drawn. None of it changes what the file means, all of it is stored in the file, and it is what a person sees on opening the graph. `create` and `update` take it as `graph`; a describe reports it, and so does a `detail` listing, which is how a whole graph's layout is read in one call.

refusedInputs.reason: an occurrence of a table in another file is created with 'table' qualified by the data source's name -- 'table':'Inventory::Widgets' -- or with 'dataSource' and 'tableId' when that file cannot be opened from here. 'externalDataSource' is the name of the CATALOG that registers a file reference -- create:externalDataSource -- not of the key on this op.

semanticChecks: 'graph.bounds' width and height must be greater than zero: a node zero points wide is invisible on the graph, which is the worst way to find that out.

'graph.color' is six hex digits with an optional leading '#' -- "#4A90D9". It must be fully OPAQUE: eight digits are accepted only when the last pair is 'FF', because a node's colour on the graph is an opaque swatch and an alpha could not be reported back by a describe. Three-digit shorthand is not accepted.
notes: `create:table` ALREADY MINTS a same-named occurrence, so creating a table and then an occurrence of the same name is `tableOccurrence_exists` -- which is otherwise baffling, since nothing in the op grammar hints that the first op made two things.

EXACTLY ONE of `table` and `dataSource` is given. `table` names a base table in THIS file, or one in another file qualified with the data source's name -- `"table":"Inventory::Widgets"`, which is resolved by reading that file's table catalog. `dataSource` names a FileMaker file reference and rides with `tableId`. An op with neither is `missing_field` and one with both is refused.

THE QUALIFIED FORM NEEDS THE OTHER FILE TO BE OPENABLE, and openable means what it means in FileMaker Pro: the path resolves, the account and password this file opened with also exist in that file, and its File Access privileges permit this file to open it. A hosted reference is opened on the same terms as a local one. When it cannot be opened the answer is `tableOccurrence_unavailable`, naming which of those it was, and `dataSource` plus `tableId` is the way through: an id needs nothing opened.

`tableId` IS NOT CHECKED. Ids are per FILE, and this form is precisely the one for a file that cannot be opened, so there is nothing to check it against. Read it from the other file first -- `read:table` run against it reports the id -- because a wrong id creates an occurrence that reads back `resolved:false` and dangles when FileMaker opens the graph. The qualified `table` form does not have this hazard, which is the reason to prefer it. Every file numbers tables from 129, so an id below that is refused as `invalid_field`: it is almost certainly a field id.
ONLY A FILEMAKER data source can back an occurrence. An ODBC or Magnolia reference is `unsupported_operation` -- those reach their tables through a shadow table whose id space this op cannot address.

A `table` value containing "::" whose left half is NOT a registered data source is refused, and so is a `table` naming a data source with no table half at all. Both point at the spellings that work rather than reporting a missing capability. `create:externalDataSource` registers a reference that is not registered yet.

`graph` places and colours the new node. Leaving it out puts the node where FileMaker would -- which for a node created outside the graph editor is the origin, so a caller building a readable graph should give one.

`position` IS THE GRAPH'S Z-ORDER as well as the occurrence order: 0 is the front, and it decides which of two overlapping nodes is drawn on top. Absent APPENDS, which puts the new node at the BACK -- FileMaker's own graph editor brings a node it creates to the front instead, so ask for `"position":0` to match it. `result` reports where the node landed.

`tags` IS AN OPEN NAMESPACE: a tag is any word, so no list of accepted values exists and none is checked. Send each tag WITHOUT the leading `#` the file stores it behind. It is not echoed on `result` -- read the occurrence back for it.

`result` is `{name,id,table,position}`, the ids being FileMaker's -- the "names in, IDs out" convention. The occurrence's id is NOT its base table's, and `graph` is not echoed: read the occurrence back for it. For an EXTERNAL occurrence `table` comes back the way a read reports one, which since the referenced files are opened means `resolved:true` with the base table's real `name` when that file could be read, and `resolved:false` with `dataSource` named and no `name` when it could not.

A `name` that is legal but cannot be used unquoted in a calculation (a leading digit, a leading or trailing space, or certain punctuation) is still created as given -- `result` then also carries a `warnings` array saying so. `warnings` is absent, not `[]`, on a clean name.
seeAlso: `fm-cli help forms` — what JSON a key's type, its requiredness and a filter's tag each take

notes: IT DOES NOT CASCADE, and that differs from `delete:table` ON PURPOSE. Deleting a table is a declaration that the whole subtree goes; deleting one occurrence out of a graph is a surgical edit, and silently taking relations the caller never named with it would be a destructive surprise.

So an occurrence a relation still anchors is refused with `in_use` naming the actionable thing -- drop the relation first. Measured 2026-07-27: the occurrence, the relation and the graph edge all survive intact, which makes it a refusal rather than a failure.

nodes.title: read:tableOccurrence
nodes.summary: Lists every table occurrence, or describes one with its neighbours
semanticChecks: 'graph.color' is six hex digits with an optional leading '#' -- "#4A90D9". It must be fully OPAQUE: eight digits are accepted only when the last pair is 'FF', because a node's colour on the graph is an opaque swatch and an alpha could not be reported back by a describe. Three-digit shorthand is not accepted.
notes: `filter` NARROWS a listing and does nothing else. Every occurrence that comes back is reported in exactly the shape an unfiltered listing gives it, so a filter changes which members appear and never what any one of them says.
`total` is how many occurrences the file has, unfiltered; `returned` counts the ones that came back. A filtered listing therefore reports both what matched and what it was matched against.
Matching ignores case, and `name` takes the wildcards `*` (any run of characters) and `?` (exactly one). There is no escape, so a literal `*` or `?` in an occurrence's name cannot be matched.
EVERY attribute given must match, so naming two of them narrows the listing further rather than widening it.

A filter matching nothing is `ok` with `"items":[]` and `returned` of 0. A filter selects rather than addresses, so filtering on a base table that does not exist is an empty answer and not an error -- which also means a misspelled VALUE looks exactly like an empty graph.

`table` matches on the base table's name in THIS file. An occurrence whose base table lives in another file has no name here to compare, so it never appears in a `table`-filtered listing whatever the table is called where it lives.

A describe reports `source` -- all four of `local`, `external`, `foreign` and `odbc`, always present rather than omitted-when-false, so a consumer never has to guess whether absence means false or means unknown. They are four independent predicates and not one enum: an ODBC table is also foreign and also external.

`related` is ONE HOP ONLY -- the occurrences a relation joins this one to directly -- and it is a list of refs rather than of names so a caller can address them without a second lookup. It is `[]` for an unrelated occurrence, never absent.
`hasCascade` says whether any relation cascades deletes FROM this occurrence. It is derived from the relations, not stored on the occurrence.

`position` is reported by EVERY read -- a plain listing, a `detail` listing and a describe -- and it is the graph's Z-ORDER as well as the occurrence order, 0 being the front. It is the only thing here that says which of two overlapping nodes is drawn on top. A listing is still ordered by id, so sort on `position` for the stacking. It is absent for an occurrence the file's order list has no entry for, which is not the same as being at the front.

`tags` is the occurrence's own tag list, one entry per tag, WITHOUT the `#` the file stores each behind, and `[]` for an occurrence with none. FileMaker's own clipboard serializer carries a tag list on every occurrence it copies, so this is where one that arrived that way shows up. An OPEN NAMESPACE -- any word can be a tag -- so no list of the values to expect exists.

`graph` reports the node's appearance -- `bounds`, `color`, `view`, `fieldListHeight` and `drawnBounds` -- always present and complete, so a caller can read a box, change one member and write the whole thing back. A describe always reports it; a listing reports it per item under `detail`, and omits the key entirely without it.

`bounds` IS THE EXPANDED BOX, whatever the `view` is. FileMaker keeps the full height there on purpose -- it is the height it restores when the node is expanded again -- so a collapsed node reports a tall `bounds` and is drawn one line high. `drawnBounds` is where it is ACTUALLY drawn: the same left, top and width, and the height the graph gives it. Use `bounds` to write a box back and `drawnBounds` to reason about the room a node takes up or about what collapsing one would free. `drawnBounds` equals `bounds` for a `full` node, and is omitted in the one case it cannot be derived -- an occurrence of a table in ANOTHER file drawn in the `related` view, whose related-field rows are counted in that file and not this one.

`detail` ON A LISTING is how the whole graph is read in ONE call rather than one per node: every item carries its box, its source, its neighbours and its cascade flag. It is opt-in only so that a caller diffing listings sees no change until it asks -- an occurrence's whole body is accessors on a member the listing already walks, with nothing to Open() and no second catalog, so there is no cost gate here.

THE EDGES ARE NOT HERE. `read:relation` lists them, once each and with their predicates, options and effects; a listing's items carry each node's own box and nothing about its neighbours. Sending both ops on one NDJSON invocation reads the whole graph -- nodes, boxes and edges -- and reports every edge once, which embedding `related` per item could not do.

`table.resolved` IS ABOUT REACHABILITY, not about which file the table is in. nodes.summary: Renames a table occurrence, retags it, repoints it at another base table, or changes how it is drawn on the graph

keys.summary: the occurrence to change -- the address, not itself a change

semanticChecks: 'graph.bounds' width and height must be greater than zero: a node zero points wide is invisible on the graph, which is the worst way to find that out.

'graph.color' is six hex digits with an optional leading '#' -- "#4A90D9". It must be fully OPAQUE: eight digits are accepted only when the last pair is 'FF', because a node's colour on the graph is an opaque swatch and an alpha could not be reported back by a describe. Three-digit shorthand is not accepted.

a `tags` entry containing a space or a `#` is refused: the file stores the whole list as one string of space-separated `#tag` tokens, so either character inside a tag would split it in two, and that format has no escape.
notes: AT LEAST ONE of `newName`, `table`/`dataSource`, `graph`, `tags` and `position` is required; any one alone is enough and all of them together are one op. An update naming none is `missing_field`.

`table` and `dataSource` REPOINT the occurrence at a different base table, and they are spelled and resolved exactly as they are on a create: `table` names one in this file or one in another qualified with the data source's name, `dataSource` rides with `tableId` for a file that cannot be opened, and at most one of the two is given. Pointing an EXTERNAL occurrence at a local `table` makes it local again.

A REPOINT DOES NOT MOVE WHAT REFERENCED THE OCCURRENCE, and this is the one consequence to understand before using it. Every stored reference into an occurrence -- relation predicates, layout objects, value lists, calculations -- is an (occurrence, field) pair, so after a repoint those field ids resolve against the NEW base table's fields. Field ids are per table and every table numbers its own from the same base, so a reference does not reliably break: it can silently come to mean a different field. This is FileMaker's own behaviour -- it is what the Specify Table dialog on a graph node does -- and neither FileMaker nor this op remaps or invalidates anything. Check what addressed the occurrence before repointing it.

The occurrence's id and its NAME are unchanged by a repoint -- an occurrence's name is its own, not its base table's. `result` is `{name,id,table,position}`, so the base table it came to point at is reported back; `graph` is not echoed -- read the occurrence back for that.

`position` RESTACKS THE NODE ON THE GRAPH as well as moving it in the occurrence order: 0 is the front. `result` reports where it ended up rather than what was asked for, so a shift the engine declined does not read as a success. Note that this order is what FileMaker's own graph rewrites when a person CLICKS a node -- so a position read out of a file someone has been working in reflects their last click, not a schema decision.

`graph`'s members MERGE: an absent one leaves the stored value alone, so recolouring a node does not move it. `bounds` is the exception and is all-or-nothing -- all four of `left`, `top`, `width` and `height` are required together, because a partial box is ambiguous.
A `newName` naming a DIFFERENT occurrence, compared case-insensitively, is `tableOccurrence_exists`.

Renaming the BASE TABLE also renames the occurrences whose names still TRACK it -- `update:table` does that automatically, which is FileMaker's own UI behaviour. So an occurrence's name can change without any op in this catalog running, and a caller holding a name from an earlier listing may find it stale.
A `newName` that is legal but cannot be used unquoted in a calculation is still applied as given, with a `warnings` array on `result` saying so -- same as create:tableOccurrence.

`tags` REPLACES the whole tag list; `[]` clears it. It is an OPEN NAMESPACE -- a tag is any word -- so no list of accepted values exists and none is checked. Send each tag WITHOUT the leading `#` the file stores it behind.

nodes.title: theme
nodes.summary: The style sets layouts wear, each a stylesheet plus the metadata that stylesheet cannot hold
notes: A THEME IS ADDRESSED THREE WAYS: by its internal name ("com.filemaker.theme.apex_blue"), by its display name ("Apex Blue") or by its id. Display names are NOT unique -- a real file can hold two themes both displaying "Enlightened" -- so an address matching two of them is refused as `ambiguous`, naming the colliding ids, rather than resolved to whichever was reached first. The id is the only spelling that always resolves.

A THEME IS NOT A LAYOUT PROPERTY THIS CATALOG DUPLICATES. Which theme a layout wears is set on the layout (`theme` on `create:layout` and `update:layout`); this catalog is the themes themselves -- what they contain and which of them exist.

`css` IS NOT THE CSS A BROWSER READS. There is no cascade, the selector and property vocabularies are closed and small, and several spellings that look standard mean something else or nothing at all. Read `fm-cli help theme-css` before writing any -- it is the whole account, and writing from general CSS knowledge instead produces a stylesheet that reports success and drops most of what it said.

THE COLOUR PALETTE AND THE NAMED STYLES' DISPLAY NAMES ARE NOT IN THE CSS. They are separate theme metadata, which is why `colorPalette` and `namedStyleNames` are separate keys: a caller who round-tripped only the stylesheet would keep every style and lose both.

THE THREE PAYLOADS ARE SEPARATE AND EACH REPLACES ITSELF WHOLE. `css` is the styles, `colorPalette` is what a colour picker offers, `namedStyleNames` is what the styles palette shows for each style. None of them merges, and none of them touches the other two.

EVERY THEME THIS CATALOG CAN MAKE IS DERIVED; there is no create-from-nothing. A theme built from an empty style set would render as the style system's bare fallbacks, which is the state this CLI's layout writes already refuse to leave a layout in.

A LAYOUT IS NEVER LEFT THEMELESS. That single rule is why `delete:theme` refuses a theme in use, why there is no create-from-nothing, and why an empty `css` is refused -- each of those is the same guarantee seen from a different verb.

ONE THEME IS THE FILE'S DEFAULT: what a `create:layout` naming no theme gets, and what a `create:theme` naming no `base` derives from. `read:theme` reports it as `isDefault`, and `update:theme` with `"default":true` moves it -- there is no separate verb, because this is the same "set as default" one action everywhere else.

`"default":false` IS REFUSED (`invalid_field`). A file always has a default theme, so there is no state "not the default" to move a theme into and no way to say which other theme should take it. To change which theme is the default, send `"default":true` on the one that should become it; the theme that held it stops being the default as a consequence.
seeAlso: `fm-cli help theme-css` — how theme CSS differs from the CSS a browser reads
`fm-cli help layout` — where a layout's theme is chosen

nodes.title: create:theme
nodes.summary: Derives a new custom theme from an existing one, or from a FileMaker built-in

keys.summary: the name a person reads, unique among the file's themes; the internal id is minted, not chosen
the theme to derive from -- one of the file's own, or a FileMaker Pro built-in to install
the theme's complete stylesheet, replacing the styles inherited from 'base'

notes: EVERY THEME THIS CATALOG CAN MAKE IS DERIVED; there is no create-from-nothing. A theme built from an empty style set would render as the style system's bare fallbacks, which is the state this CLI's layout writes already refuse to leave a layout in.

`base` ABSENT DERIVES FROM THE THEME MOST OF THE FILE'S LAYOUTS ALREADY WEAR -- the same theme a `create:layout` that names none would get. So the shortest useful create is a `displayName` and nothing else, and what it copies is whatever the file already looks like.

THAT IS NOT NECESSARILY THE THEME `read:theme` MARKS `isDefault`. The recorded default is what FileMaker Pro's own theme picker starts on; what an omitted `base` copies is what the file actually wears, which is the more useful answer for a derivation and the one that still works in a file whose default was never recorded. Name `base` explicitly whenever it matters which of the two you get.

`base` IS THE ONE ADDRESS THAT REACHES OUTSIDE THE FILE. A name matching none of the file's themes but matching one of FileMaker Pro's built-ins installs that built-in first and derives from it -- so deriving from "Apex Blue" works in a file that has never had Apex Blue. A name that is neither is `theme_not_found`.
A LISTING WILL NOT TELL YOU WHAT `base` ACCEPTS. `read:theme` reports the themes the file HAS; the built-ins it has never installed are not themes of this file yet, only names this key would take.

A CALLER NEVER CHOOSES A THEME'S ID. The new theme is minted `com.filemaker.theme.custom.<uuid>`, grouped as "custom", and given the original's name and version as lineage. `displayName` is the only name the request carries; the internal one comes back on the result.
`displayName` MUST BE UNIQUE among the file's display names. A collision is `theme_exists` rather than a silent uniquification, so two themes can never become mutually unaddressable by name.

`css` IS NOT THE CSS A BROWSER READS. There is no cascade, the selector and property vocabularies are closed and small, and several spellings that look standard mean something else or nothing at all. Read `fm-cli help theme-css` before writing any -- it is the whole account, and writing from general CSS knowledge instead produces a stylesheet that reports success and drops most of what it said.

`css` REPLACES the styles inherited from `base` rather than adding to them. Omitted, the new theme is the base's styles exactly -- which is what makes this op a starting point rather than a blank page.

A stylesheet is checked BEFORE it is written, and a write carrying one that will not parse is refused whole (`invalid_css`) with nothing changed. This is not belt and braces: FileMaker's own parser drops an unknown property or an unreadable value in SILENCE, so there would be nothing to report afterwards. Findings that are merely suspect -- a `px` length coerced to `pt`, say -- arrive on `warnings` and the stylesheet is written.

`group`, `colorPalette` and `namedStyleNames` are not create keys. A new theme is grouped as "custom" and carries the base's metadata; changing any of the three is an `update:theme` on the theme this op returns.
`result` is the new theme's `{id, name, displayName, group}`, plus `warnings` when the stylesheet raised any -- the internal `name` being the half the caller could not have predicted.
seeAlso: `fm-cli help theme-css` — the syntax `css` is written in, which is not W3C CSS

nodes.title: delete:theme
nodes.summary: Removes a theme, moving any layouts wearing it onto a replacement first

keys.summary: the theme to delete, by its display name or its internal name
the theme to delete, by the id a read reports
the theme the layouts wearing this one move to, which is what makes the delete possible

notes: A THEME IS ADDRESSED THREE WAYS: by its internal name ("com.filemaker.theme.apex_blue"), by its display name ("Apex Blue") or by its id. Display names are NOT unique -- a real file can hold two themes both displaying "Enlightened" -- so an address matching two of them is refused as `ambiguous`, naming the colliding ids, rather than resolved to whichever was reached first. The id is the only spelling that always resolves.

A THEME ANY LAYOUT WEARS IS REFUSED (`in_use`), and the refusal NAMES those layouts. FileMaker's own delete does not check, and would leave every one of them carrying a key that resolves to nothing -- which renders as the style system's bare fallbacks. This CLI guarantees a layout is never themeless, and that guarantee is what this refusal is.

`reassignTo` IS WHAT MAKES THE DELETE POSSIBLE. It names the theme those layouts move to, and they are repointed FIRST: a failure anywhere leaves the theme and its layouts exactly as they were, rather than half-migrated.

`reassignTo` MUST NAME A DIFFERENT THEME. Naming the one being deleted is `invalid_field` -- the layouts would have nowhere to go -- and naming a theme the file does not have is `theme_not_found`, on the same three spellings the address takes.

`reassignTo` ON A THEME NOTHING WEARS IS ACCEPTED AND MOVES NOTHING. Whether the delete needed it is a fact about the file rather than about the request, so a caller who supplies it defensively is not refused for being right.

DELETING THE FILE'S DEFAULT THEME IS ALLOWED, and the default always lands on a theme that still exists. With a `reassignTo` it follows the layouts to that theme; without one it goes to a remaining theme and a warning NAMES which, so the choice is never silent. Only deleting a file's last theme leaves it with no default, and the next theme added takes the role.

ONE EXCEPTION: the compatibility theme is never chosen as the default, so reassigning onto it moves the layouts while the default goes to a remaining theme instead (`update:theme` refuses it outright, and this is the same rule at the other door). The delete still succeeds and the warning says which theme took the role.
A DELETE THAT MOVED LAYOUTS SAYS SO in `warnings`, with the count and the theme they moved to -- so a caller can see the second half of what their one op did.
`result` echoes the removed theme's `{id, name, displayName, group}`, captured before the deletion, so a caller can log what went away.
seeAlso: `fm-cli help forms` — what JSON a key's type, its requiredness and a filter's tag each take

nodes.title: duplicate:theme
nodes.summary: Copies a theme under a new display name; the copy is always custom

keys.summary: the theme to copy, by its display name or its internal name
the theme to copy, by the id a read reports
the name a person reads for the copy, unique among the file's themes

notes: A THEME IS ADDRESSED THREE WAYS: by its internal name ("com.filemaker.theme.apex_blue"), by its display name ("Apex Blue") or by its id. Display names are NOT unique -- a real file can hold two themes both displaying "Enlightened" -- so an address matching two of them is refused as `ambiguous`, naming the colliding ids, rather than resolved to whichever was reached first. The id is the only spelling that always resolves.

THE ADDRESS MUST NAME A THEME THE FILE ALREADY HAS, unlike `create:theme`'s `base`. Duplicating a built-in the file has never installed would install it and immediately copy it, which is `create:theme` wearing the wrong verb -- so it is `theme_not_found` here.

THE COPY IS ALWAYS CUSTOM, whatever was copied. A copy keeping the original's internal id would put two members in the catalog under one name, which neither this CLI nor FileMaker Pro could then address.

A CALLER NEVER CHOOSES A THEME'S ID. The new theme is minted `com.filemaker.theme.custom.<uuid>`, grouped as "custom", and given the original's name and version as lineage. `displayName` is the only name the request carries; the internal one comes back on the result.

THE COPY CARRIES THE ORIGINAL'S STYLESHEET, PALETTE AND STYLE NAMES. There is no `css` key here on purpose: changing the styles is an `update:theme` on the copy, which is also the one place the stylesheet gets checked.
NO LAYOUT MOVES. A duplicate adds a theme and repoints nothing, so the original keeps every layout it had and the copy starts with none.
`result` is the COPY's `{id, name, displayName, group}`, never the original's -- the copy is the thing the caller has no other way to name.

nodes.title: read:theme
nodes.summary: Lists the file's themes, or describes one with its whole stylesheet
notes: A THEME IS ADDRESSED THREE WAYS: by its internal name ("com.filemaker.theme.apex_blue"), by its display name ("Apex Blue") or by its id. Display names are NOT unique -- a real file can hold two themes both displaying "Enlightened" -- so an address matching two of them is refused as `ambiguous`, naming the colliding ids, rather than resolved to whichever was reached first. The id is the only spelling that always resolves.

The three spellings are tried in one fixed order: internal name, then id, then display name -- and the first two are matched EXACTLY while the display name is matched case-insensitively. Two consequences worth knowing before they surprise you: a theme whose display name is the decimal spelling of some other theme's id cannot be reached by that name, and an internal name in the wrong case is not found at all.

A LISTING REPORTS ONLY THE THEMES THE FILE HAS. FileMaker's built-ins that this file has never installed are not listed -- they are not themes of this file, only names `create:theme`'s `base` would accept. An empty catalog is `{"items":[]}` with `total` and `returned` of 0, never an error.

DEPRECATED THEMES ARE REPORTED, NOT HIDDEN. FileMaker no longer offers 36 of its built-ins in its own theme picker, but a file can still be wearing one; omitting it would make that theme unaddressable. `isDeprecated` says which, and every verb here works on one.
`isCustom` IS TOLD BY THE ID, not by the group. The two can disagree -- a theme's group is an editable label while its id's bundle prefix is not -- and the id is what the engine itself tests.

ONE THEME IS THE FILE'S DEFAULT: what a `create:layout` naming no theme gets, and what a `create:theme` naming no `base` derives from. `read:theme` reports it as `isDefault`, and `update:theme` with `"default":true` moves it -- there is no separate verb, because this is the same "set as default" one action everywhere else.

EXACTLY ONE THEME IS THE DEFAULT, always -- so a listing always has one `isDefault` true, and `{"filter":{"isDefault":true}}` always answers with one theme. A file gets its default when it gets its first theme, so this holds for a file made by this tool as well as one FileMaker Pro made.

`isDefault` IS TRUE FOR AT MOST ONE THEME, so `{"filter":{"isDefault":true}}` is how to ask which theme that is without reading the whole catalog -- and it comes back as an ordinary one-item listing, not as a describe.

`layoutsUsing` COUNTS LAYOUTS, and 0 is the answer that matters: it is exactly the set `delete:theme` will remove without a `reassignTo`. A describe additionally names them, under `layouts`, in the file's display order.

`detail` REPORTS EACH LISTED THEME EXACTLY AS A DESCRIBE OF IT WOULD, which means EVERY THEME'S WHOLE STYLESHEET IN ONE ANSWER. A theme's CSS runs to tens of thousands of characters and carries its images inline, so a detailed listing of a file with a dozen themes is megabytes. Ask for it when you want them all; describe one when you want one.

`filter` NARROWS a listing and does nothing else. Every theme that comes back is reported in exactly the shape an unfiltered listing gives it, so a filter changes which themes appear and never what any one of them says. Every attribute given must match, so naming two narrows further rather than widening.

`total` is how many themes the file has, unfiltered; `returned` counts the ones that came back. A filter matching nothing is `ok` with `"items":[]`, never `not_found` -- so a misspelled pattern looks exactly like a file with no such theme.

A THEME IN NO FAMILY CARRIES NO `group` AT ALL, and absent is no-match for every filter kind, so such a theme never appears in a `group`-filtered listing -- including one asking for the family it would most likely have had.

A describe's `css` can be fed straight back into an update. Images ride along INSIDE the text as `-fm-image-data(name;data:image/png;base64,...)` rather than as references to files, so a round trip through this CLI keeps them.

THE COLOUR PALETTE AND THE NAMED STYLES' DISPLAY NAMES ARE NOT IN THE CSS. They are separate theme metadata, which is why `colorPalette` and `namedStyleNames` are separate keys: a caller who round-tripped only the stylesheet would keep every style and lose both.

`css` IS THE THEME'S OWN STYLESHEET, not one assembled from what it inherited. A custom theme records its lineage but reports the complete styles it actually has, so what a describe returns is what the theme is.
A describe returns the same object a detailed listing's item carries, plus `"kind":"theme"`, so an item taken straight out of a list carries exactly the keys a describe of it will.
A read never opens the theme catalog for writing, so it cannot dirty the file.
seeAlso: `fm-cli help theme-css` — how to read the `css` this reports, and write it back

nodes.summary: Renames a theme, regroups it, replaces its stylesheet or metadata, or makes it the default

keys.summary: the theme to update, by its display name or its internal name -- not itself a change
the theme to update, by the id a read reports
the new name a person reads; the internal id is left alone
the family FileMaker Pro's theme picker groups it under; "" leaves it in none

semanticChecks: `colorPalette` and `namedStyleNames` take an object whose every VALUE is a string. The map is free-form -- its keys are the theme's own -- so no declaration can say this, and a non-string value is refused with 'invalid_field' naming the entry rather than coerced.

An empty `colorPalette` or `namedStyleNames` object DOES count as a change: `{}` empties that category, which is a request, unlike an empty options object elsewhere in this CLI that names no setting at all.
'default': false is refused (invalid_field) -- a file always has a default theme, so send 'default': true on the theme that should become it instead.
'default': true is refused (invalid_field) for the compatibility theme, which FileMaker Pro does not offer as a default either.
notes: A THEME IS ADDRESSED THREE WAYS: by its internal name ("com.filemaker.theme.apex_blue"), by its display name ("Apex Blue") or by its id. Display names are NOT unique -- a real file can hold two themes both displaying "Enlightened" -- so an address matching two of them is refused as `ambiguous`, naming the colliding ids, rather than resolved to whichever was reached first. The id is the only spelling that always resolves.

EACH KEY IS A COMPLETE REPLACEMENT OF ITS OWN CATEGORY and leaves every other alone. Sending `colorPalette` replaces the whole palette and touches no style; sending `css` replaces every style and touches no metadata.

`css` IS NOT THE CSS A BROWSER READS. There is no cascade, the selector and property vocabularies are closed and small, and several spellings that look standard mean something else or nothing at all. Read `fm-cli help theme-css` before writing any -- it is the whole account, and writing from general CSS knowledge instead produces a stylesheet that reports success and drops most of what it said.
`css` is a COMPLETE REPLACEMENT of the theme's styles, never a merge. There is no way to amend one declaration: read the theme's stylesheet, edit the text, and send the whole thing back.

A stylesheet is checked BEFORE it is written, and a write carrying one that will not parse is refused whole (`invalid_css`) with nothing changed. This is not belt and braces: FileMaker's own parser drops an unknown property or an unreadable value in SILENCE, so there would be nothing to report afterwards. Findings that are merely suspect -- a `px` length coerced to `pt`, say -- arrive on `warnings` and the stylesheet is written.

A describe's `css` can be fed straight back into an update. Images ride along INSIDE the text as `-fm-image-data(name;data:image/png;base64,...)` rather than as references to files, so a round trip through this CLI keeps them.

THE COLOUR PALETTE AND THE NAMED STYLES' DISPLAY NAMES ARE NOT IN THE CSS. They are separate theme metadata, which is why `colorPalette` and `namedStyleNames` are separate keys: a caller who round-tripped only the stylesheet would keep every style and lose both.

REPLACING THE STYLESHEET DOES NOT UPDATE THE NAMED STYLES' DISPLAY NAMES, and a `css` sent without a `namedStyleNames` beside it comes back with a warning saying so: the recorded names are kept as they were, so any that named a style the new stylesheet does not define now names nothing.
`displayName` CHANGES ONLY THE NAME A PERSON READS. The internal id is what layouts and other files store, so it is left exactly as it was -- an update never repoints anything.

A `displayName` that collides with another theme's is refused (`theme_exists`) rather than uniquified, so two themes cannot become mutually unaddressable by name. Renaming a theme to what it already displays as is not a collision.

TWO METADATA CATEGORIES ARE NOT MODELLED HERE -- FileMaker stores more in a theme's metadata blob than this CLI reports -- and an update leaves them intact. The whole blob is read, the named category replaced, and the rest written back untouched.

ONE THEME IS THE FILE'S DEFAULT: what a `create:layout` naming no theme gets, and what a `create:theme` naming no `base` derives from. `read:theme` reports it as `isDefault`, and `update:theme` with `"default":true` moves it -- there is no separate verb, because this is the same "set as default" one action everywhere else.

`"default":false` IS REFUSED (`invalid_field`). A file always has a default theme, so there is no state "not the default" to move a theme into and no way to say which other theme should take it. To change which theme is the default, send `"default":true` on the one that should become it; the theme that held it stops being the default as a consequence.

THE COMPATIBILITY THEME CANNOT BECOME THE DEFAULT (`invalid_field`). It exists to reproduce how layouts looked before themes, and a file defaulting to it would hand every new layout that appearance; FileMaker Pro does not offer it as a default either. Copy it with `duplicate:theme` and make the copy the default if that appearance is what you want.

`default` IS THE ONE KEY HERE THAT CHANGES NOTHING ABOUT THE THEME. It moves which theme the FILE points at, so the theme that was the default before is no longer it while nothing in either theme changes -- which is why `default` may be sent on its own, and why the result reports the theme exactly as the other keys leave it.
`result` is the theme's `{id, name, displayName, group}` as it now stands, plus `warnings` when there were any. It does NOT restate `isDefault`; read the theme back for that.
seeAlso: `fm-cli help theme-css` — the syntax `css` is written in, which is not W3C CSS

nodes.title: theme-css
nodes.summary: how theme CSS differs from W3C CSS: no cascade, a closed selector and property vocabulary, and a few syntaxes that only look standard
notes: There is no cascade. A selector chain is not matched against objects -- its tokens are the ADDRESS of one slot in a flat dictionary, keyed by (object type, component, state), and the parser writes the declaration block straight into that one slot. There is no specificity and no rule that a more specific selector wins, because nothing is ever compared against anything else. Write each selector chain once.

A selector chain written twice is not two rules layered by the cascade -- it is the same address written twice, and the second write silently overwrites the first with no warning. Last write wins by file order.

Selector grammar: `objectType[.class-or-component][:state]`, with a space as the only combinator (descendant). There is no `>`, `+`, `~`, `[attr]`, `:nth-*`, or `:not()`. A comma-separated list of selectors is allowed and applies one declaration block to every address in the list.

The trailing `.class` is read two different ways depending on how many tokens come before it, and nothing warns either way. Two tokens -- `field .text` -- checks the trailing name against the component list below and addresses that sub-part. One token with a class glued directly onto the object type -- `field.myStyle:normal` -- makes the parser insert a synthetic `.self` component and read the glued-on name as a CUSTOM STYLE NAME instead, never checked against components at all. So `field.text:normal { color: red }` reads as though it colors the field's text sub-part, but it actually defines a new custom style named 'text'; the field's own text is untouched. Write the two-token form whenever you mean a sub-part.

States, lowercase and run together with no separator -- 19 in all: normal, hover, pressed, focus, enabled, disabled, checked, indeterminate, focushover, checkedhover, checkedpressed, indeterminatehover, indeterminatepressed, loading, droptarget, checkedfocus, pressedfocus, placeholder, placeholderhover.

`:active` is accepted only as an alias: an unanchored substring replace turns 'active' into 'checked' before the lookup, so `:active` resolves to `:checked` and `:activehover` to `:checkedhover`. This is why shipped themes write `tab_control:active` rather than `tab_control:checked`.

`:inactive` is NOT a valid state, even though FileMaker's own theme inspector shows an 'Inactive' state for the same objects. The same substring replace rewrites the 'active' inside it too, turning 'inactive' into 'inchecked' -- which is not a registered state -- so the whole rule is silently dropped. There is no working spelling for this state in CSS.
State fallback works the way you'd expect from CSS custom properties: a property left unset in any state other than `:normal` falls back to that same style's own `:normal` value.

Components -- the sub-part named after the class token -- are a closed list of 27: self, inner_border, text, icon, baseline, repeat_border, option_item, contents, tab, tab_inner_border, row, row_alt, status_bar, progress_bar, completed, panel, panel_inner_border, scrollbar_top_button, scrollbar_bottom_button, scrollbar_track, scrollbar_thumb, tab_header, unscrollable_contents, dot, dot_container, row_active, button_bar_divider.

Object types number around 80 and most have no web analogue: field, header, body, body_alt, drop_down, tab_panel, dot_control, portal, web_viewer, leading_grand_summary, and the 16 numbered sub-summary parts among them.

Only 8 shorthand properties exist: padding, margin, border-color, border-style, border-width, border-radius, overflow, writing-mode. There is no `border`, `background`, or `font` shorthand -- write the longhands (border-top-width, border-top-color, background-color, background-image, font-family, font-size, font-weight, ...) individually. Reaching for a web shorthand that doesn't exist here is the single most likely mistake.
The default unit is `pt`, not `px`. A `px` value is accepted but coerced to `pt` with a warning. There is also a FileMaker-only `line` unit for sizes relative to a line of text, e.g. `1.2line`.
Gradients use only the legacy syntax: `-webkit-gradient(linear, 25% 0%, 25% 100%, from(rgba(...)), to(rgba(...)), color-stop(0.5, rgba(...)))`. `linear-gradient(...)` is not understood.
No at-rules at all -- no @media, @import, @font-face, @keyframes.

Around 40 FileMaker-only `-fm-*` properties cover what a web font or background can't express, e.g. `-fm-icon` (a name from a closed icon set, such as `down-arrow` -- never a URL), `-fm-icon-color`, `-fm-use-body-current-row-style`, `-fm-tategaki` (CJK vertical text), `-fm-rotation`, `-fm-override-with-classic`.

A named style's display name and the theme's color palette are stored as separate theme metadata, not in this CSS. Editing a selector's declarations never renames the style or changes what a color picker offers.

nodes.title: valueList
nodes.summary: The named value sets a field's validation or a control draws its choices from
notes: Value lists are FILE-GLOBAL: they are not scoped by a table, so no verb takes a `table` key.

There are four kinds: `custom`, `field`, `external` and `calculation`. Each takes a DISJOINT set of attributes, so a key belonging to another kind is refused rather than ignored -- silently dropping `values` from a field-based list would report ok and build something the caller did not ask for. An `external` list points at a value list in a file this one references, named `dataSource::valueList`; the reference is stored by KEY, so renaming the target in that file does not break it.

The sort spec's COLLATION is `sortLanguage`, on create and on update; its multi-level sort ORDER is not modelled at all. The override is one stored language, and which of the two fields it applies to follows from `options.sortBySecondField` rather than being named separately. A list with no `sortLanguage` sorts in the sorting field's own language, which is FileMaker's default and is what a read omits the key for.

refusedInputs.reason: 'shadow' is FileMaker-managed and cannot be set: it marks a value list as belonging to an external data source. It is reported by read:valueList but never accepted as input.

semanticChecks: 'showRelatedOnly' restricts the list to values related to a start table, so it requires 'startTable'; FileMaker checks none of it and simply produces a list it cannot evaluate.
'sortBySecondField' requires 'secondField': there is no second field to sort by.
'showSecondFieldOnly' requires 'secondField': there is no second field to show.
A custom value must not contain a carriage return: FileMaker separates the values of a custom list with CR, so it would be read back as two values.

'secondField' must name a different field than 'field', and the two occurrences must be related (or be the same occurrence) -- both are rules FileMaker's own Manage Value Lists dialog enforces that the engine's setters do not.
A malformed 'calculation' is refused with 'invalid_field' carrying FileMaker's own parse error, and nothing is created.
notes: The `occurrence` of a field spec is a TABLE OCCURRENCE -- the node FileMaker's relationship graph shows -- not a base table. Creating a table mints a same-named occurrence, so for a simple schema the two names coincide, but FileMaker stores the occurrence's key and the distinction is real.

A LINE FEED (0x0A) inside a custom value is fine and round-trips byte-exactly: measured 2026-07-26, FileMaker stores it verbatim and does not treat it as a separator. So does leading/trailing space, and so does non-ASCII text.

`[""]` reads back as `[]`. An empty list and a list holding one empty string both serialize to the same empty blob, so the format cannot distinguish them; a lone empty value is the only custom-list input that does not round-trip. `["","b"]` is fine, because the separator makes the blob non-empty.

A 'calculation' has NO DEFAULT OCCURRENCE, unlike a field's own calculation, so an UNQUALIFIED field name never resolves. Reference a field as 'Occurrence::Field', naming an occurrence and field that ALREADY EXIST in the file -- one created earlier in the same batch is not yet visible to the formula, so create it in an earlier run.

A FORMULA FILEMAKER CANNOT RESOLVE IS REFUSED, including the cases FileMaker itself treats as harmless. A bare unqualified word, or a reference to an occurrence that does not exist, is not a parse error to FileMaker -- it silently stores the whole text as a literal string, so `Name` would come back as `"Name"`. That is refused with 'invalid_field' rather than stored, because it turns a mistyped field reference into a one-value list that reports success. Quote the text yourself if a literal string is what you meant.

SPELLING IS CANONICALIZED, so a read can differ from what was sent: a function name and a field reference are both stored in their canonical case, meaning `list(` comes back as `List(` and `contacts::name` as `Contacts::Name`. Only the spelling changes; whitespace and the formula's meaning are preserved exactly.
`result` is `{name,id}`, the id being FileMaker's -- the "names in, IDs out" convention.

A FIELD MAY BE NAMED BY ITS ID INSTEAD OF BY NAME, and exactly one of the two is given. This is for a field whose occurrence is based in a file this one cannot open -- unreachable, absent, or not authorized -- because a NAME only becomes a key by being looked up in that file's field catalog, and there is nothing to look it up in. An id needs nothing opened. NOTHING VALIDATES AN ID: a wrong one writes a reference to a field that may not exist, exactly as `tableId` on create:tableOccurrence does, so prefer the name whenever the file can be reached. A read reports the id in place of the name ONLY when it could not resolve the name, so a read can always be fed straight back in.
seeAlso: `fm-cli help forms` — what JSON a key's type, its requiredness and a filter's tag each take
